author: David Huu Pham
text:
S5 COMPLETE 2026-08-28. Branch feat/dbos-v1-s5-shutdown, ONE commit 5d01c6f on top of S1 82bf21d (4 files, +640/-43). No push, no PR, no Beads close, no git hooks. Worktree and the pasture host tree are both clean.

SPEC CORRECTION HONOURED: no handle-ownership code change. The runtime owns and closes the shared handle; the two cross-referenced ownership comments (internal/engine/engine.go Shutdown and internal/handlers/controller.go:267) still name each other and the same library function. controller.go was NOT touched (S4 owns it).

(1) TYPED, ACTIONABLE SURFACE. Engine.Shutdown now returns error. Measured what v1.2 carries: dbos.go dbosContext.Shutdown builds a []string of pending components and returns a bare fmt.Errorf("shutdown timed out after %v waiting for: %s"). There is NO structured field and no exported type, so the names exist only in that text. New in internal/engine/engine.go: type ShutdownComponent with the nine names the runtime can report, in the order it waits for them (schedule reconciler, queue runner, workflow scheduler, admin server, workflows, conductor, and the three "system database ..." ones from sysdb SysDB.Shutdown); Meaning() gives one plain sentence per part and reports an unknown name as unrecognised instead of dropping it; *ShutdownIncompleteError{PerComponentTimeout, Pending, Cause} is the typed detail, reachable with errors.As; it is wrapped in a StructuredError with CategoryWorkflow, so the operator gets What/Why/Where/Impact/Fix and the exit code table gives 3. The parse is documented at the single marker constant, and its failure mode is degradation (Pending empty, cause verbatim), never a lost error. The construction-abort path in engine.New now carries the same typed detail.

(2) TESTS (both in internal/engine/engine_test.go, the subject's existing file). Timeout path: real work is held inside its durable step through the PRODUCTION seam Config.OnTransition (the same field the daemon uses for activity recording) - no test-only seam - then Shutdown(1s) is called while that work is in flight. Asserts the error names "workflows", carries PerComponentTimeout, carries *ShutdownIncompleteError, is CategoryWorkflow, maps to exit 3, and that its text carries the part AND its meaning. Clean path: a full 12-phase epoch then Shutdown returns nil. A third test pins the open end of the component list. Every wait is on a condition with a bounded ceiling; no time.Sleep and no fixed-deadline poll anywhere.
  RED EVIDENCE (five mutations, each reverted): Shutdown swallows the runtime error -> "= nil, want an incomplete-shutdown error"; Shutdown always reports a failure -> clean-path test fails; marker string changed -> "Pending = [], want it to name workflows" + missing meaning; category changed to connection -> "exit code = 2, want 3"; Meaning fallback emptied -> unknown-part test fails.

(3) BUDGET SEMANTICS - MEASURED, DOCUMENTED, NOT CONVERTED. The argument is PER-COMPONENT (v1.2 dbos.go: "Each step respects the provided timeout"; the shutdown makes up to seven sequential waits in this engine, nine if an admin server or conductor were configured, which pasture never configures). Measured with a stuck workflow: only the in-flight-work wait expires, elapsed 303ms for a 300ms budget, pending list exactly "workflows" - the pool close and the notification loops return at once. I did NOT convert the argument to a total (dividing by seven would cut a real drain from 10s to 1.4s and cause spurious incomplete stops for work that would have finished). Instead the public parameter now SAYS what it is: Shutdown(perComponentTimeout), plus exported SequentialShutdownWaits = 7 and WorstCaseShutdownDuration(perComponent) for sizing against an external stop deadline. The timeout test asserts elapsed is in [budget, worst case) so a future runtime that starts spending the budget per part fails the gate. constructionAbortShutdownTimeout no longer restates the breakdown; it references the two new symbols (define once).

(4) cmd/pastured. daemonRuntime.Close returns the engine's stop error; run returns it, so the process exits 3 instead of 0 on a stop that cut work off, and the launch-failure path joins the two errors rather than hiding either. main now takes its exit code from the error category (was hard-wired 1) and the package comment carries the exit-code table. Tests: the daemon-level test holds work through newEngineConfig + the transition seam and asserts Close reports the pending part with exit code 3 (RED: Close ignoring the engine error -> "= nil"); a subprocess test asserts the real binary exits 2 for an unusable database path (RED: os.Exit(1) -> "exit code = 1, want 2"); a subprocess test starts a real daemon, waits for its launched log line, sends SIGTERM and asserts exit 0 with a clean-stop line.
  UNPLANNED FIX (in scope, correctness, found by that last test): the daemon registered its signal handler AFTER Launch, so a SIGTERM arriving during startup hit the default action and killed the process outright. It now registers before startup. RED: that test failed with "exited with signal: terminated" until the registration moved.
  COVERAGE LIMIT, recorded in a comment above the tests rather than papered over: the single line in run that returns the stop error is not covered - both outcomes either side of it are, but forcing a real subprocess daemon to hold work past its budget would need a stall seam bought only for the test.

(1) INCOMPLETE TABLE LIST — controller.go. The ownership bullet listed workflow_status, queues, operation_outputs and application_versions but omitted workflow_schedules (dbos@v1.2.0 migrations/sqlite/102_add_workflow_schedules_application_name.sql). Rewritten as an OPEN list: "including workflow_status, queues, workflow_schedules, operation_outputs and application_versions". Open rather than closed on purpose — the five migrations 100-104 each add the column to a different table and a future release can add a sixth, so a closed list would go stale silently.

(2) CHANNEL CLOSES UNDER DURABLE RE-EXECUTION — controller_close_internal_test.go. close(entered) and close(finished) now go through sync.Once, and the cleanup's release of parked goes through a third Once behind a releaseParked helper (replacing a select/default check that was itself racy if the workflow body ever closed it). Comment records WHY: a re-executed durable workflow running the same body would close an already-closed channel and panic the whole test binary, which would surface as an unrelated-looking crash rather than a scheduling event.

(3) FAILED CLOSE IS NOW REFUSED, NOT JUST DOCUMENTED — controller.go. dbosController gains closeOnce sync.Once + closeErr error. Close is now a two-liner that runs the real work once via a new unexported shutdown() method and replays the recorded result on every later call. sync.Once also gives the happens-before edge for closeErr, so concurrent Close calls (deferred plus explicit) are race-free — verified under -race.

  --- FAIL controller_close_internal_test.go:126: second Close took 5.000508234s, at least the full 5s budget: the failed close is being re-attempted
  test duration 10.29s mutated vs 6.31s fixed
That reproduces the reviewer's measured second 5s wait exactly. The new assertions compare the error IDENTITY (retryErr != closeErr), not its text — the mutated run shows why: both messages render identically, so a string comparison would have passed while the retry still cost a second full budget.

text:
S2 IMPLEMENTATION COMPLETE 2026-08-28. Branch feat/dbos-v1-s2-queues, one commit c6a22ce on top of the S1 head 82bf21d. Three files: internal/engine/queue.go, internal/engine/engine.go, internal/engine/subworkflows_test.go (+700/-59). No push, no PR, no close, no git hooks.

DECISION 1 — CONFLICT POLICY: KEEP dbos.QueueConflictAlwaysUpdate. Measured, not assumed. All three policies were run against a live engine: a running engine limited to K=2 and saturated, a peer registering the same queue with K=4, then observing what the FIRST engine does next.
  - AlwaysUpdate: stored limit becomes 4 and the already-running engine goes on to run 4 slices at once.
  - UpdateIfLatestVersion (the runtime default): IDENTICAL result for a same-version peer. This confirms the S1 review's claim by measurement.
  - NeverUpdate: stored limit stays 2 and the running engine never reaches 4.
NeverUpdate was rejected because it makes the queue's settings depend on which process started first, which an operator cannot predict or correct, and it silently discards a deliberate change. The accepted cost of AlwaysUpdate (a starting peer re-configures a running queue) is written on the constant next to the rejected alternative, citing https://github.com/dayvidpham/pasture/issues/104. The old "open question" paragraph is replaced by that decision record.

DECISION 2 — HOT RELOAD: Engine.SetSliceConcurrency(k int) (int, error). It writes the shared queue row, then READS THE ROW BACK and returns the value actually in force. The read-back is production behaviour, not a test aid: write and read are separate round-trips, so a peer can win in between, and that disagreement is reported with both values. Test proves the effect on a RUNNING engine, not just the stored value: saturated at K=2, SetSliceConcurrency(4), then the same engine runs 4 at once. Assertions cover the returned value, Engine.SliceConcurrency(), and an independent dbos.RetrieveQueue read.
  Engine.sliceConcurrency became an atomic.Int64 because an operator can now change it while workflows read it.
  GAP, DELIBERATE AND REPORTED: there is no command-line surface that calls it from a separate process. I asked the team lead three times for a ruling on adding one (a CLI verb in new files cmd/pasture/queue.go + internal/handlers/queue.go writing the row through a DBOS client) because it overlaps S4's client subject, and had no answer by the time gates finished. The engine method is complete and tested; the missing operator surface is named in the method's doc comment with the issue URL. It is small follow-up work: the engine side is done.

DECISION 3 — RECOVERY, QUEUE SIDE: pinned by read-back of the stored queue name. CORRECTION TO THE BRIEF: v1.2 does NOT put every recovered workflow on the reserved internal queue. The recovery statement is queue_name = COALESCE(NULLIF(queue_name,''), '_dbos_internal_queue') (dbos/internal/sysdb/system_database.go:4990). Only work that ran on NO queue lands there.
  - A recovered SLICE keeps pasture-slice-queue, so the concurrency limit and pasture's 100ms cadence still govern it. The test also proves it is dequeued from that queue and completes.
  - A recovered EPOCH workflow, which never ran on a queue, lands on the reserved queue: no concurrency limit, and the runtime's fixed 1s cadence, not pasture's 100ms. So a process restarting with many interrupted epochs resumes them unbounded; the slice work they then dispatch is still bounded by K, which is where the database-writer pressure is. This is documented in the queue.go package comment.
  Queue name is stable to read: dequeue preserves queue_name (the dequeue UPDATE does not touch it), so the assertion is not racy.
  No duplication with S7: this is the queue-side proof only (which queue, and completion via it). S7 still owns recovery semantics broadly.

DECISION 4 — ERROR PROPAGATION BEYOND RegisterQueue: three new paths, all StructuredError with What/Why/Where/Impact/Fix. Non-positive limit -> CategoryValidation. Queue settings row missing (a peer deleted it) -> CategoryStorage with the cause kept. Read-back disagreement -> CategoryStorage naming requested and stored. An engine never built by engine.New reports the missing queue instead of panicking.

FINDING: the runtime accepts a worker concurrency of 0 without complaint, which would stop the queue from running any work. The guard is therefore load-bearing, not decorative.

RED EVIDENCE (each mutation applied alone, then reverted):
  1. policy -> NeverUpdate: "stored SliceQueue after the peer registered().GetWorkerConcurrency() = 2, want 4" and "condition not met within 30s" (31.2s).
  2. remove the SetWorkerConcurrency write: "SetSliceConcurrency(4): storage error: Asked for a limit of 4 ... but the stored settings now say 2." This is simultaneously the RED proof that the read-back works.
  3. remove the positive-limit guard: "SetSliceConcurrency(0) returned no error; want a validation error" — the runtime accepted 0.
  4. return the raw runtime error: "SetSliceConcurrency error is *errors.errorString, want a structured error".
  5. remove the unbuilt-engine guard: panic, nil pointer dereference.
  6. give the replacement engine a different executor identity: "recovered epoch workflow is on queue \"\", want \"_dbos_internal_queue\"" and the slice times out — proving the test really exercises recovery.

TESTS: five new tests, all added to the existing subject file internal/engine/subworkflows_test.go (no new file). The two shared-database tests use a new queueEngineOpts/newQueueEngineFrom fixture; the two old fixtures now delegate to it, so there is one construction path. No time.Sleep and no fixed-deadline wait added: every wait is waitUntil on a condition with a 30s or 60s ceiling. The gates use sync.OnceFunc so a release cannot double-close. The pre-existing fixed-2s-deadline backpressure test is untouched and passed in both full runs.

text:
S5 REVISION ROUND 1 COMPLETE 2026-08-28. NEW commit da7b181 on top of 6aca406 (6 files, +496/-49). No amend, no rebase, no push, no Beads close, no git hooks. Worktree clean.

F1 (IMPORTANT) FIXED, AND TIGHTER THAN ASKED. The literal instruction (ceiling = 2 x budget + slack) still lets a double spend through: measured, one full extra spend costs 2.03s against a 1s budget, and a 2 x budget + 500ms ceiling is 2.5s, so it would pass. The ceiling is now ONE budget + 750ms slack (1.75s), with the measurement written into the comment. Green run measures about 1.0s, so the margin for a loaded machine is 75 percent of the budget.
  RED EVIDENCE: mutating Engine.Shutdown to call dbos.Shutdown a second time (the runtime resets its one-shot flag on the timeout path, so the second call really does spend the budget again) fails with "Shutdown took 2.025834598s, at or beyond 1.75s". The same mutation PASSED the old worst-case window, which is exactly the finding.

F2 (IMPORTANT) FIXED. run now builds its startup context with signal.NotifyContext and passes THAT context to buildDaemonRuntime; both listeners (context and channel) are registered before the "pastured starting" line, so that line now means a signal is answered rather than fatal. The context is deliberately NOT released after startup: the durable runtime derives its own context from it, so releasing it would cancel the running engine (signal.NotifyContext's stop function cancels). New startupError reports a startup that ended while a signal was being answered, with exit code 3 and the underlying failure as the cause.
  MEASURED AND HONESTLY BOUNDED, please review this judgement: (a) the startup work IS context-aware where it matters - with a cancelled context, buildDaemonRuntime fails with "failed to probe sqlite_master: context canceled"; (b) the runtime does NOT keep the cancellation in the error chain (errors.Is(err, context.Canceled) is false, measured), so startupError cannot prove the signal is the cause. I first wrote "stopped because a stop signal arrived" and then corrected it: the message now says the signal arrived AND that startup then ended, with the real failure attached, because a database that is already unusable can fail at the same moment (measured: a locked database fails startup in 3ms). (c) tasks.OpenTaskTracker is not context-aware, so a signal during the audit-trail open is answered when that call returns, not instantly; that stage fails fast rather than blocking, and changing its signature is outside this slice.
  RED EVIDENCE: passing context.Background() to buildDaemonRuntime fails the source guard with 'run passes "<not a plain name>" to buildDaemonRuntime, want the signal context "startupCtx"'; removing the signal check from startupError fails the startup test with "exit code = 2, want 3" and a missing message.

F3 (minor) FIXED, plus a guard the subprocess cannot give. New TestPasturedAnswersASignalWhileItIsStillStarting starts the real binary, waits for "pastured starting" (a condition, bounded ceiling, no Sleep), signals at once, and accepts EITHER orderly ending (exit 0 with a clean stop if the signal landed after the engine was ready, or exit 3 with the startup message if it landed inside the window) while failing on the third outcome: a kill by the default action.
  MEASURED LIMIT, and how I closed it: startup on an empty local database is short, so the subprocess cannot be made to sit inside the window on demand - and I could not lengthen it honestly (a locked database fails in 3ms in a stage that is not context-aware, with or without the fix). A subprocess test alone would therefore NOT fail if F2 were reverted. I added TestRunPassesTheSignalContextToStartup, a go/ast guard over cmd/pastured/main.go (same technique as the existing blank-import guards) that reads the wiring from the source, and TestStartupTakesTheSignalContext, which runs the real startup work under a cancelled context. Together they fail deterministically on a revert; the subprocess test proves the process is never killed by the default action.
  RED EVIDENCE: moving both listener registrations back to after the "pastured starting" line fails the subprocess test with "pastured was killed by a signal instead of ending itself".

F4 (minor) FIXED. parsePendingShutdownComponents splits on "," and trims each name. New white-box table test in a NEW file internal/engine/engine_internal_test.go (package engine): the parser is unexported and engine.go had no white-box test file; the two existing ones (dbosinit_test.go, phasemap_internal_test.go) have other subjects, so a new file follows the repository's *_internal_test.go convention rather than mixing subjects. Cases: no error, no marker, one name, several names with ", ", several with "," and no space, trailing separator, marker with nothing after it, and an unknown name that must be kept. A second test pins the degrade path: empty Pending, cause reachable with errors.Is, and the runtime's own words in the message.
  RED EVIDENCE: restoring the ", " split fails with 'parsed [queue runner,workflows], want [queue runner workflows]' and 'part 0 = "workflows,", want "workflows"'.

F5 (minor) FIXED. New launchFailure(launchErr, stopErr): the launch failure alone stays in the error chain and decides the exit code; the stop failure is kept as text in the message and has already been logged in full by the engine, with the parts that were still running. New TestLaunchFailureKeepsItsOwnExitCode covers an uncategorised launch failure joined with a workflow-category stop failure, plus both single-fault cases.
  RED EVIDENCE: restoring errors.Join fails with "exit code = 3, want 1 (the launch failure's own code, not the stop failure's)".

F6 (minor) DONE. CHANGELOG.md gains an Unreleased section: the exit-code change (former blanket 1, now 1/2/3/4/5 by kind, with the note that scripts testing for exactly 1 must change), the incomplete-stop report, and the startup-signal fix. Plain user-facing wording, no internal references.

VERB: pasture queue concurrency get <queue> | set <queue> <n>. Both queue names are accepted, the short one ("slice") and the stored one ("pasture-slice-queue"), because the stored one is what an operator sees in the database and in log lines. Unknown name lists every queue it could have been (exit 1). Non-numeric or non-positive n refused before any write (exit 1). A queue no daemon has registered (exit 5) says to start pastured. Read-back is mandatory and is what is printed; a disagreement is reported, never hidden.

CLIENT CONSTRUCTION: through the EXISTING OpenEpochController(dbPath) by its current signature. The client it holds is unexported, so the new file (same package) takes it by type assertion on the returned controller. That is why no edit to controller.go was needed. DEPENDENCY ON S4: when S4 sets ClientConfig.AppName="pasture", this verb inherits it and its row reads become scoped to the same application, with no change here.

FINDING 1 — A DESIGN CONSEQUENCE THE TEST FORCED INTO THE OPEN. A daemon writes its configured limit into the shared row EVERY time it starts (that is the AlwaysUpdate policy decided in the first commit). So an operator's change lasts only until the next daemon start. I found this because my first test helper read the value back by building an engine, which silently reset the row to 8. The behaviour is defensible — a process about to serve a queue governs it, and configuration wins at start-up — but it MUST be told to the operator, so it is now in the command's help text, in the handler's file comment, and pinned by TestSetQueueConcurrency_IsReplacedWhenTheDaemonStartsAgain. The help text points at --slice-concurrency / PASTURE_SLICE_CONCURRENCY for a lasting change.

FINDING 2 — PRE-EXISTING DEFECT, NOT MINE, NOT FIXABLE FROM MY FILES. The durable runtime writes its start-up log lines to STANDARD OUTPUT when it is given no logger (dbos/dbos.go:126 builds a TextHandler on os.Stdout). internal/handlers/controller.go passes no Logger, so EVERY pasture command that opens a client interleaves runtime log lines with its own output, and "--format json | jq" fails. It is a one-line fix in controller.go (ClientConfig.Logger), which S4 owns. My CLI test extracts the JSON object and says why, citing the issue URL, so the test keeps passing unchanged once the logger is set. Recommend routing to S4.

FINDING 3 — A WEAK ASSERTION I CAUGHT WITH A MUTATION. My first not-found assertion matched the word "pastured", which also appears in the generic read-failure fix text, so swapping the sentinel from ErrQueueNotFound to ErrTimeout still passed. Both tests now assert wording unique to the never-registered case, and the same mutation now fails. Recorded because the lesson generalises: a substring assertion that also matches the neighbouring error proves nothing.

RED EVIDENCE for the new work (each mutation alone, then reverted):
  7. make the handler's write a no-op: the end-to-end test fails with "Asked for 4 concurrent jobs on pasture-slice-queue, but the stored setting now says 2" — which is simultaneously the proof that the handler's read-back works.
  8. make ResolveQueueSelector accept anything and fall back to the slice queue: the CLI unknown-queue test fails with "exit 0, want 1".
  9. classify the not-found with the wrong sentinel (ErrTimeout instead of ErrQueueNotFound): the CLI test fails on both unique strings. (This is the mutation that exposed Finding 3.)

TESTS ADDED: 4 handler tests (selector table, unknown-name refusal, read path, write-and-read-back, unusable number, never-registered, restart-replaces), 1 formatter table test (limit, no limit, JSON, unknown format), 3 CLI tests through the compiled binary (show-and-change round trip including --format json and the stored-name form, bad arguments, database with no queues), and 1 engine test (Test 17) proving a RUNNING engine adopts a change made through the command's own code path. Every wait is a condition with a bounded ceiling; no Sleep was added.

R1 BLOCKER FIXED, and the reviewer's diagnosis is confirmed exactly. The engine now lives under engineLifetimeContext(startupCtx) = context.WithoutCancel, so the runtime's own stop keeps its private cause and work in flight is left PENDING, not CANCELLED. Startup stays interruptible by bounding the WAIT for it, not by cancelling the engine: buildDaemonRuntime runs in a goroutine, run selects on that result against startupCtx.Done(), and a signal that wins the race hands over to abandonStartup, which waits up to startupAbandonTimeout (30s) for the abandoned step to land and then closes the half-built daemon. author: David Huu Pham
text:
S6 ITEM 1 — BOOTSTRAP-RACE PREDICATE RE-VERIFICATION against dbos-transact-golang v1.2.0.

Method: cloned repo at ~/codebases/dbos-transact-golang, `git archive v1.2.0` into a scratch dir, and read the extracted tree. No /nix/store search.

Each matched string, with its v1.2.0 producer:
- "failed to run sqlite migrations" -> dbos/internal/sysdb/sqlite_pool.go:172 (newSqliteSystemDatabase wraps the migration run with %v). CONFIRMED at the line the S3 note named.
- "failed to create migrations table" -> dbos/internal/sysdb/sqlite_migrations.go:238 (the lost probe-then-create window). CONFIRMED at the line the S3 note named.
- "already exists" also reaches us from dbos/internal/sysdb/sqlite_migrations.go:281 ("failed to execute migration %d"), which is a migration body re-creating a table or index. SQLite supplies the "already exists" text.
- "duplicate column name" -> same line :281, for a migration body that re-adds a column.
- "UNIQUE constraint failed: dbos_migrations" -> dbos/internal/sysdb/sqlite_migrations.go:288 ("failed to insert migration version %d"). That INSERT runs only when lastApplied == 0; a database that already carries a version row is UPDATEd at :293 instead.
- "database is locked" / "database table is locked" -> SQLite's own busy text; can wrap any statement above.

Structure re-read and still true in v1.2.0:
- probe-then-create outside any transaction: sqlite_migrations.go:227-240 (RunSqliteMigrations).
- one transaction per migration, %v on every failure: sqlite_migrations.go:261-296 (applySqliteMigration).
- the library's own retry cannot see the driver error: dialect.go:399-412 (SqliteDialect.IsRetryable reads the driver error code) and system_database.go:6664-6675 (Retry, whose condition chain is the two dialects' IsRetryable). The %v formatting severs the typed driver error, so migration failures are never retried by the library.
- migration bodies: dbos/internal/sysdb/migrations/sqlite holds 47 files; 14 use IF NOT EXISTS, 33 do not. Versions present: 1-9, 11-13, 15-19, 21-37, 40-42, 45-47, 100-104, 106, 107.

The race predicate does not match that. This is deliberate and safe here: an immediate re-attempt does not repair a spent start-up budget, and the timeout text is actionable on its own. Pasture leaves SystemDBStartupTimeout unset, so the library default of 2 minutes applies (dbos/dbos.go:63, :131-132) — far more than a bootstrap needs.

author: David Huu Pham
text:
S6 ITEM 2 — MISSING-DRIVER NEGATIVE TEST + the actionable error it needs.

HOW THE REAL ERROR WAS OBTAINED: a throwaway program (deleted afterwards, never committed) opened a modernc sqlite handle and called dbos.NewContext and dbos.NewClient WITHOUT the driver blank import. Both returned the same failure, verbatim:
  DBOS Error Initialization: Error initializing DBOS Transact: SQLite support is not linked into this binary: add import _ "github.com/dbos-inc/dbos-transact-golang/dbos/driver/sqlite" to register the SQLite driver
Shape: *dbos.Error with Code == dbos.ErrorCodeInitialization. Producer chain in v1.2.0: sqlite_driver.go:47-53 (registeredSQLiteDriver) -> sqlite_pool.go:141 (the check that runs even for a caller-supplied handle, which is pasture's case; :72 is the other caller) -> dbos.go:636-638 (re-wrapped as an initialization error).

GAP FOUND: pasture surfaced this as "Couldn't initialize the durable-execution context / DBOS rejected the shared SQLite handle or its configuration" from engine.New, and the epoch controller returned the library text unchanged. Both point the reader at the database or the machine; the real cause is a defect in the build that no operator can work around.

CHANGE: internal/engine/dbosinit.go gains isMissingDBOSSQLiteDriver plus the exported DescribeDurableStartupFailure(where, err), which replaces the causes pasture can name and returns every other error unchanged. newDurableContext runs every non-race failure through it, so the engine path is covered; internal/handlers/controller.go calls it with its own location, so lifecycle commands get the same account. The new error is a StructuredError, CategoryStorage (exit 5), and says: what (this build cannot open a database, its SQLite support is missing), why (the driver lives in a registry that only the driver package's init fills, so nothing names it and neither the compiler nor the linker can notice), where (the caller's own file and function), impact (no epoch can start; nothing was read or written), and fix (report it with the version, or in a source checkout add the named blank import to internal/engine/engine.go or internal/handlers/controller.go and rebuild).

NO RETRY: the refusal is permanent for the life of the process, so it must never enter the bounded schema-bootstrap retry. TestNewDurableContext_UnlinkedSQLiteDriverIsNotRetried scripts the real failure followed by a SUCCESS, so a retry would show up as a pass with two attempts; it asserts exactly one attempt, that isDBOSBootstrapRace does not match the refusal, and that the runtime's own error stays reachable as the cause. TestIsDBOSBootstrapRace gains the same case in its table.

S1's blank-import guards are UNTOUCHED and unweakened (testutil.RequireBlankImport in internal/engine/dbosinit_test.go and internal/handlers/controller_test.go). The engine guard now reads the production constant dbosSQLiteDriverPackage instead of a second copy of the package path, so the path cannot drift between the guard and the fix text.

TESTS ADDED (all in the subject's existing file, internal/engine/dbosinit_test.go; no new test file, no sleeps, no deadline polls): TestUnlinkedSQLiteDriverFailureShape, TestNewDurableContext_UnlinkedSQLiteDriverIsNotRetried, TestNewDurableContext_UnlinkedSQLiteDriverIsActionable, TestDescribeDurableStartupFailure (4 sub-cases: nil, described, wrapped-and-described, unnamed-cause-passed-through).

RED EVIDENCE (one mutation at a time, each reverted straight after):
1. newDurableContext: `if !isDBOSBootstrapRace(err)` -> `if false` (retry everything). FAIL TestNewDurableContext_UnlinkedSQLiteDriverIsNotRetried: "got success, want a failure on the first attempt".
2. DescribeDurableStartupFailure: missing-driver branch deleted. FAIL TestNewDurableContext_UnlinkedSQLiteDriverIsActionable ("error type = *models.Error, want *errors.StructuredError") and both TestDescribeDurableStartupFailure sub-cases.
3. dbosMissingSQLiteDriverMarker reworded to "SQLite support is not compiled into this binary" (a library reword nobody noticed). FAIL TestDBOSVersionPinMatchesRacePredicate: "isMissingDBOSSQLiteDriver no longer matches the unlinked-driver refusal of the pinned version".
4. recorded failure shape: Code Initialization -> Timeout. FAIL TestUnlinkedSQLiteDriverFailureShape on the rendered text.
Tree restored and re-run green after every probe.

FINDING, and it was a good catch: incompleteShutdownError was written for the epoch controller and my queue verb then surfaced it verbatim. An operator running "pasture queue concurrency get slice" through a slow stop was told three untrue things at once — that the EPOCH CONTROLLER had stopped, a Where naming dbosController.Close which never ran on that path, and a Fix asking them to re-read an epoch by an id they never gave.

FIX: the report now depends on which operation held the client, because only the caller knows what the operator was doing. The choice is a typed value, releaseSite, passed by the caller and threaded through openClient and releaseClient — not a guess made inside the error. A third caller therefore has to choose deliberately rather than inherit whichever wording was written first.
  QUEUE WORDING, and it is materially different from the controller's, not just re-worded: the setting shown was read back from the database BEFORE the stop began, so it stands and nothing this command did was left half-finished. What the failure does tell the operator is that the database is under strain or held by something that will not let go, which will affect their next command too. The Fix asks them to confirm with "pasture queue concurrency get <queue>" and to find the other writer with pgrep. No epoch id anywhere.
  CONTROLLER WORDING IS UNCHANGED, deliberately: for that caller the original text is right — work in flight may never have been recorded, so the epoch state must be re-read.

TESTS: TestReleaseClient_ReportsAnIncompleteShutdown now asserts the caller-specific wording the way the control refusal asserts its phrases — the What and Impact must contain "work-queue command" and "read back from the database before the stop began", the Where must name queue.go, the Fix must point at a queue command, and the whole report must NOT contain "epoch-id", "epoch controller" or "the controller". The same test also asserts the controller's own wording still points at "pasture status --epoch-id", so the two cannot be collapsed into one again by accident.
  Note on placement: the CLI test cannot carry this. A CLI-level assertion would need a client whose stop really times out, which needs a workflow parked inside that client, and the queue verb's client hosts no workflows. The white-box test is where the failure can be produced honestly, so that is where it is asserted.

It calls the provenance library's public gate, provenance.RequireSupportedDBOSSystemSchema, on the exact *sql.DB, and translates the result. A refusal that matches provenance.ErrSupersededDBOSSystemSchema becomes a StructuredError of storage category (exit 5) that says what (an older build wrote this database), why (clean cut, no upgrade path), where (the caller's own site), impact (nothing opened, started, or changed) and how to fix it (stop the processes, confirm no first-ever start-up is running, rm the file with its -wal and -shm companions, or point --db elsewhere). BLOCKER 1 (ordering) FIXED. engine.New now runs: open the shared handle -> schema gate -> open the forensic trail -> ensure the projection table -> durable context. The gate's refusal branch closes the handle only, because no trail exists yet. The comment above the new order states WHY it is load-bearing: opening the trail migrates the file, and a refused database that carries a newer trail schema is readable by neither build (internal/audit/migrate.go refuses a recorded version newer than the build knows), which contradicts the refusal's own promise that nothing changed and that the older build can still read the history.
  PINNED BY A WHOLE-FILE DIGEST, not a table list: TestEngineNew_RefusesADatabaseAnOlderBuildWrote now compares the sha256 of the file before and after the refused construction, and names the tables present on failure. A digest covers every writer at once, including one added later; the durable-runtime table probe and the recorded-version check stay as more specific assertions beside it.
  FIXTURE SHAPE CORRECTED IN THE SAME CHANGE: writeSupersededDurableDatabase now writes through dbconn.OpenSharedDB, the production opener. A fixture written on plainer pragmas is converted to WAL by the first production open, and that conversion alone rewrites the file header, which would read as a writer the gate failed to hold back. Real pasture databases are WAL, so this is also the more faithful fixture.

IMPORTANT 2 (untested branch) FIXED. New TestRequireSupportedDurableSchema_ReportsALayoutItCannotRead: a database carrying another program's table of the durable runtime's name (columns that hold no version), so the layout can be neither read nor judged. It asserts a storage-category StructuredError, that the error does NOT match the older-build sentinel, and that the report names the file, the integrity check, and the --db alternative.

MINOR 3 (wrong account of the cause) FIXED. supersededDurableSchemaError now names both conditions that produce a below-floor version: an older build wrote the file, or a first start of THIS build was interrupted (the runtime applies its layout steps one transaction at a time). Fix step 2 splits the three cases: an older build wrote it (read the history with that build first, then delete); an interrupted first start (nothing to keep, the file never finished being created); a first start still running in another process right now (let it finish, delete nothing). The doc comment above the function records the same split.

MINOR 4 (no ceiling) RECORDED. A comment block beside RequireSupportedDurableSchema states that the gate is a floor and not a range: a database written by a future build is accepted and handed to this build's runtime. That is the library's contract, the consequence is a downgraded binary opening a database it does not understand, and a ceiling has to come from the library that owns the layout contract. It is on the provenance follow-up; the comment says to re-read it when that gate gains a ceiling.

A. Old order restored, trail opened before the gate and closed on refusal. FAIL TestEngineNew_RefusesADatabaseAnOlderBuildWrote: "the refused database changed on disk", and the failure lists the 13 tables the trail created: agent_kinds, agents, agents_software, audit_events, audit_schema_meta, context_edges, lifecycle_occurrence_bindings, lifecycle_occurrences, lifecycle_payload_blobs, pasture_agent_categories, pasture_well_known_agents, session_entries, sqlite_sequence (beside the fixture's own dbos_migrations). So the old order was also a handle leak away from hiding its own damage. The new order removes both the leak and the write.
B. unreadableDurableSchemaError swallowed (return nil). FAIL TestRequireSupportedDurableSchema_ReportsALayoutItCannotRead: "the gate accepted a database whose durable layout it could not read". The mutation the reviewer reported as surviving is now caught.

ITEM 1 (main-file-only digest) FIXED. databaseDigest hashes the main file together with its -wal and -shm sidecars, each length-prefixed so bytes cannot be rearranged between the parts, and a missing sidecar counts as empty (the normal state after the last handle closes). Reason recorded in the helper's doc comment: under WAL journal mode a writer's pages sit in -wal until a checkpoint, so a migration can be complete and durable while the main file is untouched, and any later reader — including the older build — replays that sidecar on open.
  MEASUREMENT PROBLEM FOUND AND FIXED IN THE SAME CHANGE: the digest must be taken BEFORE any assertion opens a handle of its own. An open connection under WAL keeps a 32768-byte -shm and a 0-byte -wal alive, so the first version of the sidecar-aware assertion failed against the CORRECT production order. Measured on this host: after the last handle closes, both sidecars are gone; with a handle open, -wal is 0 bytes and -shm is 32768. The engine-level test now captures the digest immediately after engine.New returns; the gate-level test closes its handle first, exactly as the production refusal path does. Production leaves no sidecar behind, because the refusal closes the only handle it opened.

RED EVIDENCE, mutation D2 (the one that survived before): trail opened BEFORE the gate and its handle NOT closed on refusal. FAIL TestEngineNew_RefusesADatabaseAnOlderBuildWrote: "the refused database changed on disk", listing the 13 tables the trail created (agent_kinds, agents, agents_software, audit_events, audit_schema_meta, context_edges, lifecycle_occurrence_bindings, lifecycle_occurrences, lifecycle_payload_blobs, pasture_agent_categories, pasture_well_known_agents, session_entries, sqlite_sequence) beside the fixture's dbos_migrations. Under the previous main-file-only digest this mutation was GREEN. Mutation reverted at once; gofmt clean afterwards.

ITEM 2 (commit wording) DONE. The new commit message states the claim only where it now holds: "With that, the one assertion really does cover every writer at once, including one added later", and explains the WAL-resident write it previously missed.

ITEM 3 (MINOR 5, over-claim in the message) FIXED. supersededDurableSchemaError's Impact now reads: nothing was opened or started, and no pasture data was written -- no epoch, no history, and no layout step; opening the file does normalise its journal mode, so its header can differ, but the records inside it do not. unreadableDurableSchemaError's Impact is narrowed the same way. The engine.New comments no longer say "byte-for-byte as it arrived" or "nothing was changed": they say no pasture DATA was written and name the journal-mode normalisation as the one byte-level exception, which happens on the gate's own first query, before a refusal is possible. The fixture comment in the test names the same case as the one change the digest cannot cover by construction, and explains that writing the fixture through the production opener keeps it out of the way of every other assertion.

S2 UNSET-SITE GUARD + A LOST-WORK INCIDENT 2026-08-28. Commit 617137f. Chain on main 08d5cf7:

THE ITEM. The typed clientSite had the epoch controller as its ZERO value and both readers chose with an if-else, so a third caller added later would have inherited the epoch controller's wording silently — and, now that the same value also picks the Where shown when a client refuses to START, a location naming a file it never ran. FIXED: the zero value is clientSiteUnset and names no caller; both readers (incompleteShutdownError and startupWhere) choose with a switch; an unhandled caller gets NEITHER report.
  WHY REFUSING BEATS DEFAULTING, and this is written in the code, not only here: the two reports tell an operator OPPOSITE things. The queue report says the value you were shown stands and nothing was left half-finished. The controller report says do not trust what you read, because work in flight may never have been recorded. Handing a new caller one of those at random looks exactly as authoritative as handing it the right one. So the refusal says pasture cannot name the command, carries the underlying failure so the real problem is not lost, and tells the reader it is a defect to report rather than something to work around on their machine.
  startupWhere now returns (string, error); openClient joins a site error with the runtime's own failure rather than replacing it.
  TEST: TestUnhandledClientSiteIsRefused covers the zero value AND a value past the defined ones; asserts neither caller's wording appears anywhere in the report; asserts the cause survives; and asserts the two KNOWN sites still work, so the guard cannot be satisfied by refusing everything.
  RED EVIDENCE (restore the old else-branch behaviour): the unknown site takes the epoch controller's wording and its Where — five assertions fail, including 'the report borrows another caller's wording ("The epoch controller stopped")' and 'startupWhere returned "Opening the epoch controller ..." for a site it cannot describe'.

INCIDENT, reported because it affects the whole team, not only me. The supervisor has operated in this worktree before by their own message, so a git command run there by another agent is the likeliest explanation. I have asked them directly and asked that nobody run git in this worktree while I am working in it.

Nothing was lost. The lesson I am applying for the rest of this slice: commit as soon as a change builds and its own tests pass, and run the long gates on the committed tree.

WHAT IS PINNED, and the first version of this test was NOT good enough — recording that because it is the useful part.

  So the test proved almost nothing. Rewritten:

    - An unregistered directory sits beside the registered ones throughout, so a remover that swept the neighbourhood cannot pass by deleting more than it was given.
    - The empty-path guard is explicitly NOT claimed as tested. The test says so in its comment: the guard is cheap defence, no test can show it doing work, and asserting it would be theatre that passes with the guard deleted.

author: David Huu Pham
text:
ITEM 1 ROOT CAUSE + FIX 2026-08-28. Branch feat/dbos-v1-s7-validation, worktree pasture/worktree/dbos-v1-s7, one commit 3042bce (9 files, +281/-37), base main 08d5cf7. No push, no PR, no close, no git hooks.

ROOT CAUSE, traced not guessed. The three failing writes are all in ONE file and ONE code path: internal/audit/sqlite.go. "record audit event" is the INSERT at sqlite.go:395, "register agent" is the INSERT at sqlite.go:713, "record agent name" is the INSERT at sqlite.go:739. All three run on SqliteAuditTrail's own plain *sql.DB. They do NOT go through provenance runScopedTransaction and they have NO retry loop. Their only defence is the busy_timeout in the connection string, which dbconn builds from profile.SQLiteBusy() (internal/dbconn/dbconn.go:42).

THE DEFECT: engine.New opened that trail with audit.NewSqliteAuditTrail / NewSqliteAuditTrailWithOptions(WithSkipMigrations()) and NEVER passed cfg.Timeouts (internal/engine/engine.go, the trail block before the shared-handle open). The audit option audit.WithTimeoutProfile already existed and internal/tasks/open_unified.go:174-176 already used it; the engine was the one caller that did not. Result: the shared durable-runtime handle got the caller's profile (engine.go:242) while the audit trail on the SAME FILE was pinned to the production 500 ms. A caller could not widen the budget for the overlap it created, and the audit writes were always the first to give up. That is exactly the observed failure set.

WHICH FIX, AND WHY: BOTH halves, and neither changes a production default.
 (a) Production wiring: engine.New now passes cfg.Timeouts to the trail. A caller that sets no profile still gets timeouts.ProductionProfile on both handles, so production behaviour is byte-identical.
 (b) The test owns its profile: TestDBOSConcurrencySpike_IsolatedEnginesCanOverlap starts 8 engines at once (16 writers against production 2), so it multiplies every wait in the production profile by spikeWorkers=8 (4s SQLite lock wait) and passes it through the public seam engine.Config.Timeouts. The load is created by the test, so the budget belongs to the test. Load was NOT reshuffled: the test still starts the same 8 workers on the same shape of work.
I did not raise the production default because nothing shows production runs 8 overlapping engines on one machine; raising it silently would hide a real stall behind a longer wait.

The constructor now refuses a workflow-result wait at or below ingress or start_slice, with the reason in the message: a caller that stops waiting before an inner window closes reports a timeout for work that was still inside its own budget, which hides the real state. text:
S7 COMPLETE 2026-08-28. Branch feat/dbos-v1-s7-validation, worktree pasture/worktree/dbos-v1-s7, rebased onto main afd4d8b (S2/PR #121 merged; rebase clean, no conflicts). TWO commits. No push, no PR, no close, no git hooks.
  8098a0d  fix(engine): let the audit trail wait for the database lock as long as the caller asked   [item 1: 1ifoef + z4i742 production half]
  a60bef8  test(engine): pin what recovery costs and what limits it, for both kinds of interrupted work   [item 3: recovery/queue semantics]

ITEM 1 and the z4i742 production half are reported in full on 1ifoef and z4i742. Summary: engine.New never passed cfg.Timeouts to the audit trail it opens, so the trail on the SAME FILE as the durable-runtime handle was pinned to the production 500 ms lock budget while the runtime handle honoured the caller. The three CI failures (record audit event, register agent, record agent name) are all on that plain handle. Fixed at the root plus the spike test now owns a budget scaled by the overlap it creates. Production defaults unchanged.

ITEM 3, RECOVERY AND QUEUE SEMANTICS UNDER THE CORRECTED MODEL. Two tests, both added to the existing subject file internal/engine/subworkflows_test.go beside the queue-recovery test S2 wrote. No new test file.

WHY NOT recovery_test.go, since the brief named it: that file is build-tagged `recovery`, forks subprocesses and SIGKILLs them, and does NOT run in the normal suite, so tests placed there could never satisfy "stays green under -count=3". It also carries a guard, TestRecoveryTestsDoNotUseSkipMigrations, that forbids GoldenUnifiedDBPath and WithSkipMigrations in that file; my in-process tests use the golden database like every other test in subworkflows_test.go, so placing them there would have tripped it. Reported rather than decided silently.

TEST 18, TestRecovery_EpochWorkflowResumesWithinTheReservedQueueCadence. An epoch workflow never runs on a queue, so recovery puts it on the reserved queue. Measurement is read back from stored state, not inferred: started_at is the DEQUEUE time (dbos/internal/sysdb/system_database.go), so a workflow that never ran on a queue has none, and a non-zero value after recovery can only have been written by a dequeue from the reserved queue. Latency = wall clock from the start of the replacement engine to that read-back, a condition wait with a bounded ceiling, no Sleep. CEILING 5s = five times the reserved queue cadence of 1s (dbos/internal/models/queue.go DefaultBasePollingInterval = 1s). MARGIN IS DOCUMENTED IN THE CODE and deliberately wide, because the number is a ceiling and a tight one reports machine load as a defect. SECOND READ-BACK, non-timing: dbos.RetrieveQueue on the reserved queue must fail, proving it has no stored settings row, which is WHY pasture cannot change its cadence or give it a limit (dbos/queue.go keeps it in process, not in the queues table; engine Config.QueueBasePollingInterval reaches pasture's two queues only, internal/engine/engine.go:419+433).
  HONEST LIMIT, written into the test comment: the MEASURED wait is about 100-140 ms, well under one cadence, because the queue runner polls once as soon as it starts and recovery has already enqueued the work by then. The 1s cadence is the bound for work that MISSES that first poll, which is the case on a busy restart. I did not assert that case: a test cannot force the runner to miss its own first poll without reaching into the runtime. The comment says this instead of claiming the cadence was observed.

TEST 19, TestRecovery_RecoveredSlicesObeyTheLimitTheRestartedEngineSets. Hot reload as a first-class feature, across a crash. Crash an engine running 4 slices at once (gated at the SliceStarted hook, high-water mark asserted == 4 before the crash), restart at 2, assert at most 2 run together. THREE READ-BACKS of the limit: Engine.SliceConcurrency(), the stored queue row via dbos.RetrieveQueue, and the observed high-water mark. Every recovered slice's queue name is read back as the pasture slice queue, because the limit only applies there. Crash order matters and is commented: the engine stops FIRST, then the dequeued slices are marked as still running through an independent handle, so a slice that finishes during shutdown cannot write its own result over the mark.
  FINDING, the substantive one: the limit in force after recovery is the RESTARTED engine's, not the crashed engine's. The queue settings are a shared row and pasture registers with the always-overwrite policy (internal/engine/queue.go), so restarting at a new limit is how an operator changes the limit for work that was ALREADY interrupted. The test states this as the behaviour, not as an accident.

RED EVIDENCE, one mutation at a time, each reverted.
  Test 18: ceiling lowered to 50 ms -> "the recovered epoch workflow was picked up after 101.115618ms, above the ceiling of 50ms". Proves the ceiling assertion is live and the measurement is real.
  Test 18, NEGATIVE RESULT REPORTED: removing markWorkflowPending does NOT turn the test red. Shutdown already leaves an in-flight non-queued workflow in that state. I kept the mark anyway and said why in the code: the test states the crash state it needs instead of depending on a shutdown detail it does not control.
  Test 19, mutation A: restart at the crashed limit of 4 -> "restarted engine reports a limit of 4, want 2" and "stored slice-queue limit after the restart = 4, want 2". Both read-backs live.
  Test 19, mutation B: restart with no limit change AND the two read-back assertions disabled, to isolate the concurrency bound -> "4 recovered slices ran at once, want at most 2 (the limit the restarted engine registered)". The bound assertion is live on its own.
  Defect found by my own mutation and fixed: the stored-limit failure message printed a pointer address instead of the value. It now prints the value, and the nil case has its own message.

ONE conflict, in internal/engine/engine.go around engine.New, resolved as instructed: S8's order kept (shared handle -> schema gate -> trail -> projection -> durable context) and the cfg.Timeouts pass-through applied at the trail open in its new position. THREE commits:
  ba33e8b  fix(engine): let the audit trail wait for the database lock as long as the caller asked      [item 1]
  c1e58b4  test(engine): pin what recovery costs and what limits it, for both kinds of interrupted work  [item 3]
  b5f26aa  fix(pastured): give the daemon one timeout profile, and correct what the recovery tests claim [this round; 9 files, +564/-153]

F1 RATIONALE CORRECTED. The reviewer is right: testutil.GoldenUnifiedDBPath copies the golden database into a fresh temporary directory per call, so the eight workers never queue on one lock. The multiplier is kept at 8 and re-justified in the terms that are true: about 2*spikeWorkers writer goroutines share the machine against two in production, so a writer that ALREADY HOLDS its file lock is descheduled far more often and holds it longer, and the peer on the same file absorbs a wait that grows with the oversubscription. The budget is scaled by the same factor as the load. The commit message says this too.

F2 FIXED FOR REAL, AND IT WAS A REAL GAP. cmd/pastured opened the tracker with tasks.OpenTaskTracker (production profile, no seam) and injected it as engine.Config.Trail, so the engine wiring reached only the trail==nil path. The daemon now resolves ONE profile at ONE call site, daemonTimeouts(), and passes it to initAuditTrail (which opens the tracker with tasks.WithTimeoutProfile) AND to newEngineConfig. The value is unchanged, so no production behaviour moves; what changes is that the three writers on one file can no longer disagree. Engine.Timeouts()'s doc now states plainly that it does NOT reach a trail supplied through Config.Trail, and why.
  NEW TEST TestInitAuditTrail_GivesTheDaemonTrailTheConfiguredLockBudget in cmd/pastured/main_test.go. It is behavioural and has no race to win: another writer holds the lock for the WHOLE call, so the write is certain to fail, and what the test reads is HOW LONG it waited. RED: revert the daemon to tasks.OpenTaskTracker -> "the daemon trail waited 516.390587ms for the file lock, above the ceiling of 250ms; it was opened with a budget of 25ms".

F3 FIXED. The spike profile now scales only the three inner tiers; workflowResult keeps the production 30 s. waitSpikeProjection and runSpikeEpoch are back to a 30 s ceiling instead of 240 s.

F4 FIXED, AND THE PRESCRIPTION NEEDED ONE ADDITION - REPORTED, NOT WORKED AROUND. holdWriteLock now returns release and waitUntilFree; the failing half holds the lock until the write has returned, the succeeding half releases on a short timer. That removed the timing coupling. Every comment of mine that said epoch workflows recover on the reserved queue is corrected.

A slice dispatches its start hook inside a durable step, so a recovered slice whose hook step already recorded a result never fires it again; counting hooks measured step memoization, not concurrency. The gate is kept only to hold running slices still long enough to be sampled. The read-back also sees MORE than the hook counter did: the isolating mutation now reports 6 slices at once where the hook count reported 4.

A-G ALL DONE. (A) the clock starts after the replacement engine is built and the build time is logged separately; it was the larger half, measured at 57-150 ms. (B) the ceiling comment now states the mechanism accurately - SEE THE CORRECTION BELOW. (C) TestReservedQueueFactsMatchThePinnedRuntime pins the reserved queue's name and cadence against the runtime version they were read from, and internal/engine/dbosinit_test.go points at it. (G) the reserved-queue lookup asserts the runtime's typed dbos.ErrQueueNotFound, not any error and not a string.

CORRECTION TO FINDING B, reported rather than repeated. The cited line is the ERROR-backoff branch, not an idle backoff. dbos/queue.go, queueRunner.runQueue doubles the interval only when a poll hit a database-contention error, and SCALES IT BACK on every clean poll; an idle queue does not slow down. The ceiling comment states the accurate version: the interval grows only after a contention error, and a restart builds a fresh runner that starts at the base interval and has never backed off, which is why one cadence bounds the wait here and would not bound it on a long-lived process.

CONFLICT ON FINDING E, reported rather than worked around. Adding the "only if still running" guard to markWorkflowPending BROKE the accepted S2 test TestSliceQueue_RecoveryKeepsEachWorkflowOnItsOwnQueue, which deliberately runs a slice to COMPLETION (so it can read back the queue it completed on) and then marks it pending. S2's test now calls the loud form with a comment saying why. Nothing is resurrected silently.

author: David Huu Pham
text:
REPRODUCED ON DEMAND (S7, 2026-08-28). The cold-role forensic write was measured at 438.193296ms against a 25 ms budget: a ratio of 17.5. This is a controlled measurement, not an outlier caught in passing, and it is the fact this task exists for.

HOW TO REPRODUCE, exactly. In internal/engine/concurrency_spike_test.go, TestEngineAuditTrail_UsesTheConfiguredSQLiteLockBudget, delete the warm-up RecordEvent that runs before holdWriteLock (that warm-up is what makes the shipped test measure ONE blocked statement). Then the failing half writes for a role whose agent rows do not exist yet, while another writer holds the file lock for the whole call, and the test logs how long the write waited. Run:
    nix develop -c env CGO_ENABLED=1 go test -race -count=3 -v ./internal/engine/
Conditions of the run that produced 438 ms: the WHOLE engine package (not -run filtered), -count=3, -race, CGO_ENABLED=1, GOMAXPROCS default on a 32-core host at load average 4-7 shared with other work. The engine test, not the cmd/pastured one.

MEASUREMENTS, three runs of the command above, nine samples, ratio against the 25 ms budget:
  run 1: 438.193296ms (17.5x), 180.059279ms (7.2x), 188.537048ms (7.5x)
  run 2: 244.823952ms (9.8x),  97.969174ms (3.9x),  114.191819ms (4.6x)
  run 3: 245.379619ms (9.8x),  55.242212ms (2.2x),  49.292495ms (2.0x)
PATTERN WORTH NOTING: the FIRST repetition of each run is the slowest every time (438, 245, 245). The package's parallelism is at its peak then.

THE STRUCTURAL FLOOR, measured separately so load and structure are not confused. Same cold write with -run limited to this one test, so almost nothing else runs:
  GOMAXPROCS default: 59.028586ms (2.4x), 46.687565ms (1.9x), 50.66283ms (2.0x)
  GOMAXPROCS=2:       45.847189ms (1.8x), 46.163875ms (1.8x), 45.390664ms (1.8x)
So about 2x the budget is STRUCTURAL - the cold write blocks on more than one statement, each with its own budget, and no overall deadline caps the sum. Everything above 2x is machine load stacked on that structure. This also explains why a reviewer on 2 pinned CPUs measured 45-51 ms and could not see the effect: at that core count the rest of the package barely runs in parallel, so only the structural floor shows.

CONTROL, to show the fix direction works: with the warm-up in place, so the measured write is a SINGLE blocked insert, the same full-package command gives 25.5, 25.6, 25.7, 25.5, 25.6, 33.7, 25.6, 25.5, 25.7 ms - one budget plus scheduling, maximum 1.35x. Collapsing the cold write to one statement (one transaction, or a bounded retry around the group) removes the multiplier entirely.

WHAT THIS MEANS IN PRODUCTION, in the same terms: the production budget is 500 ms, so the same cold-role write can spend several times that before it fails a phase transition, and it fails with CategoryStorage rather than retrying. The shipped test is NOT affected: it warms the path on purpose, so it measures one budget and its 400 ms ceiling holds with about twelve times the observed maximum in hand.

No production code was changed to obtain this. The instrumented file was restored; the branch tree matches c6accb5 exactly.

STRUCTURE SEPARATED FROM LOAD, which is the part that matters for the follow-up.
