author: David Huu Pham
text: FIXED at e8a53f3aab2f07f0fed15098fd18a35de13854bf, with your requested shape. ForFault takes a typed closed FaultStage whose Unset zero value is REFUSED: arms are not-recorded and record-unknown. Pre-work faults (environment, positional arguments, flag error, panic before dispatch) pass not-recorded; the deadline expiry and any post-commit failure pass record-unknown. The Impact follows the stage: record-unknown reads that an occurrence MAY OR MAY NOT exist and names both places to look, the lifecycle occurrence journal and the fault record file beside the database. The same distinction is written into the record line as faultStage. Your ruling on the tier is honoured: 5s is unchanged. MUTATION-RED: forcing the record-unknown branch to the not-recorded text turns TestTheImpactFollowsWhatPastureKnows RED; forcing the deadline branch to pass not-recorded turns the built-path abandonment test RED.

text: FIXED at e8a53f3aab2f07f0fed15098fd18a35de13854bf, using the seam you identified. (1) The four states are enumerated in the test file itself, with the orphan blob named as legal by design. author: David Huu Pham
text: FIXED at e8a53f3aab2f07f0fed15098fd18a35de13854bf. The seam was BUILT, not raised: the architect ruled option 1. HookLifecycleNative now calls a named CommitBarrier after the durable receipt commits and before the host is told anything; production wires a pass-through barrier and there is no test-only branch and no environment variable. THE INVARIANT WORDING WAS RESTATED BY RULING: the pair is not exhaustive, so what is proven is the stronger claim the code states, that an occurrence never names an absent blob, over the four legal states. TWO PROOFS, and each is reported as what it is. (1) Through the production command with the barrier held open: the receipt IS committed, the host receives NO continuation, the diagnostic says the occurrence may or may not exist, and the state is read back through the production read path. That run produces the COMMITTED-RECEIPT-WITH-NO-CONTINUATION outcome, deterministically, every time; it is a one-case proof by construction, not a hedge. (2) At the commit sequence with the journal seam: the orphan-blob state, the invariant, and the orphan count. RESIDUAL GAP, stated plainly: neither proof kills an operating-system process mid-write. What is left is SQLite crash behaviour, which is the database engine guarantee and not pasture. That limit is in the test doc comment, in the code comment at the deadline, and in the fix report.

author: David Huu Pham
text:
# S0 FIX ROUND REPORT — worker-s0-fix1

FINAL SHA: e8a53f3aab2f07f0fed15098fd18a35de13854bf
Branch: slice/rp2tju-s0-failure-modes, three commits over 3de1beb, 22 files.

  e8a53f3 test(lifecycle): make three unmutatable claims structural
  c48bb54 docs(lifecycle): state the two unreclaimed surfaces and pin the manifest divergence
  fe9e5f0 fix(hook): a fail-open fault lets the host continue on every harness

GATES, all on an ARCHIVE COPY of e8a53f3 (git archive + git init + origin remote + one commit):
  go build ./...                        PASS
  go test -race -count=1 ./...          PASS, every package, no data race
  make generate                         ZERO DRIFT (git status clean)
  nix flake check --no-build            PASS (cgo-disabled-build, race, installer)
  make fmt                              clean

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
## 1. THE BLOCKER, AND THE DESIGN CONSEQUENCE THE LEAF ASKED ME TO SURFACE

### The shape chosen: ForFault is NOT harness-aware

The leaf predicted that making fail-open true on every harness would make
ForFault harness-aware, cost the package its purity, damage the 24-cell table
and move ForFault toward the encoder boundary that S3 owns. I did not build
that, and here is the shape I built instead with the trade stated.

ForFault takes a typed Continuation: the exact bytes THIS host reads as
"you may continue", supplied by the caller. hostexit therefore knows nothing
about a harness, stays pure, and the 24-cell table is unchanged and still runs
without a store, a clock or a harness. The harness table lives in
nativeresponse.FaultContinuation, beside the encoders that already own the
byte shapes, which is where reviewer-c predicted this knowledge would migrate.
The migration happened; it just did not drag ForFault with it.

WHAT THE TABLE COST. The 24 cells are unchanged in count and meaning. Each
now also asserts the BYTES: the two blocking cells write nothing, and the 22
continuing cells write the continuation they were given. The table gained a
dimension only in the sense that the outcome it asserts is richer.

WHAT THE SIGNATURE COST. ForFault took four positional parameters and now
takes one struct, because it grew two more required members and three of them
are closed enums whose zero value is refused; naming them at the call site is
what stops a caller passing the wrong one by position.

THE ONE REAL RISK, AND HOW IT IS CLOSED. A Continuation is a value with a SET
flag, not a byte slice. One legitimate continuation is the EMPTY body, because
Claude Code reads empty stdout as a proceed. If "no bytes" also meant "the
caller forgot", then a forgotten continuation would silently reproduce this
exact defect on OpenCode. ForFault refuses an unset Continuation, so a
forgotten one is a loud programming error at the call site. That refusal is
mutation-tested.

### The split is not blurred

A fail-open fault emits proceed bytes and is STILL A FAULT. Three things keep
that true where it can be kept: every record line carries outcomeClass=fault
plus the bytes the host was given; the diagnostic says the event was not
evaluated; and no decision record is written on this path. ForDecision is
still the only door an evaluated answer passes, and that is now STRUCTURAL: a
test parses its declaration and refuses any mention of the fault policy, the
failure evidence or the blocking predicate.

What CANNOT be kept is a distinction in the bytes. The host reads one channel,
and on OpenCode the only accepted body is the proceed object. So the fault
bytes and the evaluated-proceed bytes are identical, deliberately, and a test
asserts they are identical for every harness and event class rather than
letting them drift apart by accident.

### Layer 2, the belt
The generated plugin now reads an empty body at exit 0 on a named callback as
"not evaluated, continue" and reports on the console. A non-empty body it
cannot accept still throws. This covers an OLD binary, which the Go fix cannot.

### The fail-closed deny object was NOT built, and why
The leaf required S0 to emit a typed deny object under PASTURE_HOOK_FAIL_CLOSED
so the opt-in would stop being a no-op on OpenCode. Finding aura-plugins-4b248h,
as restated by reviewer-b after the earlier ruling, required the opposite: that
S0 STATE the limitation and pin it, because the deny object does not exist until
S3 and its shape is S3's to define. I did not choose between them. I escalated,
built the 4b248h shape so the round was not stalled, and said I would change it.
The architect ruled OPTION A and the leaf was corrected. Sequence recorded as
fact, not as a deviation taken.

REVIEWER-B'S REASON FOR WITHDRAWING ITS OWN EARLIER FIX, recorded here because
it is the same class of user-facing wrongness as the blocker: making an OpenCode
ExitBlock non-zero would collide with the ratified refusal contract, because the
generated plugin reads any non-zero exit as a broken pasture installation and
prints "verify PASTURE_BIN". A policy refusal would then reach the user as a
broken install.

THE ARCHITECT ANSWERED THE UNDERLYING QUESTION, one line for S3 to inherit: may
a FAULT, an event that was never evaluated, use the REFUSAL channel at all? YES,
under fail-closed, but with its own closed reason distinct from every policy
reason, so that both the host and the durable record say "not evaluated" and
never "denied by policy".

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
## 2. C-I5 (aura-plugins-iy5kj8): WHICH OUTCOME EACH RUN PRODUCED

The seam was BUILT, not raised: the architect ruled option 1 and the supervisor
withdrew the instruction to raise it. handlers.CommitBarrier is a named typed
boundary called ONCE after the durable receipt commits and before the host is
told anything. Production wires a pass-through barrier. No environment variable
and no test-only branch.

THE INVARIANT WORDING WAS RESTATED BY RULING, so the pair is not what is proven.
The receipt is TWO durable writes in a deliberate order, so a third legal state
exists, and the proven claim is the stronger one the code states: AN OCCURRENCE
NEVER NAMES AN ABSENT BLOB, over the four legal states.

TWO PROOFS, and each run produces ONE outcome deterministically. Neither is a
hedge that records whichever side a race landed on.

RUN 1 — the production command with the barrier held open, in
cmd/pasture/hook_lifecycle_failuremode_test.go. OUTCOME PRODUCED, every run:
A COMMITTED RECEIPT WITH NO CONTINUATION. The receipt is committed, the host
receives no bytes, the diagnostic says the occurrence may or may not exist, and
the occurrence is read back through the production read path and found. It is a
one-case proof BY CONSTRUCTION: the barrier holds the invocation past the
deadline, so this outcome is not one of two possibilities, it is the only one.

RUN 2 — the commit sequence with the journal seam, in
internal/engine/budget/abandonment_test.go. OUTCOME PRODUCED, every run:
AN ORPHAN BLOB WITH NO OCCURRENCE, followed by a committed retry that adopts
its own orphan and leaves none. Again deterministic: the journal signals that
the append has begun and the test cancels exactly there.

A SECOND ENFORCER FOUND WHILE PROVING IT, which no reviewer listed: the
occurrence projection carries a FOREIGN KEY to the payload blob table, so the
corrupting state is refused by the SCHEMA as well as by the write order. The
mutation that removes the blob write does not produce a bad row; the projection
rebuild refuses it.

THE RESIDUAL GAP, stated where a later reader meets it — the code comment at the
deadline, the test doc comment, and here. Neither proof kills an operating-system
process mid-write. What is left is SQLite crash behaviour, which is the database
engine's guarantee and not pasture's: the blob transaction has already committed,
and an uncommitted journal transaction is rolled back from the write-ahead log
when the next connection opens the file. I report this as what it is.

ONE ITEM NOT DONE. The "one step, one transaction" assertion for the migrator is
NOT added. It belongs to internal/audit/migrate.go, and the rewritten leaf
forbids touching any retry site. Raised for the task that owns the ceilings.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
## 3. THE ORPHAN MEASUREMENT, IN THE REQUIRED FORMAT

BYTES PER ORPHAN: the raw host payload of that invocation. Measured 386 bytes
for the Claude SessionStart fixture. The per-orphan BOUND is the ingress payload
cap, 1 MiB (1048576 bytes), which is the worst case a single orphan can reach.

ORPHANS PER STORM: exactly ONE per abandoned invocation, asserted, not estimated.
The orphan is content-addressed, so a retry of the SAME delivery adopts the
existing blob rather than adding a second, and the retry leaves none behind.

IS IT MATERIAL? NOT for a single fault, and not for a repeated fault on the same
payload, because the content address collapses repeats. It becomes MATERIAL only
under a sustained storm of DISTINCT payloads: every wired event of every tool
call, each with a different body, each abandoned. At a typical few hundred bytes
that is small; at the 1 MiB cap it is not. I state the numbers and stop there; no
remedy is designed here.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
## 4. C-I3 (aura-plugins-wdvank): THE ANSWER PER ASSERTION

The six assertions the reviewer named, each answered with MUTATION PRODUCED or
TICK STRUCK, and the one that cannot be mutated by construction named.

1. TestLifecycleFaultRecordIsBestEffort — MUTATION PRODUCED. Making a failed
   record write change the outcome turns it RED ("Not equal" on the exit).

2. TestForDecisionIsNotRejudged — TICK STRUCK, then REPLACED. This is the
   assertion that CANNOT BE MUTATED BY CONSTRUCTION, and reviewer-c is right:
   ForDecision takes neither the policy nor the evidence, so no input can tell a
   correct implementation from one that ignores them. Naming it explicitly, as
   the re-review checklist requires: THIS ONE. It is now renamed to what it
   proves, TestForDecisionCarriesTheDecisionVerbatim, and the invariant is made
   STRUCTURAL in TestForDecisionCannotSeeThePolicyOrTheEvidence, which reads the
   declaration. That structural test HAS a mutation: making ForDecision consult
   the fault policy turns it RED.

3. TestHookEnvironmentRefusesAMissingLookup — MUTATION PRODUCED. Accepting a nil
   lookup turns it RED with a nil pointer dereference.

4. TestHookEnvironmentZeroValueIsUnusable — MUTATION PRODUCED. Making the unset
   fault policy valid turns it RED ("Should be false").

5. TestFailureModeIsTheOnlyFailureVocabulary — TICK STRUCK for the name, and the
   missing half BUILT. The test proves the arms of THIS enum are distinct and
   its zero value refused; it cannot prove no SECOND enum exists, which is the
   claim its name makes and the way the tree acquired three of them. A new
   structural test, TestNoSecondFailureVocabularyIsDeclaredAnywhere, asserts the
   absence over the module source. MUTATION PRODUCED: declaring a second
   failure-mode type in another package turns it RED.

6. TestAntigravityStillRefusesActionably — MUTATION PRODUCED, PARTIALLY. Making
   the contract return nil turns it RED ("An error is expected but got nil"), so
   the refusal itself is proven. The text assertion is NOT isolatable: it checks
   that the message contains "unsupported", and TWO sources supply that word, the
   headline and the wrapped sentinel, so removing either leaves the test green.
   Reported as a partial rather than a tick.

MUTATIONS FOR THE NEW ASSERTIONS OF THIS ROUND, 20 in all, each restored:

  M1  fail-open emits no bytes again -> the 24-cell table, the per-harness
      continuation table and the fail-closed pin all RED.
  M2  an unset Continuation is accepted -> "continuation never set" RED.
  M3  an unset FaultStage is accepted -> "unset stage" and "stage above the last
      arm" RED.
  M4  the abandoned invocation claims nothing was recorded -> the honesty test RED.
  M5  the OpenCode fault continuation goes back to empty -> the per-harness table
      and the matches-the-evaluated-proceed test RED.
  M6  the plugin belt is removed -> the Bun belt proof RED with the ORIGINAL
      DEFECT text: "pasture hook lifecycle response is not JSON: SyntaxError:
      Unexpected EOF".
  M7  the goroutine recover is deleted -> the test PROCESS CRASHES with the
      injected panic.
  M8  the main recover is deleted -> the test process crashes with the injected
      nil-context panic.
  M8b one statement is inserted before the recover -> the position test RED.
  M9  the deadline branch passes not-recorded -> the abandonment truth test RED.
  M10 the commit barrier is not called -> the abandonment proof RED (the
      invocation finishes without reaching the boundary).
  M11 the blob write is removed -> the state-3 assertion, the orphan count and
      the projection rebuild RED together.
  M12 the fault record calls itself a decision -> the built-binary OpenCode proof RED.
  M13 the deadline cause goes back to the generic fault text -> the path-specific
      assertion RED ("does not contain hook-invocation deadline").
  M14 a divergent row is dropped from the pinned set -> the divergence test RED.
  M15 one executable core.hooksPath line is added to a source file -> the source

author: David Huu Pham
text:
SANITY CHECK OF THE TRIGGER REASONING, requested at the S0 round-2 review (axis C).

CONCLUSION FIRST: I agree this leaf should stay DORMANT, but not for the reason
given. The stated reason is wrong, and if it is recorded as the closing reason it
will mislead whoever revisits this.

WHAT I VERIFIED IN THE MEASUREMENT
- Content-addressing is real: the orphan is keyed by digest.FromBytes(delivery.Body),
  so repeated faults on the SAME payload collapse to one blob. Correct.
- 386 bytes for the Claude SessionStart fixture, bounded above by the 1 MiB
  ingress cap. Correct.

TWO CORRECTIONS
1. "EXACTLY one orphan per abandoned invocation" is AT MOST one. The measurement
   asserts it for state 3, the abandonment between the blob commit and the
   journal append. An invocation abandoned BEFORE the blob commit leaves none.
   The arithmetic for this trigger should use at-most-one.
2. "MATERIAL only under a storm of DISTINCT payloads" reads as though the storm
   were exotic. It is the NORMAL case for this fault. The orphan appears when the
   journal append waits, which is exactly what a locked database causes, and a
   session under a lock fires a stream of DIFFERENT events carrying DIFFERENT
   identities, so the payloads are distinct almost by definition. The storm
   condition COINCIDES with the fault condition; it does not qualify it.

SO WHY DORMANT IS STILL RIGHT
It is the SIZE that saves this, not the rarity. Hundreds of abandoned
invocations during a long lock cost a few hundred kilobytes at the measured
size, which no user notices. The honest trigger is a RATE times a SIZE against a
threshold, with the fact that nothing reclaims stated plainly:
  orphans per unit time under a sustained lock, times payload size, against a
  stated threshold, growing without bound because nothing reclaims them.
Worst case is not the 386 bytes but the 1 MiB cap: a storm of large distinct
payloads under a long lock reaches tens of megabytes, still slowly.

CHANGE REQUESTED
Close this leaf dormant, and quote the CORRECTED reasoning as the closing reason:
at most one orphan per abandoned invocation, distinct payloads are the normal
case rather than the exception, the measured size makes the growth immaterial at
the observed payload size, the growth is unbounded over time because nothing
reclaims, and the number that would activate this leaf is a rate times a size,
not a rarity judgement. That way a later reader who meets a bigger payload or a
longer lock has the right quantity to re-measure.

author: David Huu Pham
text:
CONTENT-ADDRESSING SANITY CHECK, as asked, because it decides whether the reclaim leaf activates.

THE MECHANISM IS CORRECT. receipt/journal.go inserts the blob with ON CONFLICT(digest) DO NOTHING, and the key is digest.FromBytes(body), so a repeated fault on a byte-identical payload adopts the existing orphan and adds nothing. One orphan per distinct payload, exactly as stated.

THE PRACTICAL SCOPE IS THE OPPOSITE WAY ROUND FROM THE FRAMING. "Material only under a sustained storm of DISTINCT payloads" reads like an exotic case. It is the ordinary case, because host payloads are distinct by construction: a Claude PreToolUse body carries session_id, prompt_id and tool_use_id, an OpenCode callback carries sessionID and callID, and a Codex body carries session_id and turn_id. Two tool calls in one session never produce the same bytes. The byte-identical repeat that content-addressing protects against is the RARE case - the same delivery replayed - and not the storm case.

So the storm arithmetic is: a database that stays locked or broken produces one orphan per faulting invocation, each holding the full raw body, bounded by the 1 MiB ingress cap and about 386 bytes for the small fixture measured. A busy session firing several wired events per tool call reaches thousands of orphans in a working day, none of them reachable from any occurrence and none swept, since retention and reclaim are deferred out of this epic.

MY READ FOR THE ACTIVATION DECISION: activate the reclaim leaf, or state a bound. It does not have to be a sweeper. A cheap and honest alternative is to make the orphan COUNTABLE and SAYABLE - one query that reports blobs with no referring occurrence, named in AGENTS.md beside the fault record - so a user whose database grew can see why, and the deferred retention work inherits a measured number instead of a surprise. What should not ship is the current pair of statements together: "reclaimable" in the code and nothing that can reclaim or even count them.

The rest of this finding is RESOLVED. The stronger invariant, that an occurrence never names an absent blob, is the right thing to prove, and the second enforcer the worker found - the foreign key from the occurrence projection to the payload blob table - is a better guarantee than the write order alone, because it holds even if a future caller reorders the two writes.

author: David Huu Pham
text:
ARCHITECT RULING recorded, on reviewer-b finding aura-plugins-58ynqt (B14), which was raised at the S0 round-2 review and handed to this leaf.
THE RULE: the fail-open continuation applies ONLY when NO decision was committed. Once a consultation record carrying a DENY is committed, the host MUST receive that harness's deny bytes. The encoder runs on the COMMITTED DECISION, so a deadline expiring AFTER the commit emits the committed decision, NOT the fault continuation.
THE BOUNDARY IS THE CommitBarrier that S0 built: after AfterCommit returns, EXPIRY CANNOT CHANGE THE BYTES. That is where the outcome becomes fixed.
THE OTHER WINDOW - a deadline expiring BEFORE the commit - is the FAULT path and is fail-open by decision D4. The two windows are the whole space; there is no third.
TEST THROUGH THE SEAM, both directions: block AFTER the commit past the deadline and assert the host receives DENY; block BEFORE the commit past the deadline and assert the host receives the fail-open continuation with ReasonEvaluationFault.
This is an S3 obligation. S0 carries only two sentences in the hostexit doc naming the hazard, and no code change.
NOTE FOR WHOEVER IMPLEMENTS THIS LEAF: the seam you need already exists because S0 built it for a different reason - proving the abandonment invariant. It was justified as a design change on its own merits, and this is the second obligation it now carries.

author: David Huu Pham
text:
CORRECTION BY THE AUTHOR, after the round-3 worker raised a collision with B9.

TWO ERRORS IN THIS FINDING, both mine.

1. I TREATED TWO TESTS AS ONE KIND. This finding says "the two deadline proofs
   each pay the full production tier". They are not the same kind of test:
   - the abandoned-after-commit proof runs IN PROCESS and calls lifecycleOutcome
     directly, so a parameter shortens it with no loss;
   - the locked-store proof runs the BUILT BINARY, which no parameter can reach.
   Shortening the second needs an environment variable or a flag, which is the
   seam B9 refused.
   I described the pair without enumerating it, which is the exact error this
   epoch has now recorded three times.

2. I WITHDRAW THE CONFIGURABILITY HALF. This finding also argued that the tier
   is "the one number an operator might need to move" and that having no way to
   supply one was a gap. That is wrong and B9 is right. A hook that can be TOLD
   to use a different deadline stops proving the thing the host pays for, and the
   failure is asymmetric: a user who can lengthen it can freeze their own
   session, which is what the tier exists to prevent. The tier being immovable
   from outside is a PROPERTY, not a gap.

WHAT STANDS: the TEST-COST half only, and it is satisfied by injecting the
in-process proof alone.

WHAT MUST NOT HAPPEN: converting the built-binary proof to an in-process test to
save the other 5 s. Its two assertions -- below the tier plus process start, and
below the 10 s smallest host budget -- are host-budget claims that are true ONLY
at the production tier and ONLY through a real process. It is the only
end-to-end measurement in this slice. Converting it would satisfy this finding's
words and delete its substance, and I would raise that as a finding.

ACCEPTED RESOLUTION: the tier becomes a parameter of lifecycleOutcome,
production by default, with no environment variable and no flag; the in-process
proof runs injected and asserts the same path wording and state; the
built-binary proof keeps the production tier and says WHY it cannot be injected.

author: David Huu Pham
David Huu Pham
text:
STRENGTHENED by reviewer-b after reviewer-c's round-3 finding. Suggestion accepted, and I am recording the stronger reason here rather than leaving it in a code comment on one test.

## The reason this finding gives is the weaker one
B9 justified the hard-coded tier as a TESTING cost: no test can shorten the deadline, so every expiry proof pays a real 5 s wait. That is true and it is not the point.

## The stronger reason, which is reviewer-c's and which I adopt
The tier being IMMOVABLE FROM OUTSIDE THE PROCESS is a USER-SAFETY PROPERTY, not a gap.
- A user who can SHORTEN it stops proving the budget the host actually enforces: the number would no longer be the one the host pays for, and the proof would pass while meaning nothing.
- A user who can LENGTHEN it can FREEZE THEIR OWN SESSION. That is precisely the failure the tier exists to prevent, and it is the failure that was MEASURED at 31.4 s against a 10 s host budget. Handing that dial to the environment would hand the user the defect back.

So the absence of an environment variable and of a flag is a deliberate refusal, and a later reader who meets this finding while wondering why the deadline has no knob should meet that reason first.

## What this does NOT forbid, and the guard it needs instead
An IN-PROCESS parameter is not the same thing as a user-reachable knob. reviewer-c's narrowed C-M6 makes the tier a parameter of lifecycleOutcome with NO environment variable and NO flag, and that is compatible with everything above: the property is immovability from outside the process, and a Go parameter is not reachable by a user.

The two deadline proofs are also not the same kind of test, which is the fact both my finding and C-M6 had missed. The in-process proof loses nothing by being injected. The built-binary proof CANNOT be injected without the seam I refused, and it carries the A21 host-budget claim itself — elapsed below the tier plus process start, and below the 10 s smallest host budget — which are true only at the production tier and only through a real process. Converting it would keep a passing test and lose the claim.

Requested, replacing the "state the choice in a comment" ask:
1. Keep the refusal and record the user-safety reason where the parameter is declared, not only on the test.
2. Pin the single production call site the way finding S0-B15 asks for the commit barrier: one assertion that the command path passes the PRODUCTION tier, so an in-process parameter cannot drift into a behaviour switch later.
3. Leave the built-binary proof at the production tier with its elapsed assertions unchanged.

text:
WAVE-1 CONSTRAINT carried from the S0 review (reviewer-b). When two findings CONTRADICT each other, the worker SURFACES THE CONTRADICTION rather than choosing a side, AND SURFACES IT TO THE SUPERVISOR AS INTEGRATOR, NEVER TO ANOTHER WORKER DIRECTLY.

WHAT IT IS: ONE READ of this slice's leaves against IMPL_PLAN section 6, on reviewer-b's axis, searching the named targets in order — an assertion asked for WITHOUT ITS MUTATION first; then the contradiction rule and its address clause, ownership statements that widen without being updated in the same commit, operator-facing text as a truth claim, and constraints written as PREFERENCES rather than MECHANISMS.

author: David Huu Pham
text:
PRE-DISPATCH RE-READ (reviewer-b, architecture and data model). IMPORTANT — this leaf describes a guard shape that S0 has already replaced.

## What is wrong
The test list says: "the no-change subject: adding a fake Gemini destination turns it RED; ADDING A FILE UNDER .git/hooks TURNS IT RED", and the ownership line says the guard is "moved from S0 if S0 created it". S0 created it, and then S0 round 2 SPLIT it, for a reason this leaf pre-dates.

S0 now ships TWO tests, deliberately separate:
- TestPastureSourceInstallsNoGitHook, which is a property of the CODE: it walks the module and fails when an executable line contains core.hooksPath, .git/hooks or "pre-commit install". Comments are exempt, because a comment that names the forbidden act in order to forbid it is the opposite of the defect.
- TestThisRepositoryHasNoInstalledGitHook, which reports the STATE of the checkout and must NOT blame pasture, because a developer or another tool may install a hook and that is not a pasture defect.

A worker following this leaf literally would re-create the single-test shape, and the message would blame pasture for somebody else's hook — the exact defect S0 finding B6 removed.

## Concrete change
1. Restate the ownership line as a fact: the guard EXISTS at internal/codegen/no_change_guard_test.go as two tests; this leaf MOVES the enum-sync helper and leaves the guard shape as S0 landed it.
2. Replace "adding a file under .git/hooks turns it RED" with the SOURCE mutation: add a line that writes into a hooks directory, outside a comment, and show the source guard turns RED naming the file and the line.
3. Keep a separate line for the repository-state test and state that it may fail for a reason pasture does not control.

## Why it is IMPORTANT and not a BLOCKER
It does not stop S1 being implemented, and the worker will meet S0's committed code before it meets this text. Under the section 6 contradiction rule that worker must surface the difference rather than choose; this comment means it does not have to.

author: David Huu Pham
text:
PRE-DISPATCH RE-READ (reviewer-b, architecture and data model). IMPORTANT x2, MINOR x1.

This leaf is the one I most wanted to read, and its reasoning is sound: the orphan is legal by design, the write order must not change, and the bound is a safety valve rather than a retention policy. Three gaps.

## IMPORTANT 1 — the most dangerous bound has no named mutation
Four bounds are stated. Two have mutations (remove the age threshold; remove the cap). The bound with NO mutation is the one whose failure is catastrophic rather than merely wasteful: "a blob that an occurrence NAMES is NEVER reclaimed, at any age". Deleting a named blob manufactures exactly the corrupting state the blob-before-journal write order exists to prevent — an occurrence naming an absent blob — and the projection foreign key would then refuse to rebuild.
NAME IT: make the reclaim ignore the named-by check and show that the named-blob test turns RED, and say that the rebuild also fails, because both enforcers should fire.

## IMPORTANT 2 — where the reclaim runs is ambiguous, and the two readings differ in blast radius
The scope says "on the NEXT SUCCESSFUL INVOCATION, inside the EXISTING STORE OPEN PATH". Those are not the same place. Every pasture command opens the store; only the hook has an invocation and a HookInvocation budget. Under the wide reading, `pasture task list` performs DELETEs, bounded by a budget that does not exist for it. Under the narrow reading, only a successful lifecycle hook reclaims.
STATE WHICH, and if it is the store open path, state which budget bounds it for a non-hook command and add a case proving a non-hook command stays inside it.

## MINOR — ownership is not a path
"the store open path that performs the reclaim, and its test subject" cannot be checked. Name the files, as the other S1 leaves do. S1 creates files that the Wave-1 ownership table later references by path, so a vague statement here becomes a vague row there.

author: David Huu Pham
text:
PRE-DISPATCH RE-READ (reviewer-b, architecture and data model). IMPORTANT — the property that makes this leaf worth having is the one property no mutation tests.

The leaf states the reason for its own existence: 73 new events land in Wave 1, so the guard "is DATA-DRIVEN from the registration tables, so a new event is covered the moment it is registered. It must not need an edit per event."

The three named mutations — a free-text field on a target row, a tool-argument field, an inlined body — all prove the guard REFUSES the forbidden content. None proves it is DATA-DRIVEN. A guard that enumerates today's events by hand would pass all three and would then be silently blind to every one of the 73 events that arrive after it is written. That is the ship-broken-but-green case this leaf exists to prevent, reproduced inside the leaf itself.

## Concrete change
Add the fourth mutation, and make it the load-bearing one: REGISTER A NEW EVENT with a free-text field and show the guard turns RED WITHOUT ANY EDIT TO THE TEST. If the guard needs a test edit to see the new event, it is not data-driven and the mutation has found it.

Add the matching positive case: register a new legal event and show the guard covers it and passes, so the mutation cannot be satisfied by refusing everything new.

## One note on the S4/S5/S6 re-assertion
The leaf says each harness slice RE-ASSERTS the test over its own newly enabled events. If the guard is genuinely data-driven, the re-assertion is automatic and the harness leaves need only prove the guard RAN over their new rows. Say that, so a harness worker does not write a second, hand-listed copy of the same guard — which would re-introduce the per-event edit this leaf refuses.

author: David Huu Pham
text:
PRE-DISPATCH RE-READ (reviewer-b, architecture and data model). IMPORTANT x1, MINOR x1.

## IMPORTANT — the "unset" token is a pin with no mutation, and A27 depends on it
The amendment is right: an empty string cannot distinguish "derived as None" from "not yet derived", so the token must be explicit. But the leaf names only one mutation, for the parity test (wire a withheld event). Nothing turns RED if a later slice renders the empty string instead of "unset".

That matters beyond tidiness. S4-L7 checks A27 — the count of CapabilityDeny events equals the count of rows with evidence. If "unset" degrades to "", A27 can compare blanks to blanks and PASS VACUOUSLY, which is the failure mode this token was introduced to prevent.

NAME THE MUTATION: render the not-yet-derived capability as the empty string and show a report-shape test turns RED, saying that "unset" and "absent" are different states. Add the companion case: a genuinely absent evidence source renders as the empty string and is NOT the same value as "unset".

## MINOR — one ownership entry is not a path
"the OpenCode report emitter" cannot be checked against a diff. The other three entries in the same list are paths. Name the file. S1 creates the artefacts that the Wave-1 ownership table then references by path, so a vague entry here becomes a vague row there.

author: David Huu Pham
text:
PRE-DISPATCH RE-READ (reviewer-b, architecture and data model). IMPORTANT x1, MINOR x1.

## IMPORTANT — the exemption is the new assertion, and it is the one with no test and no mutation
The amendment adds a SCOPING RULE: the Clearance requirement applies to a fixture whose harnessVersion equals a frozen pin, and a fixture at an older pin is exempt. That is a new conditional in the validator and it is what keeps S1 mergeable, so it is load-bearing.

The test list does not test it. Its five cases are empty Clearance, bare task id, wrong filename, an accepted path, and the digest rewrite — every one of them at an unstated version. Neither boundary is asserted:
- a fixture at an OLD pin with no Clearance is EXEMPT and stays green;
- a fixture at a FROZEN pin with no Clearance is a HARD ERROR.
The single named mutation (relax the bare-task-id pattern) does not reach the exemption either. So the exemption could widen to every fixture, or vanish, and this leaf's tests would not notice — and S2-L3's flip to unconditional would then be flipping something it cannot see.

CONCRETE: add the two boundary cases above, and name the mutation — remove the frozen-pin condition so the exemption applies to every fixture, and show the frozen-pin case turns RED. That mutation is also what proves S2-L3 has something real to flip.

## MINOR — two different populations are both called "the existing fixtures"
This leaf says 18 fixture pairs on main (Claude 14, Codex 2, OpenCode 2). Other epic text says 14 pairs, and elsewhere 12 enabled events plus 3 controls. These are probably three different populations — every pair on disk, the pairs at the old Claude pins, and the enabled set — but a reader cannot tell which is which, and S2-L3 has to delete exactly the right one.
State the counting basis in this leaf, in one clause. I am not asserting which number is right: host-contract counts are reviewer-a's axis and PA1 has already corrected one count in this area. I am asking that the leaf say WHICH population it counted.

author: David Huu Pham
text:
PRE-DISPATCH RE-READ (reviewer-b, architecture and data model). IMPORTANT x2.

## IMPORTANT 1 — the flip is an assertion with no mutation
The leaf adds: "REMOVES the exemption ... Add a test that proves an exempt fixture can no longer exist. The bridge must not outlive this slice." That is a pin, and the leaf's two named mutations are about something else (corrupt a fixture byte; remove a control).
NAME IT: restore the frozen-pin exemption, or offer a fixture at an old pin with no Clearance, and show the flip test turns RED. Without that mutation the flip test can be written in a form that passes whether or not the exemption is gone, which is precisely how a temporary bridge outlives its slice.

## IMPORTANT 2 — "coverage must never silently drop" is written as a preference, not a mechanism
The escape says an event that cannot be re-triggered is RAISED TO THE USER before its old fixture is deleted, and that if the user withholds a currently-enabled event the 8/2/2 exit criterion is "restated in the S2 report with the user's decision quoted, rather than quietly missed". Every part of that depends on the worker following it. Nothing refuses the bad state.

The slice already has the mechanism to hand: enabled counts are generated data that a test reads. Make the property a gate.
CONCRETE: assert that every event enabled at the START of S2 is, at the END of S2, either enabled again or carries a closed-set withheld reason; and that the enabled counts are 8/2/2 unless a withheld row names WithheldNoReachableTrigger, in which case the count assertion reads the documented exception rather than the literal. Then "coverage never silently drops" is enforced by the gate rather than by discipline, and the ordering rule ("raise BEFORE the old fixture is deleted") stops being the only thing standing between a user and a silent loss of coverage.

This is the section 6 check for constraints stated as MECHANISMS rather than PREFERENCES, and this leaf is the place in S2 where it has real consequences.

author: David Huu Pham
text:
REVIEWER-A PRE-DISPATCH PASS on the S1 leaf text (axis: host-contract truth and end-user behaviour). One read, as bounded. 0 BLOCKER, so nothing here holds the dispatch. 4 IMPORTANT and 1 MINOR, each naming the leaf and the concrete change. Facts below were re-measured in the tree, not taken from the leaf.

IMPORTANT — S1-L6 hqnytd: the clearance promise has two mechanisms and five procedures, and the gap is where the user's prompt text lives.
The promise this leaf makes to the user is that nothing raw reaches a remote before their ACCEPT and that free text is substituted first. Only TWO of its seven steps are mechanisms that can fail a gate: the secret scan (step 4) and the Clearance-path refusals (built in S1-L1). Steps 2, 3, 5, 6 and 7 are worker procedure. So a worker who skips the substitution can commit a fixture carrying verbatim prompt text, write `Redaction: "home-path-v1"`, and every gate stays green: the Clearance field only requires a PATH, the digest check only requires self-consistency, and the secret scan only matches token shapes, not prose.
That is a promise the mechanism cannot keep, on the fixtures that hold the content the user was most careful about.
CHANGE: turn the step-2 inventory from a report into an ASSERTION over the committed corpus, using the class detector this leaf already builds — a fixture that carries a field the detector classes as FREE TEXT must list `free-text-v1` in its `Redaction`, or the test is RED naming the fixture and the field path. Enforce step 7 the same way for the 4 KiB tool-response rule. Keep the report mode for the worker's own use.

IMPORTANT — S1-L5 gf4wdu: "checks the pinned host version" does not say WHICH contract shape, and the two readings differ for every user of Claude Code.
The Claude contract is a RANGE (mustRangeContract, internal/runtime/profiles.go) while Codex and OpenCode are EXACT. This leaf puts a version check on the LIVE hook path for the first time; today ingress records the host version without admitting it. Read as exact equality, the day Claude Code auto-updates from 2.1.251 to 2.1.252 — which it does by itself, on the user's machine, without asking — every hook invocation starts refusing, and under fail-open the user silently loses all journaling until somebody re-pins.
CHANGE: state the admission shape per harness in the leaf: range for Claude, exact for Codex and OpenCode, each following its declared contract. State that a version outside admission is a FAULT on the fail-open path with a diagnostic naming the observed and the admitted versions, never a silent drop. Add the case: a Claude patch bump inside the range is ADMITTED, and mutate it by narrowing the range to prove the case is load-bearing.

IMPORTANT — S1-L11 s6k7mg: the reclaim's age threshold does not bound every writer, so it can delete a live blob.
The bound is "older than one HookInvocation tier", and the stated promise is that "a blob whose journal append is still in flight is NEVER reclaimed". That holds only for writers that carry the 5 s deadline. `pasture hook lifecycle raw` — the import and migration path — does NOT: cmd/pasture/hook_lifecycle_raw.go carries no WithTimeout and no select on a deadline. A long raw import can therefore sit between its blob write (receipt/service.go:85) and its journal append (:122) for far longer than five seconds, while a concurrent successful hook invocation reclaims that blob. The foreign key then refuses the import, so it is a loud failure rather than corruption, but the user loses an import to housekeeping and the leaf's own promise is broken.
CHANGE: bound the age by the LONGEST blob-to-append window of any writer, not by the hook tier; the WorkflowResult tier is the honest upper bound today. State the rule as a mechanism: the reclaim age must be greater than the largest deadline any writer may hold between the two writes, and add a test that a blob written by a path WITHOUT the hook deadline is not reclaimed while its append is in flight. If that is not provable, move the reclaim off the hook path entirely and give it an explicit command.

IMPORTANT — S1-L1 5onrkf: the Clearance exemption is keyed on a version predicate rather than on the fixtures it was written for.
The exemption reads "a fixture whose harnessVersion equals a FROZEN PIN must carry Clearance; older pins are exempt". The 18 fixtures it exists for are known and countable. As written, ANY future fixture at a non-frozen pin is also exempt from the clearance requirement, which is the one enforceable half of the privacy promise above. The bridge is meant to last one slice, and a version predicate does not say so.
CHANGE: scope the exemption to the ENUMERATED existing fixtures, by name or by digest, so a fixture that is not on that list can never be exempt whatever its version. S2-L3 then deletes exactly that list and removes the exemption, and its "an exempt fixture can no longer exist" test becomes checkable against a list rather than against a predicate.

MINOR — S1-L8 rlwt8r: baseline numbers verified, no change asked. I re-measured: hooks/pasture-activation.json holds 30 rows with 8 enabled, .codex/pasture-codex-activation.json holds 10 with 2, and the OpenCode array holds 47 with 2 enabled. The leaf's statement of all three is correct, and the "unset" token wording is exactly what was asked. Recorded so the next reader knows the numbers were checked rather than assumed.

author: David Huu Pham
text:
REVIEWER-A PRE-DISPATCH PASS on the S2 leaf text (axis: host-contract truth and end-user behaviour). One read, as bounded. 0 BLOCKER, so nothing here holds the dispatch. 1 IMPORTANT and 3 MINOR, each naming the leaf and the concrete change.

IMPORTANT — S2-L2 2fyuvb: the leaf demands an upstream diff and, in the same breath, pins the answer.
It says "Counts after this leaf: Claude 30 registered events; Codex 10; OpenCode 47", and its test asserts "the registered event count per harness is 30 / 10 / 47". Those are the counts at the OLD pins. The leaf's whole purpose is to re-derive three catalogues at NEW upstream versions and report the events ADDED, REMOVED and RENAMED. If Claude 2.1.251 added one event, the true count is 31, and the worker must then either drop a real upstream event or fail the leaf's own test. That is a host-behaviour number asserted in advance with no citation, and it makes the honest outcome unrepresentable — in the leaf that also says "an undiffed rename is a silent coverage loss".
CHANGE: assert what the leaf actually wants: the registered count EQUALS the size of the re-derived catalogue, every native name resolves, and the diff is reported with its documentation reference or inspected source revision for each added, removed and renamed event. State 30 / 10 / 47 as the PRE-bump baseline that the diff is measured against, not as the expected result. A count that changes is a finding for the supervisor, not a test failure for the worker to engineer around.

MINOR — S2-L3 462y6n: "The exact pins reject the old files anyway" is false for Claude.
The Claude contract is a RANGE, not an exact pin (mustRangeContract, internal/runtime/profiles.go), so the 2_1_222 Claude fixtures are NOT rejected by version admission; only the Codex and OpenCode exact pins reject theirs. The DECISION to delete all 14 Claude pairs is right and the leaf gives the true reason first — one capture set per pin — so only the justification is wrong.
CHANGE: delete the sentence or correct it to name which harnesses it is true of. This is the third appearance of the range-versus-exact confusion in this epic, which is why it is worth one line.

MINOR — S2-L1 rhpl01 and S2-L3 462y6n: the probe and the capture are separated in time, and one of these hosts updates itself.
S2-L1 probes the three versions and stops on drift; S2-L3 then runs live capture sessions later, possibly on another day. Claude Code updates itself by default. If it moves between the probe and the capture, the new fixtures carry a harnessVersion outside the frozen pin, and the corpus refuses them at the end of a capture session the user has already paid an hour for.
CHANGE: S2-L3 re-records `claude --version`, `codex --version` and `opencode --version` immediately BEFORE each capture session, and a drift is a STOP-and-raise, never a silent re-pin and never a capture kept "because it is close enough". State it as the same mechanism S2-L1 uses, so the rule does not depend on the worker remembering.

MINOR — S2-L6 vwy7zt: the recipe list is what the user reads before agreeing to be recorded, and it does not say that.
The leaf publishes the trigger recipes and the time estimate for the user to accept. The recording itself is described in the S1 capture leaves, which the user does not read. A person is being asked to run real sessions whose raw payloads are written to disk and later committed after their approval.
CHANGE: the published list states, in one sentence at the top, that each session records the raw host payloads into a directory outside the repository, that the binary prints a notice while it records, and that nothing is committed or pushed before the clearance step and their ACCEPT. The estimate and the recipes are then an informed agreement rather than a schedule.

NOT RAISED, checked and correct: the escape-before-deletion order in S2-L3 and S2-L6, the 8/2/2 exit criterion being restated with the user's decision quoted rather than quietly missed, the PA1 withdrawal carried in both S2-L2 and S2-L5, and the S2-L5 report contents. CORRECTION to the previous comment, posted by the supervisor against itself.

The previous comment is CORRUPTED. I wrote it with double quotes around text containing BACKTICKS, so the shell EXECUTED the backticked fragments before bd ever saw them. Two command names were replaced by their own CLI help output, which is why that comment ends in a wall of flag descriptions that have nothing to do with the review. This is a known trap that is already recorded in my own operating notes, and I walked into it anyway. The rule is: NEVER put backticked text inside a double-quoted bd argument. Use a QUOTED HEREDOC, as this comment does.

That is the ambiguity reviewer-b raised: "the next successful invocation" and "the existing store open path" are different places, and only the hook carries the budget the leaf cites.

author: David Huu Pham
text:
ROUND 3 REPORT (worker-s0-fix3, resumed after the round-3 worker stopped mid-item).
Final SHA 707ba8f, five commits over 7ec2940. Nothing pushed, no task closed.

GATES, on a git archive copy of 707ba8f with an initial commit:
  go build ./...                      PASS
  go test -race -count=1 ./...        PASS (no FAIL line in the whole tree)
  make generate then git status       CLEAN (no drift)
  nix flake check --no-build          PASS (cgo-disabled-build, installer, race)

===========================================================================
FINDING 1 (the most important of this round): THE BRANCH I INHERITED WAS RED.
===========================================================================
TestWithheldOpenCodeEventIsNotAdmittedByBuiltCLI FAILED at 7ec2940, the
inherited HEAD, before I changed anything. I proved it on a separate archive
copy of 7ec2940, so it is not an artefact of my tree.

Cause: ba6bf42 made an OpenCode OBSERVATION fault write nothing, and the
built-binary proof of the withheld path still asserted the old
{"decision":"proceed"} bytes. Round 3 changed behaviour and did not run the
gates, so the red test was committed and left.

I did NOT weaken the assertion. I resolved it on evidence, then strengthened
the comment. The evidence:
  - session.updated carries surface "opencode-catch-all-sse" in the generated
    plugin metadata, NOT "opencode-named-output". Nothing on that surface reads
    standard output.
  - the generated plugin already has its own empty-body arm: at exit 0 with an
    empty body it logs "Pasture did not evaluate <event> ... the host continues
    unevaluated" and continues. It throws only on a non-zero exit, on non-JSON,
    or on a named-output body that is not exactly the canonical object.
So the empty body is correct here, and the old comment ("an empty body would
make a named callback throw") gave the GATE reason for an OBSERVATION event and
was false on both counts for this event. The gate arm stays pinned: an OpenCode
gate fault (tool.execute.before) still asserts the canonical object.
MUTATION-RED: disabling the observation arm in nativeresponse turns the repaired
assertion RED. Commit 9647744.

===========================================================================
FINDING 2: THE INHERITED UNCOMMITTED DIFF DID NOT COMPILE.
===========================================================================
Asked for: review it, finish or correct it, commit it as my own with evidence.
What I found, on `go vet ./cmd/pasture/`:
    hook_lifecycle_failuremode_test.go:794:12: undefined: printer
The new pin used printer.Fprint without importing "go/printer". The package did
not build, so NONE of the inherited work had ever been run.

Its DESIGN was sound and I kept it: the tier as a parameter, production passing
ProductionProfile(), a zero profile normalized to production, no env var and no
flag, the in-process proof moved to DeadlineTestProfile with the elapsed number
removed from the assertion, and a structural pin on the single call site.

What I corrected beyond the missing import:
  (a) the user-safety reason was NOT at the declaration. The parameter doc said
      only "the reason is beside the deadline below" - a forward pointer, not
      the reason. Item 6b asks for it AT the declaration. Both directions are
      now recorded there: shortening stops proving the budget the host enforces,
      lengthening can freeze the user's own session, measured at about 31s
      against a 10s host budget. The duplicate paragraph at the deadline site is
      reduced to a pointer back, so the two cannot drift apart.
  (b) added the reason a supplied profile is NOT re-validated: timeouts.New is
      the only constructor, the fields are unexported, and New refuses an
      out-of-order hook-invocation tier, so the only unconstructed profile is
      the zero one, which is normalized. There is no third state.
  (c) the built-binary proof carried no refusal. Its comment now NAMES the two
      shortcuts and refuses each BY MECHANISM, never by saying "cannot":
        - convert to in-process: a parameter cannot cross a process boundary, so
          reaching it DELETES the process - no build, no start, no separate
          opener contending for the real lock - and the elapsed bounds would
          then bound one function call, which is not what a host waits for;
        - add an env var or a flag: that is the ONLY way a value reaches a
          separate process, and creating one hands the dial to every user, which
          is what the declaration refuses. There is no version of that change
          that shortens the tier for the test alone.
Commit 9067d32.

THE SIX CHECKS ON THE TIER
1. Production 5s UNCHANGED; TestProductionHookInvocationSitsBelowTheSmallestHostBudget
   still asserts 5s and the 2s headroom under the 10s budget. THE TIER DID NOT MOVE.
2. Parameter of lifecycleOutcome, production by default via IsZero normalization,
   no env var, no flag. Verified by grep and by the source-level pin.
3. In-process proof runs on DeadlineTestProfile and asserts the SAME path wording
   and state; the "5s" literal is gone from it and NO elapsed number replaced it.
   It gained two assertions instead: "abandoned the work", and NotContains of the
   store-error wording, so it cannot pass on a fast store failure.
4. Built-binary proof keeps the production tier and every elapsed assertion, and
   now carries the A21 host-budget claim in its own comment plus both refusals.
5. Ordering invariant holds for a supplied profile structurally: New is the sole
   constructor, fields unexported; TestNewRejectsAHookInvocationDeadlineOutsideItsOrder
   covers all six inversions. Recorded at the parameter so no one adds dead validation.
6. Call site pinned: exactly ONE lifecycleOutcome call in production sources, and
   it must pass handlers.PassThroughCommitBarrier{} AND timeouts.ProductionProfile()
   by rendered source text.

===========================================================================
THE ORPHAN COUNT (item 1) - and one DEVIATION I need judged
===========================================================================
Delivered: `pasture hook lifecycle orphans`, text and JSON, read-only, deleting
nothing. receipt.SQLiteBlobStore.ReclaimableCount answers it from the SAME
predicate Reclaimable enumerates, unbounded (a count that stopped at the 256
reclaim batch would under-report exactly when the number matters). Commit aa9a412.

DEVIATION, surfaced rather than decided: the leaf said add the count TO the
listing command. I put it on a SIBLING subcommand of the same lifecycle read
group instead, for a reason I could not get around:
  - the leaf ALSO requires "reports zero on a clean store", so the line cannot
    be conditional on a non-zero count;
  - TestNativeListReadBackGoldenBytesUnchanged pins `hook lifecycle list` output
    BYTE-IDENTICAL in BOTH renderers to a committed baseline. An unconditional
    footer breaks it, and regenerating that golden would defeat the invariant
    the test exists to hold. I will not weaken it.
A sibling subcommand keeps both, is MORE discoverable than a flag (it appears in
`hook lifecycle --help`, which is now pinned by a golden of its own), and does
not perturb a machine-readable record stream with prose. If the reviewers want it
on `list` regardless, say so and name what should happen to that golden.

A CORRECTNESS TRAP I HIT, worth recording: lifecycle_occurrences is a DISPOSABLE
PROJECTION rebuilt from the journal. The count is a LEFT JOIN against it, so a
count taken WITHOUT a rebuild reports EVERY blob as an orphan - the largest and
most alarming wrong number this store can produce, and precisely the false alarm
the wording exists to prevent. The command rebuilds first, exactly as `list`
does. This also rules out `manifest` as the home: manifest documents itself as
strictly read-only and a rebuild writes derived rows. And it rules out `status`,
which is about epoch workflows, not store facts.

THE EXACT OPERATOR WORDING, so it can be judged without running it.
Text output is two lines:

  orphan payload blobs: 3
  what this number means: An orphan is a payload blob that no recorded
  occurrence names. One is left behind by a hook invocation that was abandoned
  between its two durable writes, and at most one arises per abandoned
  invocation. This is expected and reclaimable, not damage: the blob is written
  before the journal row deliberately, because a spare blob can be reclaimed
  later while a journal row naming an absent blob could not be repaired at all.
  A large number therefore does not mean the store is corrupt. It means
  invocations were abandoned repeatedly, so the thing to investigate is the
  store contention that caused the abandonment, such as another writer holding
  the pasture store.

(the note is one line in the real output; it is wrapped here only to be read.)
JSON is {"orphanPayloadBlobs":3,"note":"<the same string>"}. The note travels in
JSON deliberately: a dashboard that renders the number alone reproduces the
misreading the sentence exists to prevent.
The note is printed AT ZERO TOO, on one code path, because an operator meets the
term for the first time whichever number is beside it, and a term whose meaning
appears only above a threshold is learned at the worst possible moment.

The three required claims map to it: (1) "a payload blob that no recorded
occurrence names ... abandoned between its two durable writes ... at most one
arises per abandoned invocation"; (2) "expected and reclaimable, not damage",
with the WHY, so it is not an assertion to take on trust; (3) "does not mean the
store is corrupt ... the thing to investigate is the store contention that
caused the abandonment".

The `orphans --help` Long text says the same three things in the same order and
is now pinned byte-for-byte by testdata/help-golden/hook-lifecycle-orphans.txt.

AGENTS.md carries the count beside "reclaimable": what an orphan is, that it is
expected and reclaimable, what a large number means, why the count agrees with
the invariant, why it rebuilds first, and why it is never on the hook path.

===========================================================================
MUTATION-RED EVIDENCE (every mutation applied, observed RED, then restored;
the tree was verified clean by git status after each)
===========================================================================
M1 command path passes timeouts.DeadlineTestProfile() instead of Production
   -> RED: "hook_lifecycle.go must pass the production timeout profile ..."
M2 command path passes a stub CommitBarrier instead of PassThroughCommitBarrier{}
   -> RED: "hook_lifecycle.go must pass the pass-through commit barrier ..."
M3 production hook-invocation tier lowered 5s -> 3s
   -> RED: profile_test.go:129 "production hook-invocation deadline = 3s, want 5s"
M4 ReclaimableCount returns count+1
   -> RED on BOTH: the built-binary count test (0 read as 1, 3 read as 4) and the
      agreement test ("the count and the enumeration read one predicate ...")
M5 the large-number sentence removed from the note
   -> RED twice: "the misreading must be refused by name" and "the reader must
      leave with the action to take"
M6 the identifier ReclaimableCount planted on the hook path
   -> RED: "hook_lifecycle.go is on the hook path: counting orphans there spends
      the invocation deadline reading the very store that contends ..."
M7 the OpenCode observation arm disabled in nativeresponse
   -> RED: the repaired withheld-observation assertion

===========================================================================
OTHER ITEMS
===========================================================================
ITEM 3 (yjb0jq, the Codex note direction) - ALREADY DONE at e8a53f3, VERIFIED
by reading the source, not by trusting the comment. hostcontract/codex_0_146_0.go
now says the source "declares a BLOCKING failure mode for all 7 of its gate rows
while the runtime profile now declares none ... So this source OVER-CLAIMS
blocking relative to the runtime profile; it does not merely simplify it", and
names the runtime profile as the authority. No change made.

ITEM 4 (a4ldt7) - READ, NOT TOUCHED, as instructed. The NotContains that
distinguishes the deadline path from a store-error path is unchanged in both
proofs. It will fire when the retry ceilings become context-aware; that work is
outside this epic.

ITEM 5 (B13 ownership) - each commit names the files it adds to the statement.
New this round, please fold into the slice statement:
  cmd/pasture/hook_lifecycle_orphans.go (new)
  cmd/pasture/hook_lifecycle_orphans_test.go (new)
  internal/handlers/hook_lifecycle_orphans.go (new)
  cmd/pasture/testdata/help-golden/ (hook-lifecycle.txt modified, orphans added)
  internal/lifecycle/receipt/journal.go
  internal/tasks/lifecycle_identity.go
  cmd/pasture/hook_lifecycle_production_test.go
  cmd/pasture/hook_lifecycle_docs_test.go
CHANGELOG.md and AGENTS.md were already listed.

===========================================================================
TWO MORE THINGS I FIXED THAT NOBODY FILED
===========================================================================
A. THE CHANGELOG WAS WRONG AGAIN, THE SAME WAY eu2zu1 WAS (commit 707ba8f).
   The A2 note written at 7ec2940 says pasture answers with the host's own
   carry-on bytes on OpenCode, without exception. That was true when written and
   stopped being true ONE COMMIT EARLIER in the same round: an OpenCode
   observation now writes nothing. It is the same class of defect eu2zu1 filed -
   a truth surface that did not follow the fix under it - so I corrected it
   rather than leave a user to discover it by running the hook. The note now
   separates the two OpenCode surfaces in a user's terms.
B. THE UPDATE_GOLDEN ESCAPE DID NOT EXIST (commit 3bf3c3a). The help-golden
   guard's failure message told a reader to "run UPDATE_GOLDEN=1 go test" and
   nothing implemented it. A reader told to run a command that does nothing
   hand-edits the bytes instead, which is how a golden stops meaning anything.
   It is implemented, writes only when asked, and an ordinary run still cannot
   bless a diff by accident.

===========================================================================
FOR THE NEXT REVIEW ROUND
===========================================================================
- judge the DEVIATION above (orphans as a sibling subcommand, not a footer on
  `list`) and the byte-identical golden that forced it;
- judge the exact operator wording quoted above as a truth claim;
- note that this round's red test means a fix-free clean round has NOT yet
  happened on this slice, and the exit condition still requires one.

text:
SUPERVISOR VERIFICATION of round 3, done independently before round 4.

MEASURED: HEAD 707ba8f, FIVE commits over 7ec2940, worktree CLEAN, NOTHING pushed, NO Beads task closed. The production tier is STILL 5 s and its pin still asserts 5 s, so the trap held. The orphan count exists as a SIBLING SUBCOMMAND (cmd/pasture/hook_lifecycle_orphans.go), not on the listing command.

I INDEPENDENTLY REPRODUCED THE RED BRANCH, on my own archive copy of 7ec2940, before accepting the worker's claim. TestWithheldOpenCodeEventIsNotAdmittedByBuiltCLI FAILED at the inherited HEAD with the diff -{"decision":"proceed"} / +<empty>. So the claim is TRUE: commit ba6bf42 changed what an OpenCode observation fault writes and did NOT update the built-binary proof of it, and the branch sat RED across the usage-limit interruption.

THIS IS A PROCESS FINDING, not only a code one. The round-3 commits that landed before the interruption were committed WITHOUT RUNNING THE GATES. The every-slice rule requires gates on an archive copy, and a worker that commits without them can leave a red branch that the NEXT worker inherits and must diagnose. It cost this round real time. It also means the interrupted worker's own report, had it survived, would have claimed work that did not pass.
WHAT SAVED IT: the fresh worker ran the gates on the INHERITED HEAD rather than only on its own final SHA. That is worth making a rule.

THE REPAIR WAS ON EVIDENCE, NOT BY WEAKENING: session.updated carries surface opencode-catch-all-sse, not opencode-named-output, and the generated plugin already has its own empty-body arm that continues. The gate arm stays pinned at the canonical object. Mutation-RED recorded.

SECOND INHERITED DEFECT: the uncommitted diff DID NOT COMPILE - a missing go/printer import - so NONE of it had ever been run. The worker kept the design, fixed the import, and closed three real gaps: the user-safety reason was a forward pointer instead of sitting AT the declaration; the built-binary proof carried no refusal of the two shortcuts; and nothing said why a supplied profile is not re-validated.

ALSO FIXED AND SELF-REPORTED AS UNFILED: the CHANGELOG A2 note was wrong AGAIN in the same way finding eu2zu1 was - it claimed OpenCode always gets carry-on bytes, which the observation arm had made false one commit earlier. And the help-golden UPDATE_GOLDEN escape was named in a failure message but never implemented.
ITEM yjb0jq was ALREADY CORRECT at e8a53f3; the worker verified the SOURCE rather than the comment and made no change. Item a4ldt7 read and left untouched as instructed.

author: David Huu Pham
text:
TEAM-LEAD DECISIONS on the round-4 arrangements.
1. EPHEMERAL REVIEWERS ACCEPTED for round 4 and for the rest of S0. The Beads record is the continuity. One reviewer holds the gate-runner role. EXPLICIT: do NOT re-engage the old named reviewers if any of them later resolve - ONE TEAM PER WAVE, NO DOUBLE REVIEW.
2. THE INHERITED-SHA RULE IS ADOPTED and is now in IMPL_PLAN section 6: a worker resuming a branch it did not write GATES THE INHERITED SHA on an archive copy BEFORE its own work, and committing without gates is a STOP-AND-REPORT VIOLATION. author: David Huu Pham
text:

aura-plugins-y9mxs6. SHA 707ba8f, reviewed READ-ONLY on my own git archive copy
with one initial commit. I replace the round-1..3 holder of this axis; every

VOTE: REVISE. 0 BLOCKER / 2 IMPORTANT / 2 MINOR.
  IMPORTANT aura-plugins-ccp746 (C4-I1) the orphan note is pinned as a constant

1. internal/timeouts/profile.go:132 ProductionProfile still carries 5s, and
   profile_test.go:122 TestProductionHookInvocationSitsBelowTheSmallestHostBudget

   HookInvocation reference in the tree: profile.go and one call site. NO

ONE JUDGEMENT I RECORD RATHER THAN FILE. The in-process assertion narrowed from
"stopped waiting at its 5s hook-invocation deadline" to "hook-invocation
deadline", and by the standing rule a pin that LOOSENS is a finding until its
mutation is re-run. I rule it NOT a finding, and here is the reasoning so the

=====================================================================

and Reclaimable carry the SAME predicate, byte for byte, in

    lifecycle_payload_blobs b LEFT JOIN lifecycle_occurrences o
    ON o.payload_digest = b.digest WHERE o.journal_id IS NULL
and TestOrphanCountAgreesWithTheEnumerationTheInvariantTestUses asserts the two

(corruption detected / damaged / data loss / inconsistent) is a good addition.

renderer, which nothing reads.

4. THE TWO STANDING CHECKS

COMMENTS AS WELL AS DESCRIPTIONS: done. I read the C-M6 narrowing by its own
author (both halves withdrawn) and check 6b added by reviewer-b, and I judged
against the NARROWED text, not the description.
OWNERSHIP: satisfied as far as a worker can satisfy it. EVERY commit in the
range carries an explicit "Ownership:" paragraph naming what it adds to the
statement, and the round-3 report lists the eight additions for the supervisor
to fold into the slice text. B13 did not recur.

=====================================================================
5. RULING ON THE DEVIATION: THE SUBCOMMAND IS RIGHT. THE LEAF IS SUPERSEDED,
   NOT DEVIATED FROM. NOTHING HAPPENS TO THE GOLDEN.
=====================================================================
I verified BOTH of the worker's reasons rather than accepting them.

(a) TestNativeListReadBackGoldenBytesUnchanged at
cmd/pasture/hook_lifecycle_readback_production_test.go:83 pins `hook lifecycle
list` with require.Equal against a committed baseline in BOTH renderers. The
leaf also requires the count to report ZERO on a clean store, so the line cannot
be conditional. An unconditional footer therefore breaks the text golden AND the
JSON golden, and regenerating them would retire the one invariant that test
exists to hold. Worse than the golden: the JSON golden is a MACHINE-READABLE
RECORD STREAM, and putting a 90-word prose note in it would be wrong even if no
golden existed.

(b) The projection reason is real and it is the stronger of the two.
lifecycle_occurrences is disposable and the count is a LEFT JOIN against it, so
a count taken without a rebuild reports EVERY BLOB AS AN ORPHAN. That is the
exact false alarm the wording exists to prevent, and it also rules out
`manifest`, which documents itself as strictly read-only.

WHAT THE LEAF ACTUALLY REQUIRED. Item 1 offered a CHOICE of home ("the
`pasture lifecycle` readback or `pasture status`"), and its binding constraint

where THE MEASUREMENT CANNOT PERTURB THE MEASUREMENT". The load-bearing property
is being OFF THE HOOK PATH, and a sibling read subcommand in the same lifecycle
read group has that property identically. The sibling is also MORE discoverable
than a footer or a flag, because it appears in `hook lifecycle --help`, which is
now pinned by a golden of its own.

So the leaf text is superseded by a fact it did not have. It needs no
re-litigation and the golden needs no change. THE ONE THING THE SUBCOMMAND COSTS
IS DISCOVERABILITY OUTSIDE `--help`, and that cost is exactly why C4-I2 (the
missing CHANGELOG entry) is IMPORTANT rather than MINOR: choosing the home that
nobody stumbles onto puts the whole weight of discovery on the release note.

=====================================================================
- THE RED-BRANCH REPAIR IS ON EVIDENCE. I verified the mechanism in the SOURCE,
  not in the comment: internal/runtime/lifecycle_profiles.go builds every
  OpenCode row through two constructors, openCodeNamedMapping (gate + named

- THE CHANGELOG A2 SENTENCE IS NOW TRUE against that same structure: the named
  callbacks get the carry-on bytes and the watched stream gets nothing.
- THE UPDATE_GOLDEN ESCAPE IS REAL AND SAFE. It writes only on UPDATE_GOLDEN=1
  and an ordinary run cannot bless a diff. NOT A FINDING, one observation for the

  failure messages tell the reader "UPDATE_GOLDEN=1", which works for both, so no

- The command creates a database on a fresh path, exactly as `hook lifecycle
  list` does. Existing convention, not this slice.
- No Git hook, no core.hooksPath, no time.Sleep, no internal process reference in
  any shipped .go or .ts file in this range.

=====================================================================
7. EXIT CONDITION
=====================================================================
NOT MET. This round applied no fixes, so a clean round would have closed S0; it
is not clean. Two IMPORTANT and two MINOR stand. A fix round is needed, and then
