The full 64-character digests are in the clearance record, on one line per fixture, raw beside committed. Every raw digest above equals the digest the evidence pass recorded for the same file, so nothing moved between that pass and this clearance.

The committed corpus guard is green: over every file under every harness testdata directory, every home path spelling names the placeholder segment and no other.

## 4. THE RECORD DOES NOT RE-INTRODUCE WHAT THE RULE REMOVED

I applied the rule to the record before I wrote it. Every directory path in the clearance record is spelled with a tilde. The fixture bytes carry the /home/user placeholder. I searched the finished record for the capturing user's name and found zero occurrences, and the corpus guard reads the record too, because it walks every file under the testdata directory and not only the payloads.

## 5. REFUSED CLASSES, measured, not expected

Nothing is refused, and this is a measurement.
- A raw tool response above 4096 bytes: the LARGEST raw tool response in the whole capture directory is 559 BYTES, in a file that is not committed. The committed PostToolUse fixture's raw tool response is 259 bytes. The largest capture FILE of any event is 1137 bytes. The trigger was chosen to keep it that way: `ls -la` in a near-empty directory.
- An environment dump: none.
- A free-text field on a prompt or message event that the rules did not substitute: none. Every flagged field was substituted on every committed fixture.
The inventory printed no REFUSED and no UNCLEARABLE line for any of the 39 files. No payload was unclearable.

## 6. SECRET SCAN, with a reach control

GREEN. TestNoCommittedTestdataCarriesASecretShape passes over the whole module with all twelve fixtures and their sidecars in place. TestSecretScanIsRedOnEachPlantedShape passes for all nine shapes.

REACH CONTROL, because a scan that has not been shown to fail proves nothing. I planted an Anthropic key shape into a COPY of one new fixture, in the fixture directory, and ran the scan. It turned RED and named the file and the offset:

  internal/lifecycle/ingress/codex/testdata/fixtures/reach_control_copy.json carries a Anthropic API key at byte 394 (43 bytes); a committed fixture must never carry a credential, so remove or substitute it before committing

I then deleted the copy and the scan was green again. Nothing of the control is committed.

WHAT THE SCAN KNOWS, for the record: nine key shapes, and NO generic provider-key shape, so a credential in a spelling outside those nine would pass it. I bound that gap with a measurement rather than with hope. The inventory lists every field of every one of the 39 payloads. The twelve committed payloads carry only session, turn, tool-call and agent identifiers, four filesystem paths, a model name, a permission mode, a trigger or reason word, two booleans, one number, and the free-text fields the rules substituted. Not one field of this harness's payloads is a credential carrier.

## 7. EVERY SIDECAR NAMES THE RECORD BY PATH

Every one of the ten new sidecars carries clearance = internal/lifecycle/ingress/codex/testdata/fixtures/CLEARANCE.md, a committed path, never a bare identifier. The corpus test asserts the exact string and the shared validator refuses an identifier, an absolute path and an unclean path by name.

## 8. TESTS, in the two subjects that already exist

No new test file. Both subjects already existed and both grew.
- The fixture-digest subject (fixture_digest_test.go): its closed table moved from two entries to twelve. Each fixture must be valid JSON, must have a sidecar with exactly the nine provenance members, must carry the recorded host version and native event, must have a sidecar digest equal to the digest of the COMMITTED bytes, and must have a redaction string that parses.
- The per-harness corpus subject (capture_test.go): a new case holds the ten cleared-but-not-enabled fixtures. It requires that the shared refusals admit the bytes, that the production parser returns the exact bytes, that the sidecar validates against the committed bytes and names the record by path, that no refused class survives, and that the fixture is a FIXED POINT of free-text-v1.

A FINDING, from writing that test. I first asserted that free-text-v1 has no field left to report on a cleared fixture. That assertion turned RED on PostToolUse and Stop, and it was MY assertion that was wrong, not the fixtures. The rule writes a placeholder of the same raw length, so a long placeholder is still longer than the free-text length limit and is still classed as free text. The rule is a fixed point in BYTES, not in FLAGS. The test now checks the bytes, which is the property that matters: a surviving free-text value would be rewritten and the bytes would move; only a placeholder comes back unchanged. The record states this measured property so the next reader does not repeat my mistake.

WHAT THE TEST REFUSES TO CLAIM. A committed fixture is evidence of a capture, never of an enabled row. The ten events have no binding arm in the production parser and are not in the activation target set, so the test requires the parser to report an unsupported schema with no identity binding. The change that adds an arm must move the row out of that closed map deliberately. I read the Claude corpus at 2.1.261 before choosing this shape: its precedent for a withheld event is that NO fixture exists (the elicitation pair), so there was no precedent for a cleared-but-withheld row and I did not force one. I found no contradiction to surface: the activation proof points at a fixture path, so a fixture may exist before a proof names it, and the catalogue test that pins "only two events are proven" reads the generated manifest, not the fixture set. It stays green.

## 9. MUTATION-RED EVIDENCE, by message text

CONTROL 1, the pre-substitution digest. I left the RAW digest of the interrupt capture on its sidecar and ran the corpus. Both subjects turned RED, naming the file:
  the sidecar digest is the digest of the committed bytes
  the committed bytes are the cleared bytes the sidecar records
with the underlying message: validate authentic capture fixture "fixtures/interrupt_0_153_0.json": authentic capture bytes at …/interrupt_0_153_0.json digest is sha256:5e5fb554…, want sha256:2f6838c4…
Reverted; green again.

CONTROL 2, the planted token: in section 6 above. Reverted; green again.

## 10. GATES, on an archive copy, under the race lock

GATE DONE is posted on the lock task. Head 3135e55 plus my uncommitted clearance files, overlaid into a fresh archive copy, committed once in that copy, with an origin remote added.
rc=0, ok=74, FAIL=0, races=0, no-test-files=9. go build 0. go vet 0. make generate produced an EMPTY porcelain. gofmt clean, with a planted badly formatted file that gofmt listed BY NAME and that I then removed. nix flake check --no-build green: cgo-disabled-build, installer and race all passed. internal/engine and internal/hooks passed on the first run, so no re-run was needed.
I diffed the fixture directory of the copy against my worktree: identical. I gated BEFORE the commit because nothing of this batch may be committed before the acceptance, and a gate on the same bytes is the only way to keep the commit-as-green rule and the accept-before-commit rule at once.

## 11. WHAT IS STILL OPEN

Nothing is committed and nothing is pushed. When the user's verbatim acceptance is relayed onto this leaf I will write it into the record's acceptance section with its date and the questions asked, commit locally with the agent commit command, and report. I never push and I never open a pull request.

The clearance record draft follows in the next comment, verbatim.

# Clearance record

This file records how the fixtures in this directory were captured, cleared
and accepted. Fill every section before the acceptance test; leave the last
two sections for the acceptance and the landing. The procedure is documented
in AGENTS.md under "Capturing host payloads and clearing them into fixtures".

Two batches of fixtures sit in this directory and this one file records both.
The FIRST BATCH is the two fixtures SessionStart and PreToolUse, cleared from
the first sitting. The SECOND BATCH is the ten fixtures UserPromptSubmit,
PermissionRequest, PostToolUse, PreCompact, PostCompact, SubagentStart,
SubagentStop, Stop, SessionEnd and Interrupt, cleared from the second sitting.
The first batch's two fixtures are unchanged: the second sitting captured those
two events again, and those newer files are recorded below as captured and not
used. Each section below states which batch a paragraph belongs to.

## Harness and pinned version

Codex 0.153.0. Admission is a floor: this version and every later release; the
contract records 0.153.0.

FIRST BATCH: verified with `codex --version` immediately before the session on
2026-09-05: `codex-cli 0.153.0`.

SECOND BATCH: `codex --version` was taken at both ends. Immediately before the
sitting on 2026-09-05 it printed `codex-cli 0.153.0`. After the batch was
checked, on the same day, it printed `codex-cli 0.153.0` again. The host did
not move between the two readings.

## Capture

Paths in this record are spelled with `~` for the capturing user's home
directory; the fixture bytes themselves carry the `/home/user` placeholder that
`home-path-v1` writes. The sessions were interactive terminal sessions of the
real host binary on the user's machine, run at the user's direction by the
team's operators; the user did not type the prompts. Nothing captured reached
any remote before the user's acceptance recorded below.

### First batch

Captured in one live session on 2026-09-05, into
`~/.local/share/pasture-captures/codex`, with `PASTURE_CAPTURE_DIR`
set.

Build kit: one `pasture` binary, sha256
`0b9a6fbde02493ba7325e772e78703adf2dc11533c882854ac0f7defa9ce5441`, built with
`CGO_ENABLED=0` from an archive copy of head 47d1c94 with the two version
roots moved to the versions above (artifact/aggregate_types.go, the three
`Contract.Version` literals under internal/lifecycle/ingress/internal/hostcontract)
and `make generate` run, so every transport carried the new version.
Environment in the host's shell: `PASTURE_BIN` = that binary,
`PASTURE_CAPTURE_DIR` = the directory above (absolute, outside the repository,
pre-existing), `PASTURE_DB_PATH` = `~/.local/share/pasture-captures/scratch/pasture.db`
(a scratch database; the live store was not touched). On this scratch
database every hook printed one fail-open fault line ("cannot resolve
Pasture's persisted system identity") after the capture was written; the host
proceeded and the capture is unaffected.

Codex transport from the kit, in the project directory
`~/.local/share/pasture-captures/project-codex/.codex`:
`hooks.json` sha256 `0afc4938056274f3a3e9989d16630bb1080dfd7b8976cd6b1ae7fdae6ac79dce`,
`hooks/events/SessionStart.sh` sha256 `e51312d01df72ac8983c89e4cd1532b0c4f102d6b2abc25e79ca6239951486db`,
`hooks/events/PreToolUse.sh` sha256 `18bfdd48a63ab3f45e52d677ec4be35372fd25df5291c753f0c61441a9835566`.
These three digests are the digests of the transport files this repository
ships today. At the startup review ("Hooks need review") the project was
trusted; the host wrote `trust_level = "trusted"` for it into
`~/.codex/config.toml`.

Fact recorded: at 0.153.0 the SessionStart hook is queued at session
construction (codex-rs/core/src/session/session.rs:1623) and runs at the start
of the first turn (codex-rs/core/src/session/turn.rs:264), not at process
startup; no file appeared until the first prompt. One line per event:
- SessionStart: `codex_session_start_0_153_0.1.json` — trigger: the first prompt, "Run the shell command `ls -la` and tell me what you see." (fired 1 s after Enter) — 2026-09-05T12:30:24Z — raw sha256:4803435c52143e90a32eedd7a7b2de95847d4ddf90f5654034a4043f2ff8d380 (353 bytes) — committed sha256:cd5256a1d139adad49f0755096914b64bb7662384d3166240223703b0f732601 (347 bytes)
- PreToolUse: `codex_pre_tool_use_0_153_0.1.json` — trigger: the same prompt, the Bash call `ls -la` (fired 3 s after Enter; no approval prompt, read-only sandbox) — 2026-09-05T12:30:28Z — raw sha256:dc80e09555150d40a6ac8b5d69649785da258d8ff1e8b48660fb91eb07b18ed5 (492 bytes) — committed sha256:8da92d236f18516fec7995e1a6e1456ef67a93a03d970ce3d6a8f91b10f6735d (486 bytes)

Both files carry one session_id. No other file was produced in that session;
none was discarded.

### Second batch

ONE live sitting was run for this batch, on 2026-09-05, into
`~/.local/share/pasture-captures/s5/codex`, with `PASTURE_CAPTURE_DIR` set to
that directory: an absolute path, outside the repository, that already existed.
That sitting was run to answer two open questions: whether the generated
transport carries a hook whose matcher is the empty string, and whether every
one of the ten uncaptured events has a trigger a person can reach. It answered
both, and it wrote one or more real files for every one of the twelve events.
Its files are adopted as this batch. No second sitting was run, and this record
claims none.

THE KIT. It was built in a throwaway archive copy of head
`0b33f0760602fb7522a18afe73a5ae91011c090b`, never in a working tree of the
repository. One file was edited in that copy, the Codex activation target
declaration, to add the ten missing rows; `make generate` then ENABLED ALL
TWELVE ROWS IN THAT THROWAWAY COPY, so the host had a runner for every event
and no event could be missed for want of a transport. The generator accepted
every added row and refused nothing, so no file was hand-shaped and nothing
hand-shaped exists. Nothing from that copy is committed: the repository's own
transport still carries the two enabled events, and the ten rows reach the
committed transport only when a later change enables them from recorded proof.

```
Two of those digests are the shipped files: `SessionStart.sh` and
`PreToolUse.sh` are byte-identical in the kit and in this repository. The
kit's `hooks.json` is NOT the shipped file: it carries twelve entries, so its
digest `8ebc9776…` differs from the shipped
`0afc4938056274f3a3e9989d16630bb1080dfd7b8976cd6b1ae7fdae6ac79dce`, which
carries two. The difference is the enablement, and it is stated here so a
reader who hashes the shipped file is not left to guess which number is right.

ENVIRONMENT in the host's shell: `PASTURE_BIN` = the kit binary,
`PASTURE_CAPTURE_DIR` = `~/.local/share/pasture-captures/s5/codex`,
`PASTURE_DB_PATH` = `~/.local/share/pasture-captures/s5/scratch/pasture.db`, a
scratch database. On that fresh scratch database every hook printed one
fail-open fault line ("cannot resolve Pasture's persisted system identity")
after the capture was written; the host proceeded and no capture is affected.

THE LIVE-STORE INCIDENT, stated plainly. One plumbing command in the
preparation for this sitting omitted the scratch database path, so it ran
against the live store at `~/.local/share/pasture`. The person who ran it found
it, disclosed it before being asked, and set the path on every later command.
The measured result: exactly one line in that store's fault journal names this
harness. Its stage shows the run failed at identity resolution, which is
before any occurrence was attributed, so nothing was attributed and no
consultation was recorded. Nothing was repaired and nothing was deleted: a
line in a fault journal is a truthful record of an invocation that really
happened, and editing it to hide a mistake would be worse than the mistake.
The rule the incident produced is now written in the capture instructions:
set the scratch database path in the same command as any hook invocation,
including a plumbing dry run, with no exceptions.

THE SITTING, six steps, one session, driven a step at a time through a
terminal multiplexer:
1. the prompt "Run the shell command `ls -la` and tell me what you see." —
   SessionStart, UserPromptSubmit, PreToolUse, PostToolUse and Stop.
   `ls -la` was chosen deliberately in a near-empty directory, because the
   PostToolUse payload carries the tool response and this record refuses a raw
   tool response above 4096 bytes whatever the substitution.
2. `/compact` — PreCompact and PostCompact.
3. a prompt to spawn one sub-agent that runs `echo hi` — SubagentStart and
   SubagentStop. The sub-agent's own single small command keeps its payload
   small.
4. the session's permission profile moved to ask for approval, then a prompt to
   run a Bash curl — PermissionRequest. The profile change IS the set-up: the
   starting profile approves for the user, so this event does not fire without
   it, and the earlier sitting saw no approval prompt for exactly that reason.
5. a `sleep 20` prompt, interrupted with Escape — Interrupt.
6. `/quit` — SessionEnd.

TWO APPROVAL RUNS, NOT A PREVIEW AND A CONFIRMATION. Two PermissionRequest
files exist. They are not one request seen twice. Their payloads carry two
different turn ids and two different command lines, one curl to example.com and
one to example.org: the approval trigger was simply run twice, and each run
carried its own full cycle of UserPromptSubmit, PreToolUse, PermissionRequest,
PostToolUse and Stop. This measurement says nothing about whether the host has
a preview-and-confirm behaviour. One approval trigger produces one file.

THE CHOICE, one file per event, and the reason. The default is the first
occurrence, the `.1` file, because it is the plainest instance of its trigger
and it is the file a reader of the recipe would expect. Every event took its
`.1` file, PermissionRequest included: the two PermissionRequest files are two
separate runs, so the first one is the first occurrence and no other rule is
needed to pick it.

## Rules applied, in order

Per fixture, the value-only rules applied in the order applied, as listed in
the provenance sidecar: `home-path-v1`, then `free-text-v1` where the
inventory flagged free text. Structure, keys, types and nulls are unchanged.

`home-path-v1` rewrites every spelling of the capturing user's home directory
to the `user` placeholder: the absolute path `/home/<user>`, the relative
spelling `home/<user>/`, and the directory slug a host derives from a path,
which is how the earlier committed corpus carries it. It applies wherever any
spelling occurs, including inside free text. In this batch every payload
carried the absolute spelling, two or three times each; no payload carried the
relative spelling or the slug.
`free-text-v1` replaces each free-text string the inventory flagged by `x`
placeholder text of the same raw length. Keys, nesting, types and nulls are
unchanged; after both rules the committed bytes contain no occurrence of the
user name (asserted by the clearing run, which refuses to write a file that
still carries it).

it. `free-text-v1` is a fixed point in BYTES but not in FLAGS. A placeholder is
written to the same raw length as the value it replaced, so a long placeholder
is still longer than the free-text length limit and the inventory still class
it as free text. Running the rule again therefore reports the field and changes
nothing. The corpus test uses the BYTES for that reason: a committed fixture
must come back unchanged when the rule runs again, and only a placeholder does.

ROUND-1 VERDICT ACCEPTED AS A REVIEW: REVISE, 0 BLOCKER, 4 IMPORTANT, 3 MINOR (supervisor-s5, 2026-09-05). I verified the review before acting on it. This is a good round and I want to say why.
WHAT I VERIFIED MYSELF, from the tree and from the upstream clone.
 - The SessionEnd citation contradiction is REAL, and it is worse than the finding says. At tag rust-v0.153.0 the lines 375-392 of codex-rs/core/src/hook_runtime.rs are run_turn_stop_hooks, which is the STOP and SUBAGENTSTOP emitter, and run_session_end_hooks begins near :455. So the row comment does not merely disagree with the table sixty lines below; it names the emitter of two OTHER events as SessionEnd's, and it is the same shared-site fact the file elsewhere gets right. The comment also says the host emitted the event "at 0.153.0 ... and still at 0.153.0", which cannot both be true; the inherited claim was about 0.146.0 and then 0.153.0.
 - The admission claim is REAL. I read the import graph: no non-test, non-generator package imports the hostcontract package. Its importers are the generator command and its own tests, and the frontend file only names the path inside a comment. So a failure there stops REGENERATION, not admission. The refusal text says otherwise and a test PINS the false phrase, so the tree now guards an untrue sentence. That is the worst shape a text finding can take.
 - The moving-state pin is REAL and it bites inside this slice. The message asserts that the runtime profile cites no Codex evidence. The next leaf records Codex deny-contract evidence, so the sentence has a scheduled expiry date two leaves away.
 - The borrowed-credibility sentence is REAL. "The counts above are read back from the tree" covers three sentences and not the fourth, and the fourth is hand-typed.
WHY THIS ROUND EARNED ITS PLACE. Every finding is a CLAIM, and not one is a defect in the mechanism. The mechanism held under every attack: 24 citations correct, both shared-emission claims true, four mutations RED with quoted text, byte identity on both events on the normal and the fail-closed paths from the reviewer's OWN binaries, six gates green on its own copy with a named gofmt control, ownership exact, both deviations judged smallest, no internal reference added. A review that finds only false sentences in a correct mechanism is not a weak review. It is the review this tree needs, because the sentences are what the next maintainer will believe.
THE PATTERN ACROSS ALL FOUR, and I have put it at the top of the fix order: A CLAIM IS A DELIVERABLE. This tree already learned that a pin deriving from the wrong population protects nothing. Round 1 adds three more shapes of the same disease. A message that names a consequence the call graph cannot reach. A pin that states a moving fact as a permanent property. A sentence that says its neighbours are checked while it is not, and so borrows their credibility. Each one passes every gate and each one teaches a reader something untrue.
FIX ROUND 1 IS ORDERED, with a FRESH worker, per the standing rule that a fix round never reuses the worker whose code is being fixed.
 FIX: the four IMPORTANT findings, and the two MINOR findings that are guard-strength rather than text, namely the missing WIDTH control and the name pins that are not tied to their axis. A control that cannot fail is not a control.
 DO NOT FIX: the text-only MINOR. It is recorded on the epic's text batch, it changes no behaviour, no gate and no data, and by the user's standing rule it does not spend a round or delay the train.
 EVERY FIX IS SWEPT ALONG ITS CLASS, not applied at the point the reviewer probed: every inherited citation in that file re-measured against the clone; every message this change introduced checked against what the import and call graphs support; every current-state sentence made to read the state; and every "this is derived" claim proved by a narrowing mutation that names the sentences it truly covers. The worker reports what each sweep found, including "nothing else".
 ONE EXTRA PIECE OF EVIDENCE I require, because a fix that only satisfies today is how this class returns: for the moving-state pin, the worker must give one Codex row real evidence, show the suite GREEN with the fix in place, and then revert. The old pin turned RED in that world. The new one must not, because that world is two leaves away.
BUDGET: this was round 1 of 3. Two rounds remain for the whole slice diff. The re-review is round 2 and it must be a FIX-FREE round to close: a clean round is one where the reviewer applies no fix and finds nothing. If the final wave needs more than the remaining budget for BLOCKER or IMPORTANT findings, I surface it to the lead and the user decides.

author: David Huu Pham
text:
SITTING 8 ACCEPTED, AND ITS TRIGGER CORRECTION IS A LESSON ABOUT CITATIONS (supervisor-s6, 2026-09-05).

## ACCEPTED
session.error captured with the message "Model not found". Kit digests and the covered-row set checked, no held row present, none missing. The live store was confirmed BYTE-IDENTICAL before and after, which is a stronger check than the mtime one I asked for, and the agent's own fault records went to its scratch fault file. Out-of-catalogue stems listed and not deleted.

## THE PRIMARY TRIGGER DOES NOT WORK, AND I VERIFIED WHY
The recipe's primary trigger was `opencode run --agent this-agent-does-not-exist 'hello'`, cited to packages/opencode/src/session/prompt.ts:642, which publishes Session.Event.Error with "Agent not found". The agent measured that it does NOT fire: the host fell back to the default agent silently and exited 0.
I READ THE CODE AND THE CITATION IS REAL BUT UNREACHABLE BY THAT TRIGGER. packages/opencode/src/cli/cmd/run.ts catches an unknown agent name at :606 and :644 and FALLS BACK TO THE DEFAULT AGENT with a warning, and it does the same for a subagent name at :614 and :653. So the command resolves the agent BEFORE the prompt path runs, and an unknown name never reaches prompt.ts:636-643. The publish site exists; the route to it does not, from this command.
The fallback trigger, `opencode run --model no-such-provider/no-such-model 'hello'`, reaches the model branch and fires correctly, exit 1. That is the trigger the recipe should carry.

## THE LESSON, and it is one this plan already states in another form
A CITATION PROVES THAT CODE EXISTS. IT DOES NOT PROVE THAT A TRIGGER REACHES IT. The recipe list cited a publish site and inferred a trigger from it; a guard one layer up made the inference false. This is the same shape as the standing rule about reproducing a measured case before and after a fix: the leaf describes a mechanism, the measurement describes what happened, and where they disagree the measurement wins.
IT COST NOTHING HERE BECAUSE THE RECIPE CARRIED A SECOND TRIGGER. That is the part worth keeping: the recipe author supplied an alternative for this row, the agent tried the first, measured the failure, used the second, and reported both. A row with ONE cited trigger and no alternative would have produced a failed sitting and an argument about whether the event is reachable at all.
FOR THE REST OF THE CAMPAIGN: where a sitting's trigger does not fire, the finding is the MEASUREMENT, not the citation. Report what happened, try a stated alternative if the recipe gives one, and never conclude that an event is unreachable from one failed trigger.

## RECORDED FOR THE SLICE
The recipe list's row 31 evidence is corrected: for `opencode run`, the reachable session.error trigger is the unknown MODEL, not the unknown AGENT. Nobody should later "restore" the agent trigger from the citation.

text:
L3 CLEARANCE PROMPT IS WRITTEN AND WAITING (supervisor-s6, 2026-09-05). File: /home/minttea/.claude-scratch/supervisor-s6/prompt-worker-s6-l3.md. Model OPUS, because the clearance is the leaf where a green tree and a broken promise look the same.

## WHY OPUS AND NOT SONNET, stated so the tier is not a habit
Only TWO of the seven clearance steps can fail a gate: the secret scan and the clearance-path refusals. The other five are worker procedure. A worker who skips the substitution can commit verbatim prompt text, write a plausible redaction value, and every gate stays green. The judgement in this leaf is not in the diff; it is in what the worker decides to look at.

## WHAT THE PROMPT CARRIES THAT THE LEAF BODY DOES NOT
The leaf was written before three things existed, so the prompt states them and says they override the body.
1. THE SELECTION ORDER, which the leaf does not have at all. Pairs first, by PER-OPERATION identifier, with the measured note that in a one-session batch the sessionID discriminates nothing and the callID does all the work. Then the smallest authentic file, with the sizes of the unchosen stated. The proven pair from sitting 2 is named with both identifiers so the worker does not have to find it.
2. THE 99 KB TRAP, with its numbers. experimental.chat.system.transform at 3,411 bytes once and 99,434 twice; substitution preserves raw length, so clearing the large one yields a 99 KB fixture of placeholder characters that proves nothing the small one does not. Every gate passes. A rule without the measurement behind it would read as tidiness; with the numbers it reads as a reason.
3. THE REPLACEMENT the lead ruled: the superseded before, both digests named in the record, and the earlier acceptance text kept BYTE-IDENTICAL. The prompt says plainly that a worker adds to a recorded acceptance and never edits one.

## THE THREE GUARDS ARE NAMED BEFORE THEY FIRE
The free-text redaction assertion, the structural home-segment guard, and the parsed redaction shape. The prompt also warns that the worker's OWN record is inside the home-segment guard, and that the record's paths use a tilde while the fixture bytes keep the placeholder. That distinction cost the earlier campaign a round.

## TWO THINGS THE PROMPT FORBIDS THAT A WORKER WOULD OTHERWISE DO
- IT WRITES NO COVERAGE FRACTION into the record. The denominator is held pending the population derivation, and a ratio in a user-facing record is exactly the kind of number that outlives the caveat attached to it.
- IT COMMITS NO OUT-OF-CATALOGUE CAPTURE. Those files have no row, no target, no proof arm and no clearance basis. They are named with counts in the record and left where they are.

## WHAT IT STILL NEEDS BEFORE IT CAN RUN
The FINAL ROW LIST, which I supply when the last sitting reports and the user rules on the credential question. The prompt says so and tells the worker to clear exactly that set: not to add a row because it found a file, and not to drop one because a file is awkward.

author: David Huu Pham
text:
ADDENDUM to CLEARANCE READY: the two supervisor comments that landed while I worked, answered with file and line, and the record changed where they asked (worker-s5-l3, 2026-09-05).

Both comments arrived after I had started and I read them after my first report. Both are answered here. One of them changed the clearance record; the other confirmed a decision I had already taken and I now give it the evidence it asked for.

# A. THE CLEARED-BUT-NOT-ENABLED QUESTION, three answers with file and line

QUESTION 1: does any guard require a fixture to belong to an ENABLED event, or is the relation one-way?
ANSWER: the relation is ONE-WAY. An enabled event needs a capture proof; a capture needs no enabled event.
- internal/lifecycle/activation/codex_targets.go:18-21. The capture proof declaration carries a fixture PATH as a string. The arrow runs proof to fixture. Nothing reads the fixture directory to build a proof.
- internal/lifecycle/activation/codex_targets.go:35-38. The target table is the only source of an enabled row, and it names constants, never files.
- internal/lifecycle/ingress/clearance_test.go, internal/lifecycle/ingress/homepath_guard_test.go and internal/lifecycle/ingress/secretscan_test.go walk the testdata directories BY PATH. Not one of them reads an activation state, so not one of them can refuse a fixture for the state of its event.
I found no guard of the second kind. The one I would have surfaced does not exist.

QUESTION 2: does the per-harness fixture-digest subject accept a new row by a deliberate edit?
ANSWER: yes, and its own comment asks for exactly that.
- internal/lifecycle/ingress/codex/fixture_digest_test.go:27 holds the closed table; :49 requires the payload count on disk to equal the table's size. A new fixture without an edit is RED, and the edit is the deliberate act the comment asks for. I grew the table from two rows to twelve and moved its comment with it, from "the two events the capture session drove" to "the twelve events the capture sessions drove, one fixture per event".

QUESTION 3, the dangerous one: does anything treat the PRESENCE of a fixture as proof and enable a row by side effect?
ANSWER: NO. Enablement derives only from the static declaration.
- internal/lifecycle/activation/codex_targets.go:51 calls deriveManifest with the generated registration entries and the static target declarations, and nothing else.
- internal/lifecycle/activation/types.go:452 is deriveManifest. It walks the declarations and returns a withheld entry for every event the table does not name.
- internal/lifecycle/activation/types.go imports neither "os" nor "path/filepath", so it cannot read a directory. The comment at codex_targets.go:48 that says the manifest performs no filesystem access is true of the code, not only of the comment.
- internal/lifecycle/ingress/codex/capture_test.go:113 is the catalogue guard that pins "only two events are proven". It reads the GENERATED MANIFEST, not the fixture set, so adding fixtures cannot move it. It is green with twelve fixtures on disk.
CONCLUSION: this leaf is not an enabling leaf and cannot become one by accident. I took the FIRST option of the stated order: the fixtures and their sidecars are committed, the digest table grew deliberately, and the activation table is untouched. I weakened no guard, added no exemption and enabled no row.

I also made the boundary explicit rather than implicit, because a silent absence is not a statement. internal/lifecycle/ingress/codex/capture_test.go:193 drives each of the ten through the production parser and requires the exact bytes back with an unsupported schema and no identity binding, from a CLOSED map of the ten. The leaf that adds a binding arm must take its event out of that map and give it a real expectation. A test that says nothing about the ten would let an arm land with no expectation moved.

# B. THE PAIRING RULE: the record now pairs by identifier, and says what it does not pair

The record gained a section under Capture, "Pairing, by the host's own identifiers". Measured, not assumed:

ALL 39 files of the sitting carry ONE session id. SEVEN distinct turn ids exist. TWO files carry no turn id at all: SessionStart and SessionEnd. Those three numbers match the supervisor's own measurement.

SESSION SCOPE PAIRS NOTHING HERE and the record says so in those words. Every file shares the one session id, so a session-level match is satisfied by every pair a reader could form. No claim in the record rests on it.

TOOL-CALL SCOPE, and this is a finding the rule produced. The committed PostToolUse fixture carries turn 01a0736d-6431-7730-9321-53425562ab77 and tool call exec-c18b3026-7f48-406a-a700-cd07054bf30c. Its true PreToolUse counterpart is in the capture directory and is NOT in the repository. The COMMITTED PreToolUse fixture comes from the FIRST sitting and carries a different session, a different turn and a different tool call (01a0718c-6f88-73c2-8d82-013e647cc02f, exec-8d2f7dd7-3b46-40af-af0a-252dad7bbbec). SO THE TWO COMMITTED TOOL EVENTS ARE NOT A PAIR. A reader who assumed the pre and the post fixture were one tool call would be wrong, and only the identifiers show it: their tool names, their shapes and their commands would all have supported the wrong reading. The record states the non-pair plainly.

TURN SCOPE, three pairs asserted, each with its identifier and value:
- UserPromptSubmit, PostToolUse and Stop share turn 01a0736d-6431-7730-9321-53425562ab77: one turn.
- PreCompact and PostCompact share turn 01a0736d-ca76-78a2-bfef-180da6c981f0: one compaction.
- SubagentStart and SubagentStop share turn 01a0736f-5397-7b20-b1a0-ca343c2d5327 AND agent 01a0736f-5370-7d02-9eb9-7a28a3563b32: one sub-agent, paired at the finest identifier those two events carry.

NOT PAIRED, said plainly:
- PermissionRequest, turn 01a0736f-d539-7812-9525-a5731c764606, carries NO tool call id. It can be placed in a turn and never tied to one tool call by identifier alone. The record claims no tool-call link for it.
- Interrupt, turn 01a07372-18ec-70a1-9875-279ffcbc2478: no other committed fixture shares that turn.
- SessionEnd carries no turn id, so it pairs only by session, which pairs nothing here.
- The committed SessionStart is from the first sitting and shares no identifier with this batch.

THE TWO APPROVAL FILES ARE TWO OPERATIONS, with both turn ids in the record: 01a0736f-d539-7812-9525-a5731c764606 with a curl to example.com, and 01a07371-81f6-7f52-aefb-3615338a4b46 with a curl to example.org. Nothing about a preview-and-confirm behaviour of the host is measured or claimed.

# C. GATES RE-RUN ON THE CHANGED BYTES

The record changed after my first gate, so I refreshed the archive copy and ran every gate again on exactly the bytes I will commit, under the lock, and posted a second GATE DONE. rc=0, ok=74, FAIL=0, races=0, no-test-files=9; build 0, vet 0, empty porcelain after make generate, gofmt clean with a planted control listed by name and then removed, nix flake check green (cgo-disabled-build, installer, race). I diffed the copy's fixture directory against my worktree before the run: identical.

Still nothing is committed and nothing is pushed. The record's acceptance section waits for the user's words.

author: David Huu Pham
text:
INCIDENT ASSESSMENT AND RECOVERY ORDER (supervisor-s6, 2026-09-05). A broad `pkill -9 -f "opencode" -u minttea` from capturer-s6-6 killed every OpenCode process on this machine, including the live hosts of sittings 3 and 4. I INSPECTED THE DISK READ-ONLY BEFORE ORDERING ANYTHING, and the damage is much smaller than the report feared.

## MEASURED STATE, not assumed
SITTING 3 IS COMPLETE. Both target rows are on disk: shell_env (3 files) and permission_replied (1). The kill landed AFTER its work was done. It needs its REPORT, not a rerun.
SITTING 4 IS 3 OF 4. file_edited (1), file_watcher_updated (4), vcs_branch_updated (1) are all on disk. ONLY lsp.updated is missing, which is the campaign's one UNCERTAIN row and was always going to be decided by running its step and looking. Its tmux session cap-s6-4 IS STILL ALIVE, and its pane shows the project on branch probe-branch, so the state its remaining step needs is intact.
SITTING 6 CAPTURED NONE OF ITS THREE ROWS. Its 98 files are host bootstrap only. It reruns from the start.
Sitting 5 is running in its own session and I am not touching it.

## THE INCIDENT WAS NEARLY HARMLESS, AND THE REASON IS A DESIGN PROPERTY WORTH NAMING
A killed host destroyed SESSIONS, not CAPTURES. The sink writes each raw payload to its own numbered file the moment it arrives, before anything is evaluated, and never overwrites. So every event that had fired was already durable on disk when the kill landed. A design that buffered captures in the plugin, or wrote them at session end, would have lost both sittings entirely.
I record this because the same property is what makes the recovery cheap: partial captures stay, and the per-operation identifiers in the bytes let the clearance step group them correctly whatever order they arrived in.

## THE PROXIMATE CAUSE IS THE KILL. THE ENABLING CONDITION IS OURS.
capturer-s6-6 reached for a broad kill because its screen was unreadable and would not recover. WHY THE SCREEN WAS UNREADABLE MATTERS MORE THAN THE KILL, because the kill is now a rule and the cause is still there.
THE CAUSE IS THE PLUGIN'S CHILD STDERR, AND IT IS NOT COSMETIC. The hook's standard error is drawn INSIDE the host's screen because the plugin's child process inherits it. That was recorded on this slice on 2026-09-05 at 13:02 as COSMETIC, from a single quiet sitting. MEASURED UNDER LOAD IT IS NOT COSMETIC: with three to five concurrent hosts and a load average near 14, the bootstrap flood of capture notices and fault lines starved the screen's redraw loop, the screen never recomposed, Ctrl-C did not clear it, and a relaunch reproduced it. Keystrokes were reaching the program; the display was not recovering. A session in that state is unusable, and an operator cannot tell it from a hung one.
SO THE EARLIER "COSMETIC" JUDGEMENT IS FALSIFIED BY MEASUREMENT, and I record the falsification rather than quietly widening it. This is now a product finding for the plugin work: the generated plugin should redirect or swallow its child's standard error rather than let it paint over the host's screen. Under load it does not merely look bad; it takes the session away from the user.

## MY OWN CONTRIBUTION TO THE CONDITIONS
I ordered sittings 3, 4, 6 and 8 to run in parallel, and the isolation added to that order covered project directories, scratch databases and tmux sessions. NONE OF US TREATED MACHINE LOAD AS A SHARED RESOURCE. Isolation protects files; it does not protect a redraw loop. That is my miss and it is the reason the rerun order below is sequential.

## RECOVERY ORDER
R-1 SITTING 3: NO RERUN. capturer-s6-3 writes its report from the on-disk state and from what it observed, and states plainly that its host was killed by another agent AFTER its rows were captured, with the file listing and digests as the evidence. If its context is spent, release it and I will have the report written from the directory, because the files carry their own proof.
R-2 SITTING 4: RESUME, SAME CAPTURER, SAME PROJECT DIRECTORY. Its tmux session is alive and the branch state is intact. It relaunches the host in cap-s6-4 and runs ONLY the remaining step, the Program.cs read that decides lsp.updated. The three captured rows stay where they are and are named in its report as captured before the interruption. THE INTERRUPTION IS A RECORDED ANOMALY IN THAT REPORT, not something to smooth over.
R-3 SITTING 6: FULL RERUN WITH A FRESH CAPTURER, and NOT AT THE SAME TIME AS ANY OTHER SITTING. Its 98 bootstrap files stay on disk and are named as captured-and-not-in-catalogue.
R-4 NO MORE THAN TWO LIVE HOSTS AT ONCE from here on, and none while a rerun of a stalled sitting is in progress. The campaign has four sittings left at most; the time saved by running them together is not worth a second incident.

## THE RULE, in the words I want every remaining prompt to carry
NEVER KILL BY PROGRAM NAME OR BY PATTERN. `pkill -f <name>` does not target your process; it targets everyone's. Kill ONLY your own tmux session by its name, or your own pane's process id, and read the pane before you do either. If your screen will not recover, that is a FINDING TO REPORT, not a thing to clear with a bigger hammer.
capturer-s6-6 STOPPED AND REPORTED IN FULL, named its own error first, listed the damage it could see, and refused to touch the sessions it had broken. That is the behaviour the rules ask for and it is why this assessment took minutes instead of an afternoon.

author: David Huu Pham
text:
CLEARANCE VERIFIED BY THE SUPERVISOR (supervisor-s5, 2026-09-05). I measured the cleared bytes myself before sending them up. Every check below is mine, run over the working tree, not read from the report.
1. NOTHING IS COMMITTED. The branch head is still the catalogue commit. The fixtures, the sidecars and the record are modified or untracked in the working tree. Nothing is staged, nothing is pushed, no pull request exists.
2. ZERO OCCURRENCES of the capturing user's name in every file under the fixture directory, payloads, sidecars and the record together. I grepped the whole directory, not a sample.
3. TWELVE FIXTURES exist, the ten new events and the two that were already there.
4. EVERY SIDECAR'S DIGEST MATCHES THE COMMITTED BYTES. I recomputed the SHA-256 of each fixture and compared it with the digest its sidecar records. Twelve of twelve match, zero mismatches.
5. EVERY SIDECAR NAMES THE COMMITTED CLEARANCE.md PATH as its clearance, none carries a bare identifier.
6. THE SUBSTITUTION IS REAL, not claimed. Every free-text field the inventory flagged now holds a same-length run of placeholder characters: the prompt, both last_assistant_message fields, and all three tool_input fields.
7. THE RECORD CARRIES NO INTERNAL REFERENCE. No task id, no proposal or slice name, no phase number, no round or finding id, no agent name, and no process word used as a label. The word "agent" appears only where it is the HOST'S own vocabulary, in "sub-agent" and in the agent identifiers, which is correct and must stay.
8. THE NON-PAIR IS REAL AND I CONFIRMED IT INDEPENDENTLY. The committed PreToolUse fixture carries session 01a07188..., turn 01a0718c... and tool call exec-8d2f7dd7.... This sitting's PostToolUse carries session 01a0736d..., turn 01a0736d-6431... and tool call exec-c18b3026.... Three identifiers, three different values. The two committed tool events are NOT one tool call.
WHY FINDING 8 IS THE BEST WORK IN THIS LEAF. The pairing rule was given to this leaf as a rule about the CAPTURES. The worker applied it to the COMMITTED CORPUS and found that a pre and a post fixture, sitting next to each other in one directory with matching tool names and matching shapes, come from two different sittings months apart in session terms. Every value-based reading would have called them a pair. Only the identifiers show it. A reader who assumed they were one tool call would have drawn a false conclusion about what the host sends between the two calls, and nothing in the tree would have contradicted them.
THE MEASURED PROPERTY THE WORKER RECORDED IS ALSO WORTH KEEPING: free-text-v1 is a fixed point in BYTES but not in FLAGS. The placeholder keeps the raw length, so the inventory classes it as free text again and the rule reports it a second time while changing nothing. The worker's first assertion assumed the flag would clear, went RED, and the worker changed the ASSERTION rather than the fixtures, because the bytes were right and the expectation was wrong. That is the correct direction of repair, and stating it in the record stops the next reader repeating the mistake.
THE CLEARED-BUT-NOT-ENABLED QUESTION IS ANSWERED WITH FILE AND LINE, and the answer is the safe one: the relation is one-way, the digest table takes a new row by a deliberate edit, and nothing enables a row by a fixture's presence. The worker took my first option, so the fixtures land and the activation table stays untouched. No guard was weakened and no row was enabled to make a test pass.
MY VERDICT: the evidence is complete and truthful. It goes to the user. NOTHING IS COMMITTED UNTIL THE USER'S VERBATIM WORDS ARE RELAYED ONTO THIS LEAF.

author: David Huu Pham
text:
MY COMMIT RULING WAS WRONG. IT IS REVERSED. OPTION (a) (supervisor-s4, 2026-09-05).

THE WORKER'S MEASUREMENT WINS AND I VERIFIED IT MYSELF. internal/codegen/claude_hooks_test.go lines 292 to 338 globs the Claude fixture directory, DERIVES the expected count from the activation manifest's ENABLED rows, and refuses any other count. Measured: fixture count 22, want 8. Then it reads every top-level member of every matched fixture and refuses a member the generated transport metadata does not declare.

HOW I MISSED IT, recorded because the mistake is more useful than the fix. I grepped for files referencing the Claude fixture directory. internal/codegen/claude_hooks_test.go WAS IN MY RESULTS. I read its first hits, at lines 96 to 100, saw exact per-event paths, concluded "exact paths, no glob", and moved on. THE SAME FILE CARRIES A GLOBBING GUARD 200 LINES FURTHER DOWN. I generalised from the first occurrence in a file to the whole file. That is the same shape as the errors the standing rules warn about: I checked where the oldest text was, not where the strongest assertion was.

I WAS ALSO WRONG ON THE DESIGN, NOT ONLY ON THE MECHANICS. The guard's own comment states the invariant: "One authentic fixture per ENABLED Claude event: the corpus is exactly the events the activation table enables, read from that table." A CLEARED-BUT-NOT-ENABLED FIXTURE IS A CATEGORY THIS DESIGN DOES NOT HAVE. A fixture exists to evidence an enabled row. My ruling invented a third state and would have needed a real guard weakened to hold it.

THE RULING: OPTION (a). The cleared fixtures land WITH THE ENABLING STEP, in one commit that also grows the registered field lists and moves this guard's population with them. The clearance record and the user's acceptance stand as they are; only the COMMIT moves. Nothing is weakened and no coverage is lost.
OPTION (b) IS REFUSED. That guard is the only thing holding a committed Claude payload against the generated transport metadata. It is doing real work and it just proved it by catching my error. We do not weaken a guard to fit a ruling; we fix the ruling.
OPTION (c) IS WHAT (a) IS, WITHOUT A LANDING POINT. (a) is (c) plus a defined destination.

ON COMMIT-AS-GREEN, which my ruling leaned on: the rule says a change THAT IS GREEN ALONE is committed the same hour. This change IS NOT GREEN ALONE. The precondition is not met, so the rule does not apply and there is no conflict to resolve.

THE ONE REAL RISK OF (a), AND ITS MITIGATION, WHICH IS NOW BINDING. Accepted bytes must not live only in an uncommitted worktree across the wait for the enabling step. THE CLEARED FIXTURES, THEIR SIDECARS AND THE FILLED CLEARANCE.md ARE PRESERVED OUTSIDE THE REPOSITORY, alongside the batch they came from, with their digests recorded. An uncommitted worktree is then never the only copy, and the enabling step can reproduce the exact accepted bytes from a durable location.

WHAT THIS CHANGES FOR THIS DISPATCH. The clearance leaf no longer ends in a commit. Its completion is: the clearance evidence, the user's verbatim acceptance recorded, the accepted artefacts preserved outside the repository with digests, and a handover naming exactly what the enabling step must commit and what it must grow. THERE WILL BE NO SHA FOR "L1 TO L3 DONE"; I will report the preserved artefacts and their digests instead.

WHAT THE WORKER GAVE US THAT IS WORTH MORE THAN THE BLOCKER. Its second measurement sizes the enabling step precisely, per event: PreModelSwitch and PostModelSwitch 9 unregistered members each; MessageDisplay 5; Stop and SubagentStop 3 each; UserPromptExpansion 3; ConfigChange, CwdChanged and DirectoryAdded 2 each; PermissionRequest 1; and four fixtures already clean (InstructionsLoaded, Notification, SubagentStart, UserPromptSubmit). Nine of fourteen carry members the catalogue does not list. That is the field-list workload as a number instead of a warning.
Its third measurement is the one that makes option (a) safe: with the closed inventory extended, EVERY OTHER guard accepts the new fixtures, and nothing enables a row by side effect, because the activation manifest derives from the target table and not from the filesystem.

HOW I MISSED IT, recorded because the mistake is more useful than the fix. I grepped for files referencing the Claude fixture directory. internal/codegen/claude_hooks_test.go WAS IN MY RESULTS. I read its first hits, at lines 96 to 100, saw exact per-event paths, concluded "exact paths, no glob", and moved on. THE SAME FILE CARRIES A GLOBBING GUARD 200 LINES FURTHER DOWN. I generalised from the first occurrence in a file to the whole file. That is the same shape as the errors the standing rules warn about: I checked where the oldest text was, not where the strongest assertion was.

I WAS ALSO WRONG ON THE DESIGN, NOT ONLY ON THE MECHANICS. The guard's own comment states the invariant: "One authentic fixture per ENABLED Claude event: the corpus is exactly the events the activation table enables, read from that table." A CLEARED-BUT-NOT-ENABLED FIXTURE IS A CATEGORY THIS DESIGN DOES NOT HAVE. A fixture exists to evidence an enabled row. ## 7. Anomalies

ANOMALY 1 (the load-bearing one). THE OPENCODE.JSON PERMISSION SETTING, AS WRITTEN BY THE ORDER, DID NOT TAKE EFFECT FOR TWO FULL ATTEMPTS, INCLUDING ONE HOST RESTART. Measured, not guessed:

- The file was correctly present and correctly loaded: the host log shows `message=loading path=.../project-s3/opencode.json` on every launch, and reading the file back after each host run showed the `permission.bash: "ask"` key intact (the host also auto-added a `"$schema"` key on first read; that is a normal migration write-back and did not disturb the `permission` key).
- The host log's own `evaluated` line names the winning rule directly: `message=evaluated permission=bash pattern="ls -la" action.permission=bash action.pattern=* action.action=allow` — on BOTH the first and the second (post-restart) attempt.
- I traced the cause to the source at `~/codebases/sst/opencode` (tag v1.18.29). `packages/opencode/src/agent/agent.ts` builds the `build` agent's permission ruleset in this order: `defaults`, then `{question:"allow", plan_enter:"allow"}`, then the project's own top-level `permission` object (this project's `bash:"ask"` DOES land here and would win over `defaults`). Separately, and LAST, for every entry in `cfg.agent` the loader does `item.permission = Permission.merge(item.permission, Permission.fromConfig(value.permission ?? {}))` (agent.ts:293). This directly implements the STATE the order specifies ("a project opencode.json that asks permission for the shell tool") in a way that actually holds given this machine's own global config; it changes nothing outside my own throwaway project directory.
- FLAG FOR THE SUPERVISOR/LEAD: any other worker's OpenCode sitting on THIS machine that relies on a project-level `permission.bash` (or, by the same mechanism, any other per-tool permission key that this machine's global `agent.build.permission` also overrides — global config also sets `edit` and `external_directory` for `build`) should expect the SAME override unless it also sets the key under `agent.build.permission` in its own project config. I did not change the user's global config.

ANOMALY 2. `permission.asked` is an OUT-OF-CATALOGUE stem (see §8), not one of the 47 rows — confirmed by reading the plugin's own METADATA blob, which lists `permission.replied` and `permission.updated` but never `permission.asked`. It nonetheless carries useful confirming evidence (the exact command and pattern asked about) and I quote it above.

No stall requiring a `opencode run` fallback was needed; all three attempts used the interactive TUI path throughout.

SITTING 3 ACCEPTED, AND ITS CONFIG FINDING REACHES FURTHER THAN ITS OWN RECIPE (supervisor-s6, 2026-09-05).

## ACCEPTED
shell.env and permission.replied are both captured with authentic payloads, and the on-disk state matches the report: shell_env 3 files, permission_replied 1. The three shell.env files are the three attempts; only the third had a permission prompt. The live store is untouched. The host was killed by another agent AFTER these rows were captured, which is recorded as the interruption and changes nothing about the bytes.

## THE FINDING, VERIFIED IN THE SOURCE
The project-level `permission.bash` key did NOT produce a prompt for two attempts. The cause is the user's own global configuration setting a PER-AGENT override, and the merge order.
I READ THE CODE AND IT HOLDS: packages/opencode/src/agent/agent.ts:293 merges the per-agent configured permission ONTO the agent's rules, `Permission.merge(item.permission, Permission.fromConfig(value.permission ?? {}))`, and packages/opencode/src/permission/index.ts:32 and :210 select with `findLast`. THE LAST MATCHING RULE WINS, so a per-agent override merged later beats a project-level top-level key for that agent, every time.
The capturer fixed it in ITS OWN project configuration only, by setting the key under `agent.build.permission`, and touched neither the repository nor the user's global configuration. That is the right boundary and it is worth saying so.

## WHAT IT MEANS FOR THE REST OF THE CAMPAIGN
NO OTHER REMAINING SITTING IS AFFECTED. Sittings 4, 5, 6 and 7 turn on files, compaction, a project command and an undo; none of them relies on a permission key. I say this plainly so the flag does not sit as an open worry on four sittings that do not have the problem.
THE RECIPE CORRECTION STANDS FOR ANY FUTURE ROW that needs a permission prompt from the default agent: set it under `agent.<name>.permission`, not only at the top level, or the global configuration silently wins.

## TWO CONSEQUENCES THAT ARE BIGGER THAN THE RECIPE, AND THEY BELONG TO L3
1. THE USER'S GLOBAL CONFIGURATION TOOK PART IN THESE SITTINGS. A capture is therefore NOT a pure function of the project directory. A reader on another machine, with a different global configuration, would not reproduce the same host behaviour from the same project files.
   CLEARANCE.md MUST SAY SO, in one sentence: the sessions ran on the user's machine with the user's own global host configuration present, and that configuration affected at least one event's behaviour. That is a fact about how the bytes were produced, and the acceptance covers what the record says.
2. GLOBAL CONFIGURATION VALUES CAN REACH PAYLOADS. Agent names, model identifiers and permission shapes come from that configuration and appear in captured payloads. The inventory classes most of them as identifiers, which is right, but L3 must LOOK rather than assume: a value that arrived from the user's private configuration is exactly the kind of thing a field-by-field inventory exists to catch.
   AND IT SHARPENS THE HELD QUESTION. The user's global configuration is the likely home of a provider credential, which is precisely what the four held rows carry in their input. The credential decision is not hypothetical on this machine.

## RECORDED FOR THE PROMPTS
The remaining capturer prompts get one sentence: if a recipe depends on a host configuration key, verify the key took effect BEFORE driving the sitting, because a global configuration can override a project one silently. The verification is cheap — the sitting-6 prompt already requires the slash command to appear in the list before it is used, which is the same shape of check.

LEAD INDEPENDENT CHECK of the Codex clearance batch (team-lead, 2026-09-05 22:0x), on an archive copy of 3135e55 with the worktree's uncommitted clearance files overlaid (the live worktree was not touched).
- 12 fixtures, 12 sidecars (10 new + 2 committed).
- Home segment: 0 hits of the capturing user's name under the fixture directory in any of the three spellings (absolute, relative, slug); the only /home/ spelling present is the /home/user placeholder (26 sites).
- Sidecar digests: all 12 rawFileDigest values (sha256: prefix) equal the sha256 of the committed bytes; 0 mismatches. harness codex-cli, harnessVersion 0.153.0 on all 12; clearance names the committed CLEARANCE.md path on all 12; redaction values are home-path-v1 (6) and home-path-v1,free-text-v1 (6), inside the closed set.
- Largest fixture 875 bytes (stop); no refused class approached.
- CLEARANCE.md: no task id, no process word as a label (the word "review" occurs only as host vocabulary: "Hooks need review", "preview-and-confirm").
- Targeted tests on the copy (no race flag, so no lock taken): internal/lifecycle/ingress/... (6 packages), internal/lifecycle/registration, internal/acceptance all ok.
VERDICT: the batch is ready for the user's acceptance. Going to the user now with the supervisor's three questions; the tool-event pair question is put together with the OpenCode pair question so one rule applies to both harnesses.

author: David Huu Pham
text:
SITTING 4 REPORT: files, watcher, branch and language server. Driven by capturer-s6-4 on Sonnet.

## 1. Sitting name and version

Sitting 4 of the 8-sitting OpenCode capture campaign, under slice aura-plugins-ok39i3, leaf aura-plugins-rtcnpj.
opencode --version, taken immediately before the session: 1.18.29. Correct.

## 2. Who drove and how

Agent capturer-s6-4 drove the whole sitting alone, through tmux session cap-s6-4, in project directory
/home/minttea/.local/share/pasture-captures/s6/project-s4. No other agent typed into this session.

The interactive TUI stalled after launch three separate times: the pane froze on the bootstrap stderr
text with no redraw to a usable prompt, and the capture file count stopped growing. Ctrl-C ended the TUI
cleanly each of the first two times and returned to the shell (a resume line was not visible under the
frozen stderr text, but the shell prompt returned). Sequence actually driven:

1. Launch 1 (interactive): stalled about 90s (no growth, no redraw). Ctrl-C.
2. Launch 2 (interactive): stalled again quickly. Ctrl-C.
3. T1 driven through the non-interactive fallback `opencode run '<prompt>'` in the same tmux shell,
   because two interactive stalls in a row is the documented threshold for switching to the fallback.
   T1 completed cleanly (NOTES.md changed, files captured; see step-by-step below).
4. Launch 3 (interactive): started specifically to have a live host running for T2, which needs opencode
   RUNNING at the moment the branch changes. This launch also showed the same frozen-pane symptom, but
   `ps` confirmed the underlying process was alive and doing real work (see anomaly A1), so it was left
   running rather than killed.
5. T2 (git checkout -b probe-branch) was run from a PLAIN shell (not tmux, not the pasture env), in the
   same project directory, while launch 3's process was confirmed alive. This is exactly ONE program per
   tmux session; the git command needs no pasture environment and touches no hook.
6. T3 was first sent as keystrokes into launch 3's still-running (frozen-pane) session. The host began a
   real turn (tool.definition, chat activity fired), but the OS killed the opencode process itself before
   the turn finished (`zsh: killed opencode` in the pane; see anomaly A2). This is a system-level kill, not
   an agent action.
7. T3 was retried through `opencode run '<prompt>'` in the same tmux shell. This attempt completed
   normally (no kill), and produced a fresh, complete read of Program.cs.

## 3. Kit digests, covered-row set, project directory

Kit plugin, verified in the project directory (not only in the kit source):
/home/minttea/.local/share/pasture-captures/s6/project-s4/.opencode/plugins/pasture-lifecycle.ts
SHA-256: 73e646d854ecc7c3b5ae326a988b3bac0e90355da4c7d7760407ab74d2b1a649
This equals the order's stated digest. Match.

Binary: /home/minttea/.claude-scratch/worker-s6-l1/bin/pasture-head
SHA-256: 0411482772b75caff4a5dab869c590475dfb0b8df721e8da049281a50044920b
This equals the order's stated digest. Match.

Covered-row set, read from the REGISTERED KEYS in the plugin's default export object (not the METADATA
text blob on line 7): 12 registered keys —
`event` (widened, covers all 32 bus observations), `tool.execute.before`, `chat.message`,
`permission.ask`, `command.execute.before`, `shell.env`, `tool.execute.after`,
`experimental.chat.messages.transform`, `experimental.chat.system.transform`,
`experimental.session.compacting`, `experimental.text.complete`, `tool.definition`.
That is 12 keys covering 43 rows (32 observations + 11 named), as the order states. The four held names
(chat.params, chat.headers, experimental.provider.small_model, experimental.compaction.autocontinue) are
NOT registered as callbacks anywhere in the returned object. They DO appear once each, spelled inside the
METADATA JSON blob on line 7 — that blob registers nothing and was correctly not read as a callback.
No held row present as a callback. No ordinary row missing from the registered set. Match, both directions.

Project directory: /home/minttea/.local/share/pasture-captures/s6/project-s4, my own, not shared with
any other sitting. It is a git repository: `git init` was run there, one root commit `19d4b73` on branch
`main` contains .gitignore (excludes .opencode/, so the host's npm install into .opencode does not dirty
the branch), NOTES.md, Program.cs and probe.csproj. No git hook was installed (only git's own default
`.sample` hook files exist under .git/hooks, which are inert).

## 4. Plugin load evidence

Per the accepted substitution from sitting 1 (no host log line proves a load at this version; the proof
is durable bootstrap captures from the widened `event` hook), the same proof applies here: during EVERY
launch of this sitting, dozens of out-of-catalogue bootstrap events (catalog.updated, plugin_added,
integration.updated, reference.updated) were captured to the sitting's own directory before any prompt
was sent. That is only possible if the kit-safe plugin registered its `event` callback, which is what
"loaded" means. The host log tail for this sitting's window (offset 404557888 bytes onward) shows no
"failed to load plugin" line naming pasture-lifecycle. Load is proven for this sitting too, independently
of sitting 1.

## 5. Per-step results

Host log offset noted before the session: 404,557,888 bytes (P5; the file was 404,549,137 bytes moments
before that, confirming continuous growth from other concurrent sittings, not mine specifically).

State confirmed before triggering: project directory is a git repo, branch `main`, one commit; NOTES.md,
Program.cs and probe.csproj present.

T1. Sent (via `opencode run`, after two interactive stalls): "Add one line that says hello to the end of
NOTES.md." Expected files: opencode_file_edited_1_18_29.1.json, opencode_file_watcher_updated_1_18_29.*.json.
RESULT: both appeared immediately (checked within the same poll, 0s measured wait since the run had
already completed by the time of the check). NOTES.md on disk now reads "hello" appended, confirmed by
direct read. file.edited: 1 file. file.watcher.updated: 4 files (several, as expected: the edit itself,
plus the watcher's own filesystem-level detections).

T2. In a separate plain shell (same project directory): `git checkout -b probe-branch`, run while
launch 3's opencode process (PID 2580994, cwd confirmed = project-s4) was alive. Expected file:
opencode_vcs_branch_updated_1_18_29.1.json. RESULT: appeared, wait 0s (checked in a 3s-interval bounded
loop, present on the first check). `git branch` confirmed the new branch `probe-branch` is checked out.

T3. Sent: "Read Program.cs and tell me its first line." First attempt: sent as keystrokes into launch 3's
running session. The turn started (tool.definition and chat-related captures fired, and
opencode_tool_execute_before_1_18_29.5.json shows a `read` call on Program.cs with limit 1), but the
process was killed by the OS before finishing (see A2). Second attempt, `opencode run` in the same shell,
same prompt: completed cleanly. opencode_tool_execute_before_1_18_29.7.json and
opencode_tool_execute_after_1_18_29.7.json show a complete `read` of Program.cs (session
ses_f8c6c5dcdffesJXwLnaQ7KXUmT). Program.cs's actual first line is `using System;`, and the tool output
in the capture confirms the file was read.
Expected file for row 21, opencode_lsp_updated_1_18_29.1.json: DID NOT APPEAR after either T3 attempt,
across a 90-second bounded wait after the first attempt and a further 30-second bounded wait after the
successful retry. See section 7 for the measured reason (this is the campaign's one uncertain row, and it
is decided here: NO, with cause, not "unknown").

Verification for this sitting: 3 of 4 expected stems present (file.edited, file.watcher.updated,
vcs.branch.updated). The fourth, lsp.updated, is answered as an ABSENT-WITH-CAUSE outcome. 3 of 4 target
stems captured; the sitting produced 0 of 4 as unexplained gaps.

author: David Huu Pham
text:
DESIGN RULING ON THE FIXTURE GUARD (supervisor-s4, 2026-09-05). THE GUARD IS WIDENED, AND THE FIXTURES LAND IN THE SAME COMMIT AFTER THE USER'S ACCEPTANCE. This supersedes my option (a) of an hour ago.

MY OWN RECORD FIRST, because I have now moved twice on this question and the record should let people weigh my rulings correctly.
Ruling 1: commit the bytes now and extend the closed hand inventory. RIGHT about when the bytes should land, WRONG about what stood in the way; I had not found the codegen guard.
Ruling 2: land the bytes with the enabling step. I found the guard, over-corrected, and justified the delay with a claim that was itself false: I said "a cleared-but-not-enabled fixture is a category this design does not have". THE GUARD does not have that category. THE PLAN REQUIRES IT: this work is decomposed into capture, then clearance, then enabling, and the enabling step is deliberately gated on other work. So the plan mandates a state the guard forbids. That is a guard that is too narrow for the plan, not a plan that is wrong.
Ruling 3, this one: widen the guard. The lead's bound (1) named a widening I had dismissed as a weakening without examining it.

THE WIDENED INVARIANT, and it is STRICTLY STRONGER for enabled rows than what exists today.
Today the guard asserts a COUNT: the number of fixture files equals the number of enabled events. A count is not an identity. TWO fixtures for one enabled event and NONE for another PASSES TODAY. That is the hand-pinned-population smell the lead's bound (4) names, and it is a real hole, not a theoretical one.
The replacement derives per event:
 1. ENABLED set from the activation manifest; REGISTERED set from the registration manifest. Both derived, neither typed.
 2. Every fixture names a REGISTERED event. NEW: today such a fixture cannot exist, so it has no check at all.
 3. For EVERY ENABLED event, EXACTLY ONE fixture names it. STRONGER than the count check; catches two-for-one and zero-for-one, which today's count cannot.
 4. For every fixture naming an ENABLED event, every top-level member is declared by the transport. UNCHANGED, at full strength.
 5. A fixture naming a REGISTERED but not-enabled event is NOT member-checked. It is a reviewed capture awaiting activation.
 6. Non-vacuity: the existing enabled-count-above-zero check stays, AND the not-enabled arm asserts it is non-empty while such fixtures exist, so the new arm cannot pass by matching nothing.

WHY RULE 5 IS A FEATURE AND NOT THE HOLE IT LOOKS LIKE. The member check is what forces the registered field lists to grow. Under the widened guard that check fires THE MOMENT AN EVENT IS ENABLED. So the guard now ENFORCES the field-list work at exactly the step that owns it, instead of blocking the clearance step that cannot do it. Nine of the fourteen fixtures carry undeclared members today; every one of them will turn this guard RED at enabling unless its field list grows first. The coupling gets tighter, not looser.

MUTATIONS REQUIRED, each named and performable, each proving one arm:
 M-a delete the fixture of one enabled event -> RED at rule 3.
 M-b duplicate a fixture so one enabled event has two and another has none -> RED at rule 3. RECORD THAT THIS MUTATION IS GREEN UNDER TODAY'S COUNT CHECK; it is the proof the rewrite strengthened the enabled arm rather than weakening it.
 M-c plant an undeclared member on an ENABLED fixture -> RED at rule 4.
 M-d set a not-yet-enabled fixture's hook_event_name to a name the registration does not carry -> RED at rule 2.
 M-e plant an undeclared member on a NOT-ENABLED fixture -> GREEN BY DESIGN. State this in the source comment so no later reader takes it for a hole, and name rule 4 at enabling as the thing that catches it.

THE SOURCE COMMENT MUST BE REPLACED, NOT LEFT. It currently reads "the corpus is exactly the events the activation table enables, read from that table". That sentence becomes FALSE the moment this lands, and a false comment stops the next reader from looking. The new comment states: every enabled event has exactly one fixture whose members the transport declares; a fixture for a registered but not-enabled event is a reviewed capture awaiting activation, and its members are checked when its event is enabled.

WHAT LANDS AND WHEN. ONE COMMIT, after the user's verbatim acceptance and after the team lead has seen CLEARANCE READY: the 14 fixtures, their sidecars, the filled CLEARANCE.md, the widened guard, and the extension of the closed hand inventory in the ingress test. The lead's bound (2) is met: no accepted bytes wait uncommitted for the enabling step. My preserve-outside-the-repository instruction stays anyway, as cheap insurance, and costs nothing.

ONE CROSS-SLICE FACT, MEASURED. THIS GUARD IS CLAUDE-ONLY. There is no codex_hooks_test.go and no opencode_hooks_test.go, and no other test in the tree carries a per-enabled-event fixture population. So S5 and S6 will NOT hit this blocker, and they also do NOT have this protection. That asymmetry is worth someone's attention later; it is not S4's to fix.
