SITTING 4 REPORT — PART 1 of 4 (sections 1-5). See parts 2-4 for the file listing/digests and anomalies/housekeeping. (An earlier truncated 60000-byte test fragment was posted by mistake immediately before this comment; disregard it, this Part 1 supersedes it.)

SITTING 4 REPORT: files, watcher, branch and language server. Driven by capturer-s6-4 on Sonnet.

## 1. Sitting name and version

Sitting 4 of the 8-sitting OpenCode capture campaign, under slice aura-plugins-ok39i3, leaf aura-plugins-rtcnpj.
opencode --version, taken immediately before the session: 1.18.29. Correct.

## 2. Who drove and how

Agent capturer-s6-4 drove the whole sitting alone, through tmux session cap-s6-4, in project directory
/home/minttea/.local/share/pasture-captures/s6/project-s4. No other agent typed into this session.

The interactive TUI stalled after launch three separate times: the pane froze on the bootstrap stderr
text with no redraw to a usable prompt, and the capture file count stopped growing. Ctrl-C ended the TUI
cleanly each of the first two times and returned to the shell (a resume line was not visible under the
frozen stderr text, but the shell prompt returned). Sequence actually driven:

1. Launch 1 (interactive): stalled about 90s (no growth, no redraw). Ctrl-C.
2. Launch 2 (interactive): stalled again quickly. Ctrl-C.
3. T1 driven through the non-interactive fallback `opencode run '<prompt>'` in the same tmux shell,
   because two interactive stalls in a row is the documented threshold for switching to the fallback.
   T1 completed cleanly (NOTES.md changed, files captured; see step-by-step below).
4. Launch 3 (interactive): started specifically to have a live host running for T2, which needs opencode
   RUNNING at the moment the branch changes. This launch also showed the same frozen-pane symptom, but
   `ps` confirmed the underlying process was alive and doing real work (see anomaly A1), so it was left
   running rather than killed.
5. T2 (git checkout -b probe-branch) was run from a PLAIN shell (not tmux, not the pasture env), in the
   same project directory, while launch 3's process was confirmed alive. This is exactly ONE program per
   tmux session; the git command needs no pasture environment and touches no hook.
6. T3 was first sent as keystrokes into launch 3's still-running (frozen-pane) session. The host began a
   real turn (tool.definition, chat activity fired), but the OS killed the opencode process itself before
   the turn finished (`zsh: killed opencode` in the pane; see anomaly A2). This is a system-level kill, not
   an agent action.
7. T3 was retried through `opencode run '<prompt>'` in the same tmux shell. This attempt completed
   normally (no kill), and produced a fresh, complete read of Program.cs.

## 3. Kit digests, covered-row set, project directory

Kit plugin, verified in the project directory (not only in the kit source):
/home/minttea/.local/share/pasture-captures/s6/project-s4/.opencode/plugins/pasture-lifecycle.ts
SHA-256: 73e646d854ecc7c3b5ae326a988b3bac0e90355da4c7d7760407ab74d2b1a649
This equals the order's stated digest. Match.

Binary: /home/minttea/.claude-scratch/worker-s6-l1/bin/pasture-head
SHA-256: 0411482772b75caff4a5dab869c590475dfb0b8df721e8da049281a50044920b
This equals the order's stated digest. Match.

Covered-row set, read from the REGISTERED KEYS in the plugin's default export object (not the METADATA
text blob on line 7): 12 registered keys —
`event` (widened, covers all 32 bus observations), `tool.execute.before`, `chat.message`,
`permission.ask`, `command.execute.before`, `shell.env`, `tool.execute.after`,
`experimental.chat.messages.transform`, `experimental.chat.system.transform`,
`experimental.session.compacting`, `experimental.text.complete`, `tool.definition`.
That is 12 keys covering 43 rows (32 observations + 11 named), as the order states. The four held names
(chat.params, chat.headers, experimental.provider.small_model, experimental.compaction.autocontinue) are
NOT registered as callbacks anywhere in the returned object. They DO appear once each, spelled inside the
METADATA JSON blob on line 7 — that blob registers nothing and was correctly not read as a callback.
No held row present as a callback. No ordinary row missing from the registered set. Match, both directions.

Project directory: /home/minttea/.local/share/pasture-captures/s6/project-s4, my own, not shared with
any other sitting. It is a git repository: `git init` was run there, one root commit `19d4b73` on branch
`main` contains .gitignore (excludes .opencode/, so the host's npm install into .opencode does not dirty
the branch), NOTES.md, Program.cs and probe.csproj. No git hook was installed (only git's own default
`.sample` hook files exist under .git/hooks, which are inert).

## 4. Plugin load evidence

Per the accepted substitution from sitting 1 (no host log line proves a load at this version; the proof
is durable bootstrap captures from the widened `event` hook), the same proof applies here: during EVERY
launch of this sitting, dozens of out-of-catalogue bootstrap events (catalog.updated, plugin_added,
integration.updated, reference.updated) were captured to the sitting's own directory before any prompt
was sent. That is only possible if the kit-safe plugin registered its `event` callback, which is what
"loaded" means. The host log tail for this sitting's window (offset 404557888 bytes onward) shows no
"failed to load plugin" line naming pasture-lifecycle. Load is proven for this sitting too, independently
of sitting 1.

## 5. Per-step results

Host log offset noted before the session: 404,557,888 bytes (P5; the file was 404,549,137 bytes moments
before that, confirming continuous growth from other concurrent sittings, not mine specifically).

State confirmed before triggering: project directory is a git repo, branch `main`, one commit; NOTES.md,
Program.cs and probe.csproj present.

T1. Sent (via `opencode run`, after two interactive stalls): "Add one line that says hello to the end of
NOTES.md." Expected files: opencode_file_edited_1_18_29.1.json, opencode_file_watcher_updated_1_18_29.*.json.
RESULT: both appeared immediately (checked within the same poll, 0s measured wait since the run had
already completed by the time of the check). NOTES.md on disk now reads "hello" appended, confirmed by
direct read. file.edited: 1 file. file.watcher.updated: 4 files (several, as expected: the edit itself,
plus the watcher's own filesystem-level detections).

T2. In a separate plain shell (same project directory): `git checkout -b probe-branch`, run while
launch 3's opencode process (PID 2580994, cwd confirmed = project-s4) was alive. Expected file:
opencode_vcs_branch_updated_1_18_29.1.json. RESULT: appeared, wait 0s (checked in a 3s-interval bounded
loop, present on the first check). `git branch` confirmed the new branch `probe-branch` is checked out.

T3. Sent: "Read Program.cs and tell me its first line." First attempt: sent as keystrokes into launch 3's
running session. The turn started (tool.definition and chat-related captures fired, and
opencode_tool_execute_before_1_18_29.5.json shows a `read` call on Program.cs with limit 1), but the
process was killed by the OS before finishing (see A2). Second attempt, `opencode run` in the same shell,
same prompt: completed cleanly. opencode_tool_execute_before_1_18_29.7.json and
opencode_tool_execute_after_1_18_29.7.json show a complete `read` of Program.cs (session
ses_f8c6c5dcdffesJXwLnaQ7KXUmT). Program.cs's actual first line is `using System;`, and the tool output
in the capture confirms the file was read.
Expected file for row 21, opencode_lsp_updated_1_18_29.1.json: DID NOT APPEAR after either T3 attempt,
across a 90-second bounded wait after the first attempt and a further 30-second bounded wait after the
successful retry. See section 7 for the measured reason (this is the campaign's one uncertain row, and it
is decided here: NO, with cause, not "unknown").

Verification for this sitting: 3 of 4 expected stems present (file.edited, file.watcher.updated,
vcs.branch.updated). The fourth, lsp.updated, is answered as an ABSENT-WITH-CAUSE outcome. 3 of 4 target
stems captured; the sitting produced 0 of 4 as unexplained gaps.

author: David Huu Pham
text:
SITTING 4 REPORT — PART 4 of 4 (sections 7-9 and conclusion).

## 7. Anomalies

A1. THE TUI STALLED THREE TIMES. Each time the pane froze on bootstrap stderr text with no redraw, and
the capture file count stopped growing. `ps` confirmed the process itself stayed alive and functionally
connected in TWO of the three cases (checked cwd = project-s4, growing CPU time) — the "stall" is a
rendering problem, not always a dead process. The system was running at least two other concurrent
capture sittings (project-s3, project-s6) plus a shared `opencode ... serve --service` daemon at the
time; that is a plausible cause of contention, but I did not confirm it further, and I do not claim it as
the cause. `opencode run` never showed this symptom in this sitting; the two prompts sent through it both
started and finished normally.

A2. THE RUNNING OPENCODE PROCESS WAS KILLED BY THE OPERATING SYSTEM MID-TURN, NOT BY ME. During the first
T3 attempt (typed into the still-running, frozen launch-3 session), the pane showed the literal text
`zsh: killed opencode` partway through a real turn (tool.definition and message activity had already
fired). `ps` confirmed the project-s4 opencode process (PID 2580994) was gone afterward, with no exit
message from opencode itself, no relaunch attempted by me before the kill. System memory at the time:
`free -h` showed ~5GB free RAM but ~19GB of 68GB swap in use, i.e. real memory pressure, consistent with
(but not proven to be) an OOM kill from several concurrent sittings' opencode processes running at once.
I could not confirm this from `dmesg`, which needs root on this machine. I report the observed fact (the
process was killed externally, mid-turn) and flag the plausible cause without asserting it.

A3. LSP.UPDATED DID NOT FIRE, AND THE MEASURED REASON IS STRONGER THAN "NO ADMISSIBLE SERVER ON THIS
MACHINE". The order's own uncertainty was framed around PATH availability (gopls/tsserver/pyright absent,
csharp-ls present). The actual, decisive cause, read from the host's own log for this sitting's exact
time window (tail from byte offset 404,557,888): every single run in this sitting printed
`message="all LSPs are disabled"` (11 occurrences across the sitting's log window, one or more per turn),
sourced to packages/opencode/src/lsp/lsp.ts:152, `if (!cfg.lsp) { yield* Effect.logInfo("all LSPs are
disabled") }`. The `lsp` config field is `Schema.optional` (packages/core/src/v1/config/config.ts:120)
with no default-true anywhere I could find, and NEITHER the global `~/.config/opencode/opencode.json` NOR
the project directory's config sets `lsp` at all. So the LSP subsystem here is off by default, for every
file type, independent of which language-server binaries happen to be on PATH or already downloaded. This
is not a PATH problem; it is a configuration-default problem. I did NOT set `lsp: true` anywhere to test
past this, because that was not part of the ordered trigger and the order's own text tightly scopes what
I may change ("DO NOT install or download a language server"); enabling a disabled subsystem via config,
even scoped to the throwaway project, is a further environment change beyond the specified recipe, and I
was told not to guess. I report the measured, decisive cause and stop there.

A4. NO SERIALISATION-GUARD LINE. Searched the full tmux scrollback (1930 lines, `tmux capture-pane -S
-20000`) for "could not serialize the payload of": zero occurrences. No row's trigger fired without being
captured for this reason.

A5. EXTRA CAPTURES FROM THE RETRY TRAFFIC. Because of the three launches, two `opencode run` fallbacks,
and the killed mid-turn attempt, this sitting produced many more incidental captures than a single clean
run of the four target rows would: multiple sessions worth of chat.message, experimental.chat.*,
tool.definition, tool.execute.before/after, session.* rows (all IN the 47-row catalogue, just not this
sitting's four target rows) fired repeatedly. These are not findings; they are ordinary catalogue rows
this sitting's extra turns happened to also produce, and are listed in section 6's full inventory. They
are separate from the out-of-catalogue stems in section 8.

## 8. Out-of-catalogue stems

These stems are NOT in the 47-row catalogue at all (same five the sitting-1 report first measured, minus
message.part.delta which fired here too):

- opencode_catalog_updated_1_18_29 — 12 files
- opencode_integration_updated_1_18_29 — 6 files
- opencode_reference_updated_1_18_29 — 6 files
- opencode_plugin_added_1_18_29 — 270 files (one per skill/agent/plugin file the host's local trees
  discovered across the sitting's several launches)
- opencode_message_part_delta_1_18_29 — 66 files

Per the supervisor's ruling on sitting 1: these are evidence toward the true population, not findings
against this sitting, and never fixtures for any row.

## 9. Housekeeping

- tmux session cap-s6-4: killed (`tmux kill-session -t cap-s6-4`), confirmed absent from
  `tmux list-sessions` afterward.
- Dry-run directory (/home/minttea/.local/share/pasture-captures/s6/dryrun): checked, empty. This sitting
  did not use it (no hand-piped bytes were produced).
- Live store (~/.local/share/pasture) checked untouched by this sitting:
  - pasture.db mtime is from well before this sitting's window (checked with `stat`; unchanged since a
    time roughly 46 minutes before the housekeeping check, i.e. before this sitting started).
  - lifecycle-faults.jsonl in the live store DID grow during the sitting's window, but its newest entries
    are all `harness=claude-code` (this very agent session's own ambient Claude Code hook activity), never
    `harness=opencode`. The matching `harness=opencode` fault entries for THIS sitting's withheld/unknown
    rows live only in the scratch fault file at
    /home/minttea/.local/share/pasture-captures/s6/scratch/lifecycle-faults.jsonl, confirmed by direct read.
  - PASTURE_DB_PATH for this sitting was always the scratch database
    /home/minttea/.local/share/pasture-captures/s6/scratch/pasture-s4.db, exported only inside tmux
    session cap-s6-4, never the live store.

## CONCLUSION

3 of 4 rows captured: file.edited, file.watcher.updated, vcs.branch.updated. The fourth, lsp.updated, is
the campaign's one uncertain row and this sitting DECIDES it: it did NOT fire, and the measured, decisive
cause is that the LSP subsystem is off by default at this host version (config field `lsp` is absent and
unset, `if (!cfg.lsp)` short-circuits to "all LSPs are disabled" for every file type), not merely "no
admissible server on this machine". I recommend row 21 join the raised list with THIS cause recorded
verbatim, rather than the PATH-availability cause the order anticipated, so a later reader is not misled
into thinking a different C# tool on PATH would have changed the outcome.

author: David Huu Pham
text:
A LISTING TAKEN FROM A LIVE HOST IS NOT THE EVIDENCE IT LOOKS LIKE. MY PROMPT ORDERED IT WRONG (supervisor-s6, 2026-09-05).

## THE MEASUREMENT
capturer-s6-3's report states 717 files in its capture directory. I counted the directory just now: 720 files, all JSON. The three extra are not a discrepancy in anyone's arithmetic. THEY ARRIVED AFTER THE LISTING WAS TAKEN AND BEFORE THE SESSION ENDED. The host was still running, the plugin was still forwarding bus events, and the sink was still writing files.

## THE CAUSE IS IN MY OWN PROMPT, AND I RECORD IT AS MINE
My common closing steps ran in this order: C1 search the standard error, C2 take the listing with digests, C3 compare against the expected set, C4 KILL THE SESSION. So the listing is taken while the host is still alive, BY CONSTRUCTION. Every sitting run under that prompt has the same defect, and it is luck rather than design that the only measured gap so far is three files of bootstrap noise.
IT MATTERS BECAUSE THE CLEARANCE STEP WORKS FROM THE REPORT. A listing that undercounts is the evidence a later worker trusts, and a file that exists but is not in the record is a file nobody selects, nobody clears and nobody accounts for. The gap does not have to be large to be wrong: it only has to contain the one file somebody needed.

## THE FIX, APPLIED TO EVERY REMAINING PROMPT
C2 now reads: STOP THE HOST FIRST, CONFIRM IT HAS EXITED, THEN LIST. State the file count, and RE-RUN THE COUNT ONCE AFTER THE LISTING TO SHOW IT DID NOT MOVE. That second count is the cheap part and it is what turns a listing into evidence: a number that is stable across two reads of a stopped directory is a fact, and a number read once from a live one is a snapshot of a moving thing.
C4 now says the host is already stopped, so nobody stops it twice or, worse, reorders it back.

## WHAT THE ALREADY-RUN SITTINGS NEED, AND IT IS SMALL
Sittings 1, 2, 3 and 8 all took their listings under the old order. Each should RE-TAKE the count now that its directory is quiescent, and record both numbers with the reason, rather than silently replacing the first one. Nothing needs re-capturing: the files are on disk and the identifiers in the bytes are unaffected. This is a bookkeeping correction, and correcting it in the open is cheaper than a clearance step that discovers the gap later and cannot tell whether a missing file was lost or never listed.
I HAVE NOT ASKED THE RUNNING SITTINGS TO CHANGE ANYTHING MID-FLIGHT. They finish under the order they were given, and they re-take the count at the end like the rest.

## THE GENERAL FORM, because this is the third time today the same shape has appeared
A CHECK RUN AGAINST A MOVING TARGET REPORTS THE MOVEMENT, NOT THE TARGET. The gate that expected a log line the host never writes, the count that was right in total and wrong in a part, and now a listing taken while the thing being listed was still growing — all three passed their own reading and told a reader something untrue. THE DEFENCE IS THE SAME EACH TIME: state what you measured, measure it twice when it can move, and say which reading you are relying on.

author: David Huu Pham
text:
SITTING 4 ACCEPTED AT 3 OF 4, AND THE FOURTH ROW IS NOW DECIDED RATHER THAN UNCERTAIN (supervisor-s6, 2026-09-05).

## ACCEPTED
file.edited, file.watcher.updated and vcs.branch.updated are captured. The live store is untouched. The report is split across six comments because of a comment-size limit, which is the right handling and which I note below for the clearance step.

## THE lsp.updated CAUSE IS DECISIVE, AND I VERIFIED IT
The capturer traced the host log line "all LSPs are disabled" to packages/opencode/src/lsp/lsp.ts:152. I READ IT AND THE SURROUNDING BRANCH:
  `if (!cfg.lsp) { yield* Effect.logInfo("all LSPs are disabled") } else { ... }`
and the configuration schema declares the key OPTIONAL at packages/core/src/v1/config/config.ts:120. SO WITH NO `lsp` KEY SET, EVERY LANGUAGE SERVER IS DISABLED, no client can spawn, and lsp.updated CANNOT FIRE FOR ANY FILE TYPE.
THIS SUPERSEDES THE FRAMING I GAVE THE SITTING. My order said the row was uncertain because of which server binaries are on PATH, and named the C-sharp route as the one needing no download. THAT WAS THE WRONG QUESTION. The C-sharp route would have failed too, and so would every other, because the subsystem is off before any binary is consulted. A PATH survey cannot detect a feature that never asks for a binary.
THE CAPTURER DID NOT ENABLE IT, correctly: enabling a host subsystem was outside its ordered trigger, and it reported rather than widened. That is the boundary I want held.

## I RULE THE ROW CAPTURABLE, AND ORDER ONE SHORT SITTING FOR IT
The row is NOT unreachable. It needs `"lsp": true` in the project's own configuration, plus a file whose type has a server present — and csharp-ls is already installed on this machine, which is why the project carries the C-sharp files.
THIS IS THE SAME CLASS OF SET-UP AS SITTING 3's PERMISSION KEY, which I already accepted: a project-level configuration key, set in the capture project only, never in the user's global configuration and never in the repository. The bytes stay authentic because a real host produces them; the record states the configuration that produced them.
ORDER: a short sitting 4b, one project, `"lsp": true` added to that project's configuration only, open a C-sharp file, and look. IF IT STILL DOES NOT FIRE, the row is withheld with the strongest possible reason — the subsystem was enabled, a server was present, and no client spawned — and that is a far better sentence than "we could not find a trigger".

## THE SECOND ANOMALY IS THE ONE THAT CHANGES MY ORDERS
The host was killed BY THE OPERATING SYSTEM mid-turn, with about 19 GB of 68 GB of swap in use and several sittings' hosts running together. The capturer could not confirm the cause and said so rather than asserting it, which is right.
I DO NOT NEED THE EXACT CAUSE TO ACT. Together with the earlier stalls, the starved redraws and the load average near 14, the evidence is that CONCURRENT LIVE HOSTS ARE THE PROBLEM, and my parallel dispatch created them. I already tightened to two at once. I NOW TIGHTEN TO ONE.
The remaining work is a sitting 6 rerun, this sitting 4b, and sitting 7. Three short sittings. Running them one at a time costs perhaps half an hour and removes the whole class of failure that has now produced one incident, three stalls and one operating-system kill. THE TIME SAVED BY OVERLAPPING THEM IS NOT WORTH A FOURTH SYMPTOM.

## A NOTE FOR THE CLEARANCE STEP
A Beads comment has a size limit near 64 KB, and this sitting's evidence needed six comments. THE CLEARANCE EVIDENCE WILL BE LARGER than any single sitting report. L3 must plan to split it, and must state at the top of the first part how many parts there are and what each contains, so that a reader can tell a truncated record from a complete one. A record that is silently short is the failure mode here.

author: David Huu Pham
text:
THE WIDENING RULING IS WITHDRAWN. OPTION (a) STANDS (supervisor-s4, 2026-09-05). This is the reconciled ruling and the last one on this question.

WHY IT IS WITHDRAWN, PROCESS FIRST. My widening ruling and the team lead's acceptance of option (a) CROSSED IN FLIGHT. The lead accepted "the fixtures land with the enabling step" without having seen the widening. Two people ruled near-simultaneously on the same question. The standing lesson from the previous slice is exact about this case: WAIT FOR ONE RECONCILED RULING and do not implement a mid-flight ruling that may be withdrawn. A guard rewrite was landing under exactly those conditions, so I stopped the worker before it could commit to it.

WHY IT IS WITHDRAWN ON THE MERITS, WHICH MATTERS MORE THAN WHO SPOKE LAST. THE ARM I ASKED FOR WOULD BE VACUOUS ALMOST IMMEDIATELY.
All 14 cleared fixtures become ENABLED at the enabling step. The derived target is 22, and 22 is the 8 already enabled plus these 14. So the moment that step lands, the population of registered-but-not-enabled fixtures is ZERO, and the arm I specified matches NOTHING.
Worse, the non-vacuity check I myself required — assert the not-enabled arm is non-empty while such fixtures exist — would then turn the guard RED at the enabling step.
So the widening would have permanently complicated a working guard, and added an arm that dies within one step, in order to hold a state that lasts ONE HOP between two leaves. That is the wrong shape. The team lead's bound (1) invited a widening and the widening was available, but availability is not fitness. I did not ask how long the new arm would live before I specified its non-vacuity check, and that is the question that decides it.

WHAT THIS MEANS FOR TODAY'S GUARD. It stays exactly as it is. Its count-versus-identity weakness, which the lead's bound (4) named and I confirmed is real — two fixtures for one enabled event and none for another passes today — IS STILL A HOLE, and it is now a finding without an owner in this slice. I record it as such rather than fix it opportunistically inside a clearance step. The right place is the enabling step, which already moves this guard's population and already has to touch the field lists; deriving the population per event costs little there and the mutation that proves it is the duplicate-fixture one. I recommend it to that step and do not mandate it.

THE RULING: the 14 cleared fixtures land WITH THE ENABLING STEP, in one commit that also grows the registered field lists and moves the guard's derived population with them. The guard is not weakened and is not touched by the clearance step. Commit-as-green does not apply, because this fixture set is not green alone.

THE THREE REQUIREMENTS THAT MAKE THE DELAY SAFE, all binding:
1. THE MOMENT THE USER ACCEPTS, the cleared fixtures, their sidecars and the filled CLEARANCE.md are preserved OUTSIDE EVERY REPOSITORY with their digests RECORDED HERE. The enabling commit must prove BY DIGEST that it committed those exact accepted bytes. The digest list is the load-bearing link between what the user accepted and what finally ships.
2. CLEARANCE READY COMES NOW, NOT AT THE ENABLING STEP. The user's acceptance is not delayed by other work.
3. The measured per-event unregistered-member list is recorded on the slice as an accepted widening of the enabling step: 9 of 14 fixtures carry members the catalogue does not list.

THE CLEARANCE STEP ENDS WITHOUT A COMMIT, AND THAT IS THE CORRECT OUTCOME. Its product is the clearance evidence, the user's verbatim acceptance, the preserved artefacts with digests, the prepared inventory diff, and the handover.

MY OWN RECORD ON THIS QUESTION: four positions. Commit now with the inventory extended; land with the enabling step; widen the guard and land now; and finally, land with the enabling step. Two of the four moves came from measurements I had not made and one came from a ruling that crossed mine. The worker's measurements were right every time and none of them was ever contradicted. The lesson I take is the one the lead already named for the epic memory, and a second one of my own: BEFORE SPECIFYING A NEW GUARD ARM, ASK HOW LONG ITS POPULATION WILL EXIST. An arm that is vacuous after the next step is not a widening; it is debt.

SITTING 5, COMPACTION. Report by capturer-s6-5.

1. SITTING AND VERSION
Sitting name: SITTING 5, COMPACTION (two rows, per the supervisor addendum on aura-plugins-ae098k: experimental.compaction.autocontinue is HELD and not sought here).
opencode --version, taken in the launching tmux shell immediately before the session: 1.18.29.

2. WHO DROVE AND HOW
This agent (capturer-s6-5) drove a tmux session named capturer-s6-5, through the tmux-capture-driver protocol (read pane before each keystroke, text and Enter as two send-keys calls). No non-interactive fallback was needed; the interactive path ran end to end.

3. THE KIT
Plugin: /home/minttea/.local/share/pasture-captures/s6/project/.opencode/plugins/pasture-lifecycle.ts
Plugin SHA-256, verified in the project directory: 73e646d854ecc7c3b5ae326a988b3bac0e90355da4c7d7760407ab74d2b1a649 (equals the kit-safe digest in the addendum).
Binary: /home/minttea/.claude-scratch/worker-s6-l1/bin/pasture-head
Binary SHA-256, verified: 0411482772b75caff4a5dab869c590475dfb0b8df721e8da049281a50044920b.
Binary --version: "pasture version devel".
Project directory: /home/minttea/.local/share/pasture-captures/s6/project.
COVERED-ROW SET (precondition P2), checked in the project copy: the returned plugin object registers 12 keys: the one "event" key (all 32 bus observations) plus 11 named keys (tool.execute.before, chat.message, permission.ask, command.execute.before, shell.env, tool.execute.after, experimental.chat.messages.transform, experimental.chat.system.transform, experimental.session.compacting, experimental.text.complete, tool.definition). That is 43 rows, matching the order exactly: 47 catalogue rows minus chat.params, chat.headers, experimental.compaction.autocontinue and experimental.provider.small_model. No held row is registered; no ordinary row is missing. The four held names occur once each inside the METADATA data blob (line 6 of the file, a data literal that registers nothing) — expected, not a finding.

4. PLUGIN LOAD EVIDENCE
The host log (~/.local/share/opencode/log/opencode.log, filtered to run=c2b45cf2, the run ID for THIS sitting's project directory /home/minttea/.local/share/pasture-captures/s6/project) shows no "failed to load plugin" line naming pasture-lifecycle. The only failed-to-load line for this run names a different plugin: bd-prime.ts ("must default export an object with server()") — not this campaign's concern, matching the pattern the recipe predicted for an unrelated plugin.
No explicit msg="loading plugin" line naming pasture-lifecycle appears for this run (such lines appear elsewhere in the log only for npm-cache-installed plugins, e.g. opencode-claude-auth; the local file plugin under .opencode/plugins does not appear to log that message the same way). I record this as an anomaly in the log-line check, but the PLUGIN DID LOAD, proved directly: 49 capture files were written into .../s6/s5 before I sent any prompt (opencode_plugin_added_1_18_29.1..45, opencode_catalog_updated_1_18_29.1-2, opencode_integration_updated_1_18_29.1), all timestamped at session-resume start, which is only possible if the plugin's "event" callback is registered and running.

5. STEPS, IN ORDER
State: resumed the shared session by id (per the supervisor addendum), ses_f8c74e69bffeqDIe64dzbMVPc4, in project directory /home/minttea/.local/share/pasture-captures/s6/project. That session already held a completed turn (a prior sitting's "Find first line of README.md" turn), satisfying the sitting's state requirement.

Step T1 (setup, in the tmux shell, before opencode started):
  export PASTURE_BIN=/home/minttea/.claude-scratch/worker-s6-l1/bin/pasture-head
  export PASTURE_DB_PATH=/home/minttea/.local/share/pasture-captures/s6/scratch/pasture-s5.db
  export PASTURE_CAPTURE_DIR=/home/minttea/.local/share/pasture-captures/s6/s5
  unset CLAUDECODE CLAUDE_CODE_ENTRYPOINT
Verified with printenv in the same shell before launch.

Step T2: opencode -s ses_f8c74e69bffeqDIe64dzbMVPc4. The TUI came up directly into the resumed session (no trust prompt, no fresh-install wait, since the project's .opencode/ was already populated by an earlier sitting). Pane showed the OpenCode banner and a "Continue" line naming the same session id.

Step T3 (the trigger): typed the literal text "/compact" as one send-keys -l call, paused about one second, sent Enter as a separate call.
Expected files: opencode_experimental_session_compacting_1_18_29.1.json, opencode_session_compacted_1_18_29.1.json.
Both appeared. Wait: the bounded poll for opencode_session_compacted_1_18_29.1.json reported 0s waited — both files were already present in the directory listing by the time I checked, meaning they were written within the first couple of seconds of the compaction turn (screen was corrupted by drawn-over stderr in the interim; see Anomaly below). Total elapsed wall time for the compaction turn, judged from the file mtimes and the session going quiet, was under one minute.

Step T4 (close-out): sent Ctrl-C to the TUI. It ended cleanly and printed a resume line naming the SAME session id (ses_f8c74e69bffeqDIe64dzbMVPc4), confirming the session survives for sitting 7.

author: David Huu Pham
text:
RULING ON lsp.updated, AND WHY "NO REACHABLE TRIGGER" WOULD BE THE WRONG WORD (supervisor-s6, 2026-09-05).

## I DO NOT RULE THE ROW YET, AND THAT IS THE RULING
The lead asked me to place lsp.updated in the table now. I DECLINE, for one round, because a sitting is ordered that decides it. Sitting 4b sets the language-server subsystem on in its OWN project configuration, opens a C-sharp file with a server already installed, and looks. That sitting either produces the capture or produces the strongest withholding evidence available. PLACING THE ROW BEFORE IT RUNS WOULD BE A GUESS DRESSED AS A DECISION, and the whole campaign has been about not doing that.

## BUT THE CLASS IS ALREADY DECIDABLE, AND IT IS NOT "NO REACHABLE TRIGGER"
WithheldNoReachableTrigger says something about the HOST: that nothing a user can do makes the event happen. THAT IS FALSE HERE, and we know it is false before 4b runs. The event fires once per newly spawned language-server client; the host simply disables every server when the configuration key is unset (lsp/lsp.ts:152, with the key optional at core/src/v1/config/config.ts:120). A user who sets the key gets the servers, and the trigger is then an ordinary file read.
THE HONEST DISTINCTION, and I want it in the vocabulary discussion rather than smuggled into a row:
- UNREACHABLE is a property of the HOST. Nothing the user does produces the event. permission.ask is this: the host declares the hook and never calls it.
- CONFIGURATION-DEPENDENT is a property of the DEPLOYMENT. The event happens for a user who enables the feature and never for one who does not.
Recording a configuration-dependent row as unreachable would put a false statement about the host into a file we ship, which is the same defect this slice already found in the permission.ask blocking cells.

## WE HAVE ALREADY CAPTURED A ROW OF THIS EXACT CLASS, WHICH SETTLES THE PRECEDENT
permission.replied is in hand, and it fired ONLY after a permission rule was set under the agent, because the user's own global per-agent setting otherwise allows the tool and no prompt ever appears. Nobody proposed calling that row unreachable. It is an ordinary enabled row whose capture required a stated configuration.
SO IF 4b PRODUCES THE FILE, lsp.updated IS AN ORDINARY ENABLED ROW ON THE SAME FOOTING, with its configuration stated. If 4b does NOT produce the file with the subsystem enabled and a server present, the row is withheld and its reason must say THAT — enabled, server present, no client spawned — and not "no trigger was found", because a trigger was found and run.

## WHAT THIS ADDS TO THE CLEARANCE ORDER, AND I HAVE APPLIED IT
The L3 prompt now requires, PER FIXTURE, one clause naming any non-default configuration the capture needed. Two rows are known to need one: permission.replied and, if it lands, lsp.updated.
THE REASON IS NOT BOOKKEEPING. A fixture is evidence about what a host sends. A reader who does not know a non-default setting produced it will conclude the event fires for everybody, and it does not. The clause costs a line and it is the difference between a true record and a misleading one.
AND IT DOES NOT WEAKEN AUTHENTICITY, which is worth saying plainly so nobody argues the fixtures down: a real host sent the bytes. CONFIGURATION DECIDES WHETHER AN EVENT HAPPENS, NEVER WHAT IT LOOKS LIKE WHEN IT DOES. The record should say which of those two things it is describing.

The glob matches neither the three controls nor the sidecars, so 22 is the 8 committed fixtures plus my 14.

B2 A COUNT FIX ALONE WOULD NOT CLEAR IT. After the count the same guard reads every top-level member of every matched fixture and refuses a member the generated transport metadata does not declare. Measured per fixture against the generated registration:

  UserPromptExpansion: 3 (expansion_type, command_args, command_source).

author: David Huu Pham
text:
FINAL RECONCILED RULING ON THE FIXTURE GUARD: WIDEN IT, WITH MY VACUITY OBJECTION REPAIRED (supervisor-s4, 2026-09-05).

THE STATE THAT MADE THIS HARD, said plainly so nobody reads the thread as indecision alone. Two of the team lead's messages crossed two of mine, on one question. The lead accepted option (a) in one message and accepted the widening in the next; each was written without sight of the ruling of mine it crossed. So there were two live acceptances of two different options. I did not flip to the newest. I stopped the worker and reconciled.

MY OBJECTION TO THE WIDENING WAS AGAINST A DETAIL OF MY OWN SPECIFICATION, AND IT IS REPAIRABLE. I objected that the new arm would be VACUOUS: all 14 cleared fixtures become enabled at the enabling step, so the registered-but-not-enabled population goes to ZERO and, by the non-vacuity check I MYSELF specified, the guard would then turn RED. That objection is correct against MY SPECIFICATION. It is not an objection to widening the guard. THE FAULT WAS THE NON-VACUITY CLAUSE I INVENTED, not the widening the lead invited.

THE REPAIRED SPECIFICATION. Three POSITIVE rules, every one permanently non-vacuous in both the state before enabling and the state after, plus one SCOPE clause that asserts nothing and therefore needs no population.
 RULE A, over EVERY matched fixture: it names a REGISTERED event. Population is every fixture, at least 8 forever. Never dies.
 RULE B, over EVERY ENABLED event: EXACTLY ONE fixture names it. Population is the enabled set, at least 8 forever. THIS IS THE REPLACEMENT FOR THE COUNT CHECK AND IT IS STRICTLY STRONGER, because a count is not an identity: two fixtures for one enabled event and none for another PASSES TODAY.
 RULE C, over every fixture naming an ENABLED event: every top-level member is declared by the transport. UNCHANGED, full strength, permanently non-vacuous.
 RULE D is a SCOPE, not an arm: a fixture naming a registered but not-enabled event is outside Rule C. It makes no assertion, so it has no population to be empty, and it cannot go vacuous. THIS IS THE WHOLE REPAIR.
 Keep the existing enabled-count-above-zero guard against a manifest that enables nothing.
 Keep the glob exactly as it is. It ends in _2_1_261.json, so the three controls do not match it and must not start to.

CHECKED IN BOTH STATES, because that is the check I failed to make the first time.
 BEFORE ENABLING: 22 matched fixtures, 8 enabled. Rule A checks 22. Rule B checks 8. Rule C checks 8. Rule D scopes out 14. GREEN.
 AFTER ENABLING: 22 matched fixtures, 22 enabled. Rule A checks 22. Rule B checks 22. Rule C checks 22. Rule D scopes out none and asserts nothing. GREEN, and NO ARM IS DEAD.

MUTATIONS, each named, each performable, each proving one rule:
 M-a delete the fixture of one enabled event -> RED at Rule B.
 M-b duplicate a fixture so one enabled event has two and another has none -> RED at Rule B. RECORD THAT THIS IS GREEN UNDER TODAY'S COUNT CHECK. This single pair is the whole proof that the rewrite STRENGTHENED the enabled arm rather than weakening it, and it is the most important evidence in the change.
 M-c plant an undeclared member on an ENABLED fixture -> RED at Rule C.
 M-d set any fixture's hook_event_name to a name the registration does not carry -> RED at Rule A.
 M-e plant an undeclared member on a NOT-ENABLED fixture -> GREEN BY DESIGN. Say so in the comment, and name Rule C at enabling as what catches it.

REPLACE THE SOURCE COMMENT. It reads "the corpus is exactly the events the activation table enables, read from that table", which becomes FALSE when this lands, and a false comment stops the next reader from looking.

WHAT LANDS: ONE COMMIT, after the user's verbatim acceptance and after the team lead has seen CLEARANCE READY — the 14 fixtures, their sidecars, the filled CLEARANCE.md, the widened guard, and the extension of the closed hand inventory. The lead's preservation requirement stands anyway: the accepted artefacts are also preserved outside every repository with digests recorded here, so the enabling step can prove by digest that it holds the exact accepted bytes.

THE CROSS-SLICE FOLLOW-UP IS CONSISTENT WITH THIS AND CONFIRMS IT. The lead filed the missing Codex and OpenCode equivalents blocked by the enabling step, "so it follows the Claude shape". That presupposes a Claude shape exists to follow. Under option (a) no shape would exist yet.

MY LESSON, and it is the one worth keeping from four positions on one question: I SPECIFIED A NON-VACUITY CHECK WITHOUT ASKING HOW LONG ITS POPULATION WOULD LIVE, then treated my own bad clause as a reason to abandon a sound design. Test a proposed guard in EVERY state the system will occupy, not only the state in front of you.

author: David Huu Pham
text:
SITTING 5 ACCEPTED, THE RE-COUNTS ACCEPTED, AND ONE LOOP CLOSED SO IT STOPS BEING RE-REPORTED (supervisor-s6, 2026-09-05).

## SITTING 5 ACCEPTED, AND IT PROVED THE HOLD RATHER THAN ASSUMING IT
Verified on disk: experimental_session_compacting 1 file, session_compacted 1 file. Both target rows present.
AND THE PART THAT MATTERS MORE THAN THE TWO ROWS: all four held rows are ABSENT from that directory — chat.params 0, chat.headers 0, experimental.provider.small_model 0, experimental.compaction.autocontinue 0.
THIS IS A LIVE NEGATIVE TEST AT THE ONE MOMENT IT COUNTS. experimental.compaction.autocontinue fires after a compaction succeeds. Sitting 5 RAN A COMPACTION. If removing the key had not worked, that is the sitting where the file would have appeared, and it did not. Until now the hold rested on reading the plugin and counting its keys; it now rests on the host declining to produce the event at the exact operation that produces it.
chat.params and chat.headers are the same story with more force: they fire on EVERY request, so their absence across a whole sitting is a repeated negative, not a single one. The hold is a property of the file, and the file behaved.

## THE RE-COUNTS ACCEPTED, AND THE TWO OUTCOMES ARE BOTH USEFUL
Sitting 3: original 717, re-take 720, confirmed by two independent reads and a third after hashing. The three extra files are named with sizes and digests, all out-of-catalogue stems, and the TARGET-ROW COUNTS ARE UNCHANGED — shell.env 3, permission.replied 1. My own count of that directory was 720, which matches. The addendum does not replace the original report, which is the right handling: the record shows the first reading, the second, and the reason they differ.
Sitting 2: original 179, re-take 179 and 179, identical filename by filename, zero differences. A NIL RESULT, AND IT IS WORTH AS MUCH AS THE OTHER. It shows the rule is discriminating rather than always finding something, and it shows that sitting's evidence was already sound.
That pair is the whole argument for the two-read rule in one page: one directory moved, one did not, and neither could have been known without reading twice.

## LOOP CLOSED: THE MISSING "loading plugin" LINE IS NOT AN ANOMALY AND MUST STOP BEING REPORTED AS ONE
Sitting 5 flagged that no host-log line named pasture-lifecycle for its run. THAT LINE DOES NOT EXIST AT THIS HOST VERSION. I measured it when sitting 1 raised the same point: packages/opencode/src/plugin/index.ts logs plugin loading ONLY on the failure branch, at :231. There is no success log anywhere in that file, so its absence is the expected state for a plugin that loaded perfectly.
THE PROOF THAT REPLACES IT IS THE ONE SITTING 5 ALREADY GAVE: captures arriving from the widened key at resume time, before any prompt. That is direct evidence of registration.
I am closing this loop because it has now been reported twice as an anomaly by two different agents, and a known absence that keeps being re-raised costs a reader's attention every time and eventually trains them to skip the anomaly section. THE REMAINING SITTINGS SHOULD NOT REPORT IT. The load evidence is the file arrival, and the only log line that matters is a FAILURE line naming pasture-lifecycle, whose absence is the check.

## STATE
Accepted: sittings 1, 2, 3, 5 and 8, and sitting 4 at 3 of 4. Running: 6b, alone. Queued in order: 4b alone, then 7 last, because 7 deletes sessions and must run when no other sitting needs one. Sitting 7 reuses the session sitting 5 left alive.
Outstanding on the user: D-1 held pending the population derivation, and D-2, which decides whether the four held rows are ever captured. Everything else in this leaf is moving.

text:
SITTING 8 ADDENDUM: re-take of the capture-directory file count, host stopped.

REASON. Supervisor-s6's bookkeeping order: a listing taken while the host was still running may undercount. I re-ran the count and the listing after the host stopped, twice, and I report both numbers here without replacing the original report.

ORIGINAL COUNT (taken during/just after the run): 109 files.
RE-TAKE COUNT, read 1 (host stopped): 109 files.
RE-TAKE COUNT, read 2 (host stopped): 109 files.
The two re-take reads agree with each other and with the original.

FULL COMPARISON. I compared the full file list and the SHA-256 of every file, original vs re-take, name for name. The diff is EMPTY: same 109 file names, same 109 SHA-256 hashes, byte for byte. No file was added, removed, or changed between the original listing and the re-take.

NO NEW FILE. There is no file in the re-take that was absent from the original, so there is no additional SHA-256/size to report under that heading.

I did not start any host for this addendum. I did not delete or move anything.

author: David Huu Pham
text:
THE RE-COUNT SWEEP IS CLOSED, AND ITS RESULT REFINES THE RULE THAT PRODUCED IT (supervisor-s6, 2026-09-05).

## ALL FOUR DIRECTORIES ARE NOW ACCOUNTED FOR
- Sitting 1: 142 files, taken from the directory by me because its capturer may be gone. Two reads two seconds apart, both 142. Its original report said 142.
- Sitting 2: 179 original, 179 and 179 on re-take, identical filename by filename, zero differences.
- Sitting 3: 717 original, 720 on re-take, three extra files named with sizes and digests, all out-of-catalogue, target-row counts unchanged.
- Sitting 8: 109 original, 109 and 109 on re-take, an empty name-for-name digest diff.
ONE OF FOUR MOVED. THREE DID NOT.

## THE REFINEMENT, AND IT MATTERS FOR HOW THE RULE IS STATED
I wrote the rule as "stop the host first, then list", on the ground that a live host is still writing. THAT IS NOT QUITE THE CONDITION. Sitting 2 listed under the same old ordering as sitting 3 and did not move at all.
THE REAL CONDITION IS WHETHER THE HOST IS STILL EMITTING, WHICH IS NOT THE SAME AS WHETHER IT IS ALIVE. A host that has finished its turn and gone idle emits nothing, so a listing taken from it is already stable. Sitting 3 differed in one way: ITS HOST WAS KILLED ABRUPTLY BY ANOTHER AGENT while bootstrap events were still arriving, so three more landed between its listing and the end.
SO THE RULE SURVIVES, AND ITS JUSTIFICATION CHANGES. It is not "a live host always invalidates a listing"; it is "YOU CANNOT TELL FROM OUTSIDE WHETHER EMISSION HAS STOPPED". Bootstrap events keep arriving for a while after start, and nothing on the screen says when the last one has landed. Two agreeing reads of a stopped directory is the cheapest available proof, and it is cheap precisely because three times out of four it finds nothing.
I RECORD THE CORRECTION RATHER THAN LETTING THE ORIGINAL WORDING STAND, because the original reason would have a worker believing a stopped host is the whole guarantee, and then trusting a single read the moment stopping is inconvenient.

## THE THREE NIL RESULTS ARE THE POINT, NOT THE OVERHEAD
A rule that always finds something is usually measuring itself. This one found a real gap in one directory and nothing in three, which is what a discriminating check looks like. The three nil results also cost almost nothing: two reads and a diff.
AND THE ONE HIT WAS HARMLESS ONLY BY LUCK. The three missing files were bootstrap noise. They could as easily have been the last event of the sitting, and the clearance step, which works from the report, would have had no way to know it was short.

## WHAT REMAINS OF THIS THREAD
Nothing. Every capture directory that exists has a count confirmed by at least two reads, and the one discrepancy is explained, named and digested. The clearance step can now trust the listings in the reports, which was the whole purpose.

text:
SITTING 4 RESUME REPORT: relaunched the host, re-ran only the Program.cs read, lsp.updated confirmed absent. Compliance notes for H-1 and H-2 below.

## Correction to the earlier report's anomaly A2

The earlier report speculated that the opencode process was killed by resource contention (possible OOM)
during the first T3 attempt. Per the team-lead's relay, the actual cause was ANOTHER AGENT'S BROAD PROCESS
KILL (a kill by program name or pattern, hitting multiple sittings' opencode processes at once), not a
resource exhaustion event specific to this sitting. I withdraw my OOM speculation; the process ended
because of an external broad kill, not because of anything this sitting's own resource usage did. My own
kill discipline for this sitting: I killed only my own tmux session (`tmux kill-session -t cap-s6-4`) at
close, both times, never a process by name or pattern.

## State at resume

tmux session cap-s6-4 was NOT alive when I received the resume order — I had already killed it during
this sitting's own C4 housekeeping step, before the resume order arrived. The project directory's git
state was intact and unaffected: branch `probe-branch`, one commit, NOTES.md still carrying the earlier
"hello" edit. I created a fresh tmux session under the SAME name, `cap-s6-4`, in the SAME project
directory, and proceeded from there. The three previously captured rows (file.edited, file.watcher.updated,
vcs.branch.updated) remain on disk, untouched, and are NOT re-triggered; only the Program.cs read (row 21,
lsp.updated) was re-run, as ordered.

## Preconditions re-verified before the relaunch

- P1: `opencode --version` immediately before relaunch: 1.18.29. Correct.
- Env re-exported in the new tmux shell, before any hook command: PASTURE_BIN, PASTURE_DB_PATH
  (/home/minttea/.local/share/pasture-captures/s6/scratch/pasture-s4.db, the same per-sitting scratch
  database as before, never the live store), PASTURE_CAPTURE_DIR
  (/home/minttea/.local/share/pasture-captures/s6/s4, same directory as before). `unset CLAUDECODE
  CLAUDE_CODE_ENTRYPOINT` run in the same shell before launching opencode.
- P5: host log size noted before relaunch: 404,702,460 bytes.
- H-2 baseline taken BEFORE relaunch: sha256sum of ~/.local/share/pasture/pasture.db =
  3da48f08f603e306f19727976379bc918192f9716f0cd9e9ba6855344ee0b5aa, size 157081600 bytes, mtime
  1788642838 (unix).

## The relaunch and the trigger

Relaunched `opencode` interactively in the tmux session. The pane showed the same "ugly under load"
symptom noted in the order: bootstrap stderr from the widened `event` hook filled the screen and never
cleared to a clean prompt view, but this time keystrokes still landed (the underlying process was healthy,
confirmed by `ps` showing PID 2649206, cwd = project-s4, growing CPU time throughout). I did not fight the
redraw; I sent the trigger anyway, per the order.

Sent: "Read Program.cs and tell me its first line." The turn ran to completion (confirmed: new
opencode_tool_execute_before_1_18_29.8.json / .9.json show a fresh glob + read of Program.cs under a NEW
session ID `ses_f8c64c59effewlaOikae51eldR`, distinct from both earlier sessions; matching
opencode_tool_execute_after_1_18_29.8.json / .9.json show the read completed). Waited 90 seconds in a
bounded poll for opencode_lsp_updated_1_18_29.1.json: it did NOT appear. The opencode process itself was
NOT killed this time (still running and healthy after the wait, confirmed by `ps`).

## H-1 compliance: the log line is now filtered to MY OWN run, not the shared tail

The host log carries a per-process `run=<id>` correlation key on every line, and the "creating instance" /
"fromDirectory" lines carry `directory=<path>`. I found the exact run ID whose directory equals my project:

```
grep "directory=/home/minttea/.local/share/pasture-captures/s6/project-s4" <log tail> | grep -oP 'run=\K[a-f0-9]+' | sort -u
-> 4aae16ad
```

Filtering the log tail to `run=4aae16ad` only (80 lines total, none from any other sitting), the two load
facts hold on MY OWN run, not a neighbour's:
```
timestamp=2026-09-05T22:05:27.771Z level=ERROR run=4aae16ad message="failed to load plugin" path=file:///home/minttea/.config/opencode/plugins/bd-prime.ts error="..."
timestamp=2026-09-05T22:05:27.773Z level=INFO run=4aae16ad message="all LSPs are disabled"
```
No line in run=4aae16ad names pasture-lifecycle as a failed load. No other `lsp`- or `csharp`-related line
appears in this run at all. So the earlier sitting's conclusion (LSP subsystem off by default, independent
of PATH) is now confirmed as MY OWN run's fact, not inferred from the shared, interleaved tail across five
concurrent sittings.

## H-2 compliance: live-store digest, not the fault file

Checked immediately after closing this resume session:
```
sha256sum ~/.local/share/pasture/pasture.db
-> 3da48f08f603e306f19727976379bc918192f9716f0cd9e9ba6855344ee0b5aa   (unchanged from the pre-relaunch value)
stat -c '%s %Y' ~/.local/share/pasture/pasture.db
-> 157081600 1788642838   (unchanged size and mtime)
```
Byte digest and mtime are IDENTICAL before and after this resume session. The live store's
lifecycle-faults.jsonl growing (from ambient Claude Code hook activity elsewhere) is NOT read as a touched
live store, per H-2; I did not use fault-file growth as evidence either way here.

## No capture file deleted; sizes of every new file

Total files in the capture directory now: 907 (was 693 before this resume; +214 new, 0 deleted). No
numbered file was removed at any point in this sitting. lsp.updated remains ABSENT after 907 files and two
independent, complete turns (one via `opencode run`, one via the TUI) both reading Program.cs.

WHAT I MEASURED MYSELF, read-only, rather than take on trust.

V2 NO NAME SURVIVES. ZERO occurrences of the capturing user's name in ANY file in that directory, the clearance record included. All 25 payloads carry the placeholder segment.
V3 THE EXISTING ACCEPTANCE IS UNTOUCHED, AND THIS IS MECHANICAL, NOT A PROMISE. The whole change is 410 insertions and ZERO DELETIONS. A record that removed or reworded one line of the acceptance the user gave earlier today would show a deletion. There is none.

V5 THE WORKTREE HOLDS ONLY WHAT IT SHOULD: the inventory extension and the clearance record. No generator input, no generated file, no activation file, no transport, and no codegen guard.

THE JUDGEMENT ITEM GOES TO THE USER, NOT TO ME. Five committed values are the host's own bytes, because the classifier does not class them as free text and the substitution therefore did not fire. THE WORKER REFUSED TO HAND-EDIT THEM AND WAS RIGHT. A hand edit would make the committed bytes impossible to reproduce from the two documented rules, and the rules are the contract; it would have bought nothing, because the values are "ok", "ok", "ok", "/probe" and "ok". The user sees the exact bytes and decides. That is the correct handling of a judgement item: name it, do not resolve it quietly.

THE SECRET SCAN HAS THE CONTROL THAT MATTERS. The module scan passes with the fixtures in place; the nine-shape control passes; and the REACH CONTROL was run — a key shape planted into a COPY of one NEW fixture turned the scan RED naming the file and the byte offset, and the copy was discarded. That is what proves the scan saw THESE files instead of passing by doing nothing.

STRUCTURE IS PRESERVED. Every raw payload was compared field by field with its committed bytes: same paths, same types, same array lengths, same nulls, zero differences over all fourteen. Digests recomputed over the committed bytes. Two of the three home spellings occur, the absolute and the slug, and both were rewritten; the relative spelling occurs in none of the fourteen, established by search rather than by assumption.

REFUSED CLASSES: NONE. No payload carries a tool response at all. The largest whole payload is 986 committed bytes against a 4096 threshold. No environment dump.

THE COMMIT PATH IS SETTLED AND IT IS OPTION (a). The 14 fixtures land WITH the enabling step, in one commit there that grows the registered field lists and derives the guard's population per event. The count-is-not-identity hole is PINNED on that leaf rather than left ownerless, and a follow-up carries the per-event shape to the other two harnesses afterwards.
I RECORD THAT THE TEAM LEAD'S RESOLUTION IS BETTER THAN MY WIDENING. At the enabling step all 14 fixtures are enabled, so the per-event derivation lands in the only state where it is permanently non-vacuous, and the scope clause I invented for the in-between window is not needed at all. Everything I was trying to protect is achieved with strictly less machinery. My four positions on this question ended one step behind the simplest correct answer.

NEXT: the user's acceptance. On the acceptance the worker writes the verbatim text into the record, preserves the accepted fixtures, sidecars and record OUTSIDE every repository with their digests recorded here, and hands over. IT DOES NOT COMMIT; the commit belongs to the enabling step, which must later prove by digest that it holds these exact accepted bytes.

V1 COUNTS. 25 payloads and 25 sidecars in the fixture directory: the 14 new pairs plus the 11 that were already there. One sidecar per payload, no orphan either way.
V2 NO NAME SURVIVES. ZERO occurrences of the capturing user's name in ANY file in that directory, the clearance record included. All 25 payloads carry the placeholder segment.
V3 THE EXISTING ACCEPTANCE IS UNTOUCHED, AND THIS IS MECHANICAL, NOT A PROMISE. The whole change is 410 insertions and ZERO DELETIONS. A record that removed or reworded one line of the acceptance the user gave earlier today would show a deletion. There is none.
V4 THE FIVE PLAINTEXT VALUES ARE AS DECLARED: .delta "ok" on MessageDisplay; .last_assistant_message "ok" on Stop and on SubagentStop; .prompt "/probe" on UserPromptExpansion; .tool_input.content "ok" on PermissionRequest. The three substituted fields are same-length placeholder runs. The path inside PermissionRequest is the placeholder.
V5 THE WORKTREE HOLDS ONLY WHAT IT SHOULD: the inventory extension and the clearance record. No generator input, no generated file, no activation file, no transport, and no codegen guard.

THE JUDGEMENT ITEM GOES TO THE USER, NOT TO ME. Five committed values are the host's own bytes, because the classifier does not class them as free text and the substitution therefore did not fire. THE WORKER REFUSED TO HAND-EDIT THEM AND WAS RIGHT. A hand edit would make the committed bytes impossible to reproduce from the two documented rules, and the rules are the contract; it would have bought nothing, because the values are "ok", "ok", "ok", "/probe" and "ok". The user sees the exact bytes and decides. That is the correct handling of a judgement item: name it, do not resolve it quietly.

THE SECRET SCAN HAS THE CONTROL THAT MATTERS. The module scan passes with the fixtures in place; the nine-shape control passes; and the REACH CONTROL was run — a key shape planted into a COPY of one NEW fixture turned the scan RED naming the file and the byte offset, and the copy was discarded. That is what proves the scan saw THESE files instead of passing by doing nothing.

STRUCTURE IS PRESERVED. Every raw payload was compared field by field with its committed bytes: same paths, same types, same array lengths, same nulls, zero differences over all fourteen. Digests recomputed over the committed bytes. Two of the three home spellings occur, the absolute and the slug, and both were rewritten; the relative spelling occurs in none of the fourteen, established by search rather than by assumption.

REFUSED CLASSES: NONE. No payload carries a tool response at all. The largest whole payload is 986 committed bytes against a 4096 threshold. No environment dump.

THE COMMIT PATH IS SETTLED AND IT IS OPTION (a). The 14 fixtures land WITH the enabling step, in one commit there that grows the registered field lists and derives the guard's population per event. The count-is-not-identity hole is PINNED on that leaf rather than left ownerless, and a follow-up carries the per-event shape to the other two harnesses afterwards.
I RECORD THAT THE TEAM LEAD'S RESOLUTION IS BETTER THAN MY WIDENING. At the enabling step all 14 fixtures are enabled, so the per-event derivation lands in the only state where it is permanently non-vacuous, and the scope clause I invented for the in-between window is not needed at all. Everything I was trying to protect is achieved with strictly less machinery. My four positions on this question ended one step behind the simplest correct answer.

NEXT: the user's acceptance. On the acceptance the worker writes the verbatim text into the record, preserves the accepted fixtures, sidecars and record OUTSIDE every repository with their digests recorded here, and hands over. IT DOES NOT COMMIT; the commit belongs to the enabling step, which must later prove by digest that it holds these exact accepted bytes.

author: David Huu Pham
text:
MEASURED CODEX INPUT TO THE VOCABULARY QUESTION (supervisor-s5, 2026-09-05). The Codex coverage work has a concrete instance of the distinction this task is trying to name, and it was measured on the live host rather than argued.
THE INSTANCE: PermissionRequest. Codex emits it only when the session's permission profile ASKS for approval. The account default in the sitting was "Approve for me", which auto-approves anything not flagged unsafe. Under that default the event NEVER FIRES, however the command is chosen: the earlier pin-bump sitting saw no approval prompt for a read-only command, and this slice's first attempt at a network command also ran silently because the sandbox refused the network without asking. The event fired only after the operator changed the profile with the host's own command to "Ask for approval" and then asked for a command that needed to leave the sandbox.
WHY THIS IS NOT NoReachableTrigger. A trigger exists, it is documented by the host's own menu, any operator can reach it, and it produced an authentic capture. Calling that row "no reachable trigger" would be false.
WHY IT IS ALSO NOT PLAIN REACHABILITY, and this is the part worth putting in the vocabulary. The trigger depends on a HOST CONFIGURATION THE OPERATOR CHOOSES, and the common configuration is the one where the event never fires. So a row like this can be enabled, proven and honest, while a user on the default profile exercises it NEVER. Any claim of the form "this event is covered" is true of the product and misleading about the user's day, unless the row records what configuration it needs.
WHAT I SUGGEST THE VOCABULARY CARRY, offered for the joint proposal and not as my ruling: a CONFIGURATION-DEPENDENT row is one whose trigger exists and is operator-reachable, but only under a named non-default host configuration. It is ENABLED like any other row when a capture proves it. What it gains is a recorded CONDITION: the configuration the host must be in, named in the host's own words, so a reader knows why the event may be silent on a normal machine and does not read the silence as a defect.
A SECOND, WEAKER CODEX INSTANCE, recorded for completeness: SubagentStart and SubagentStop need the host's multi-agent spawn tool. It is stable and enabled by default, so it is NOT configuration-dependent in the sense above; the distinction is whether the DEFAULT reaches the event, not whether a setting exists at all.
THE LINE I WOULD DRAW: the axis is not "is there a switch" but "does the default reach it". A row the default reaches is plain. A row the default never reaches, but an operator can reach on purpose, is configuration-dependent and records its condition. A row no operator can reach at any setting is the one that takes the no-reachable-trigger arm, and by the standing rule it takes it only on a cited absence of an emission site.
EFFECT ON CODEX TODAY: none of this changes the captures or the clearance. It changes one row's RECORDED REASON at the enabling leaf, which is where this task blocks.

author: David Huu Pham
text:
SITTING 4 RESUME ACCEPTED, AND I WITHDRAW ONE OF MY OWN SUPPORTS (supervisor-s6, 2026-09-05).

## ACCEPTED, AND THE lsp FINDING IS NOW STRONGER THAN IT WAS
The resume re-ran only the remaining step, the turn completed fully, and lsp.updated still did not appear after a bounded 90-second wait.
THE H-1 COMPLIANCE IS WHAT UPGRADES THE FINDING. The capturer filtered the host log to the single run identifier whose directory matches its own project, 80 lines, zero from any other sitting, and on that filtered set "all LSPs are disabled" is logged ON ITS OWN RUN. So the disabled-subsystem fact is now measured for this sitting rather than inferred from an interleaved tail shared with four other hosts. That is the difference between a fact and a plausible reading, and it is exactly what H-1 was written for.
The live-store check is also stronger than asked: digest AND mtime, byte-identical before and after, not inferred from fault-file growth.

## I WITHDRAW A SUPPORT FOR MY OWN ORDER, BECAUSE THE FACT UNDER IT IS GONE
The capturer withdraws its earlier speculation that the operating system killed its host under memory pressure. The process was ended by ANOTHER AGENT'S BROAD PROCESS KILL, not by resource contention.
I USED THAT KILL AS EVIDENCE WHEN I TIGHTENED THE CAMPAIGN TO ONE LIVE HOST. It is no longer evidence, and I will not leave a withdrawn fact propping up an order of mine while I hold other people's claims to measurement.
WHAT ACTUALLY REMAINS UNDER THE ONE-HOST ORDER, stated honestly:
 - THREE MEASURED STALLS, in two different sittings, with the screen never recomposing at a load average near 14. That is real and it is load-related.
 - The 19 GB of swap in use, which was observed, though the kill attributed to it was not caused by it.
 - NOT the operating-system kill. That was one agent's pattern kill and would have happened at any load.
SO THE ORDER STANDS ON THE STALLS ALONE, WHICH IS THINNER THAN I IMPLIED. I keep it, for a reason that does not depend on the strength of the evidence: only two sittings remain, sequential costs perhaps twenty minutes, and the downside of being wrong in the other direction is another lost sitting. A conservative order with a thin justification is fine as long as the justification is stated at its true weight, and mine was not.

## WHAT THE SITTING LEAVES
Sitting 4 stands at 3 of 4. lsp.updated is NOT settled by this resume and was never going to be: the subsystem was still off, because enabling it was outside the ordered trigger. Sitting 4b settles it, with the subsystem on in its own project configuration and a server already present.
The directory now holds 907 files, up from 693, with the new ones listed and digested. The target-row files from before the interruption are unchanged.

author: David Huu Pham
text:
JOINT VOCABULARY PROPOSAL, S6 HALF, FOLDING IN S5's MEASURED INPUT (supervisor-s6, 2026-09-05). supervisor-s4 has not answered yet; where its rows decide something I say so and leave the choice open rather than settling it alone.

## S5 ALREADY DREW THE RIGHT AXIS AND I ADOPT IT
supervisor-s5's line is better than the one I brought: THE AXIS IS NOT "IS THERE A SWITCH" BUT "DOES THE DEFAULT REACH IT". A setting exists for almost everything; what matters is whether an ordinary user ever meets the event. I adopt that wording and build on it.

## THE THREE-WAY DISTINCTION, with each slice's measured instance
1. PLAIN. The default configuration reaches the event. Most rows. Nothing new.
2. CONFIGURATION-DEPENDENT. The default NEVER reaches it; an operator can reach it on purpose, under a named non-default configuration.
   OpenCode, measured: permission.replied fires only when a permission rule is set under the agent, because the user's own global per-agent setting otherwise allows the tool and no prompt appears (agent.ts:293 merges the per-agent permission last; permission/index.ts:32 and :210 select with findLast). lsp.updated fires once per newly spawned language-server client, but the host disables every server when the `lsp` key is unset (lsp/lsp.ts:152; the key is optional at core/src/v1/config/config.ts:120).
   Codex, measured by S5: PermissionRequest fires only under an "ask for approval" profile; the account default auto-approves and the event never fires.
   Claude, per the task text: PermissionDenied fires only when the classifier denies under the user's permission settings.
3. UNREACHABLE. NO operator reaches it at ANY configuration. OpenCode's permission.ask is the clean case: the host declares the hook key at packages/plugin/src/index.ts:261 and nothing in the host calls it, zero occurrences of the trigger in the checkout.

## WHAT EACH CASE DOES
CASE 2, WHEN WE CAPTURE IT — and this is the default, because it is cheap and it is true: the row is ENABLED like any other, and the record carries the CONDITION: the configuration the host must be in, in the host's own words, beside that fixture. S5 asked for exactly this and I have already put the per-fixture clause into my clearance order with the lead's acceptance.
  THE REASON IS NOT BOOKKEEPING. A fixture is evidence about what a host SENDS. Configuration decides WHETHER an event happens, never WHAT IT LOOKS LIKE when it does. Without the condition, "this event is covered" is true of the product and misleading about the user's day: a reader concludes the event fires for everybody, and on the default it fires for nobody.
CASE 3 keeps WithheldNoReachableTrigger, and by the standing rule takes it only on a CITED absence of an emission site.

## THE CONCRETE CHANGE I PROPOSE: RE-WORD ONE CLAUSE, AND MINT NOTHING YET
The arm's doc at internal/lifecycle/activation/types.go today reads: "records that no known action makes the host fire the event in a live session, so no authentic capture can exist."
THE FALSE CLAUSE FOR A CONFIGURATION-DEPENDENT ROW IS THE SECOND ONE. An authentic capture CAN exist; we hold one for permission.replied and S5 holds one for PermissionRequest. The first clause is only loosely wrong; the second is flatly wrong, and it is the clause a later reader would rely on.
PROPOSED, and it makes the arm STRONGER rather than vaguer: "records that no action an operator can take, AT ANY HOST CONFIGURATION, makes the host fire the event in a live session, so no authentic capture can exist. It does NOT cover a row whose DEFAULT configuration never reaches it but which an operator can reach on purpose: such a row is configuration-dependent, and it is captured with its condition recorded."
I PREFER THIS TO A LOOSER RE-WORD ("no action we will take or configuration we will impose") because that version would quietly merge two different facts — a host that cannot, and a team that chose not to — into one arm, and the first fact is the more useful one to a later reader.

## THE FOURTH ARM: NOT YET, AND HERE IS THE EXACT CONDITION THAT WOULD EARN IT
A fourth arm is needed only for a row we DECLINE to capture BECAUSE we will not impose its configuration. That case has a real home and no arm.
S6 HAS ZERO SUCH ROWS: permission.replied is captured; lsp.updated is being settled by a sitting that sets the key, and if it still does not fire with the subsystem enabled and a server present, its reason is neither of these — that is a measured environment fact needing its own sentence.
S5 HAS ZERO: PermissionRequest is captured.
SO THE DECIDING QUESTION IS S4's, and I leave it open: does S4 have rows it declines to capture because it will not impose the configuration, and how many? If several, mint WithheldConfigurationDependent and I support it. If none or one, minting it creates a vocabulary entry that later readers must interpret with no example in front of them, and the re-word above is the smaller and truer change.

## ONE WARNING CARRIED FROM THIS SLICE, FOR WHOEVER ASSIGNS REASONS
A WITHHOLDING REASON RECORDS WHY WE HAVE NO CAPTURE. IT DOES NOT CORRECT A FALSE CLAIM ELSEWHERE. OpenCode's permission.ask carries Blocking, gate-consultation and throw-fail-fast in our catalogue, which together assert that the host asks us for a decision and honours a refusal; at this version it never asks. Giving that row a truer withholding sentence does not touch those three cells, and they remain a separate item. If S4 or S5 holds a row of the same shape, the joint proposal should say so, because the vocabulary change is exactly the kind of work that looks like it closed the problem.

I am NOT stopping the whole unit: the two legality tables are unambiguous and I am implementing them now. ONE HALF OF L3 IS BLOCKED.

WHAT IS BLOCKED: the REACHABILITY column.

THE GAP, measured, not inferred. The reachability rule reads "a cell is reachable only when some ENABLED gate event MAPS TO THAT ActionClass and is not short-circuited by rule 1 or rule 2". That rule presupposes a mapping from a registered native event to an ActionClass. THAT MAPPING DOES NOT EXIST ANYWHERE IN THE TREE, and no S3 task's owned-file list creates it. Evidence: at 9ae98eb, a search for ActionClass across internal and cmd returns matches only in the package I added at L2; internal/lifecycle/gate carries WriteClass, which is the class of a pasture-side WRITE (delivery, definition activation, lineage, disclosure) and is a different subject; internal/runtime carries EventSemantic, BlockingMode and StopLoopPolicy, none of which names an action class.

SO THE DERIVATION HAS NO SOURCE. To build the reachability entries I would have to author the class of all 92 registered events by hand: 33 Claude, 12 Codex, 47 OpenCode. That is not a derivation and it is not a small judgement. It DECIDES WHICH DENY CELLS ARE REACHABLE, and the reachability column is carried into the D5 text the USER APPROVES. Choosing 92 classifications on my own judgement would put my guesses in front of the user as measured facts. The standing order is to surface a gap, not to choose, so I surface it.

WHAT IS NOT BLOCKED, and what I am doing now:
- Verdict with an invalid Unset zero; RoleActionTable 3 x 10 and PhaseActionTable 13 x 10 BUILT AT INIT from the default-allow rule plus the published exception lists; the exhaustiveness check regenerating the grid from the enum arm ranges; every exception cell reads Deny and every other cell reads Allow; Stop, Compact, Permission, PostHoc and PromptSubmit Allow in every row of both tables; an unlisted cell REFUSES and never denies; the two mutations this task names (delete the axis-reviewer worktree cell, and turn one exception into an allow).
I will commit that as its own green unit and report it, so the tables are not held behind the ruling.

WHAT I NEED, one of three; I do not start any of them without an order:
1. RULE that the event-to-action-class mapping belongs to L3 and is MINE to author. Then say whether it is authored per harness or once by native name, and accept that the classes for the 92 events are my judgement, published for the user's approval at D5. I would then also add the derived guard that every registered event on every harness either carries a class or is on an explicit "carries no action class" list, so a new registered event cannot slip through unclassified.
2. RULE that it belongs to another unit (L7 llt3k5 is the closest: it already fills per-event evidence rows and touches internal/runtime), and that L3 ships the tables plus a reachability column that is DERIVED once that mapping exists. L3 would then land without the column and a follow-up adds it.
3. GIVE ME THE MAPPING, from the plan or from the user, as data I transcribe rather than invent.

MY RECOMMENDATION: option 1, with one narrowing that makes it honest and cheap. The reachability column only needs the classes of the events that can reach a DENIED cell, which is four action classes: worktree, subagent, config-change and task-lifecycle. Nothing else is ever denied by either table. So I would classify only the events that map to those four, list every other registered event as "carries no denied-cell class", and let the derived guard prove that list is exhaustive over all 92. That is a handful of named events per harness instead of 92 judgements, every one of them checkable against the native event name, and the user sees a short list rather than a wall.

TWO MEASURED FACTS THE TASK STATES THAT I CONFIRMED AT 9ae98eb, from internal/lifecycle/registration, which is the clean production source (it does NOT depend on internal/tasks, unlike internal/lifecycle/activation, which does and therefore CANNOT be imported by gateauthority without making the cycle this package exists to break):

After the first /probe the corrupted screen still showed the text as typed, which looks exactly like an unsent Enter. The instruction that follows from it is not "be careful with the screen"; it is: THE SCREEN IS NEVER THE EVIDENCE. The evidence is a file in the capture directory or a line in the host log.

It was recorded as cosmetic from one quiet sitting. 2. ActionObservation IS ADDED to ActionClass in types.go, which is mine. Pure observations take it. POST-HOC GATES KEEP ActionPostHoc: Claude PostToolBatch, Codex PostToolUse and PostCompact, OpenCode tool.execute.after. An observation that reports a COMPLETED action of a named class, for example Claude PostToolUse, is ALSO ActionObservation, because Decide rule 1 exits on the semantic before the class is read; I state that in the doc comment. Both tables treat ActionObservation exactly like Stop, Compact, Permission, PostHoc and PromptSubmit: NEVER DENIED. I re-run the L2 exhaustiveness and zero-value cases and they must stay green with the new arm, because those lists are sentinel-derived.
3. THE REACHABILITY COLUMN DERIVES FROM THE REGISTRATION MANIFESTS ONLY: registered, AND blocking or conditionally blocking, AND not short-circuited by rule 1 or rule 2. The column is LABELLED as REGISTERED reachability. The external test package cross-checks enabled-ness through internal/lifecycle/activation, and the report states, per reachable denied cell, whether it is ENABLED today and which harness work must supply the evidence. The D5 text the user sees carries BOTH words. I state in the source why enabled-ness is not read in production: the activation package reaches internal/tasks, and reading it there would make the cycle this package exists to break.
4. THE FOUR CONFIRMED MEASUREMENTS go into the report WITH THE EXACT NATIVE EVENTS: the subagent cells are unreachable-but-mapped and are KEPT and labelled; worktree, task-lifecycle and config-change are reachable on Claude.
5. COMMIT SHAPE: the tables half is its own commit; the mapping, the new arm and the column are the NEXT commit. Each names its files. NO FILE OUTSIDE gateauthority is touched for this. A genuinely unclear class judgement for one event is LISTED HERE WITH MY READING and does not stop the unit.
Beginning: tables commit first, then the mapping, the arm and the column.
