author: David Huu Pham
text:
SECTION 3.4, THE FOURTH SWEEP OVER THE CONTROL CLASS. Delivered in e64fbfb, which is now the head. Two findings, both fixed. The full width of the sweep is below, including every control I examined and found sound.

HOW I RAN IT. I enumerated every control in the four files these commits touch, classified each by its KEY, and then ran a matrix on my own copy: THREE citation worlds (no Codex row cited, ONE cited, EVERY row cited) times EIGHT states of the tree (a green baseline plus seven breaks). Each cell establishes the world, applies the break, runs make generate, and records which controls fire, identified by their own message text and not by test name, because three of the tests hold several controls. 24 cells.
I CORRECTED THE HARNESS ONCE AND I REPORT IT. My first matrix regenerated only for the breaks that change generated input. The world itself moves the profile, so in worlds two and three the manifest was stale and every cell reported the stale-manifest state on top of the break: a swapped axis name looked as if it fired four controls. The corrected matrix regenerates after every world and every break, and those cells then fire only their own control. A harness that makes the tree look guarded when it is not is the same defect as a control that does.

THE POPULATION THE EVIDENCE RULE ACTUALLY MOVES. A row moves only if it is BLOCKING and its citation state changes: evidenceBoundFailure keeps the declared blocking arm while a citation stands and lowers it to report-and-continue without one, and a non-blocking row always takes the strict-hook arm. So the moved population is the DECLARED GATES, 8 of the 12 Codex rows, and it is 8 with no row cited, 7 with one cited and 0 with every row cited. Every control keyed on that population, or on any count derived from it, loses power as the citation work lands. That is the class.

THE TWO FINDINGS.

F1. A HAND-WRITTEN ARM IS INVISIBLE IN THE FULLY CITED WORLD, AND THE CONSTRUCTED READ CONTROL DOES NOT COVER IT. I gave the gate builder a hand-written blocking arm instead of the read and regenerated. With no row cited: five controls fire. With one cited: five fire. With EVERY row cited: NOTHING FIRES. The row equality, the arms control, the divergence subject and both doc-comment subjects all report ok, because the hand-written value equals the value the read would answer for every blocking row at once. My own read control does not see it either, and that is the part worth stating plainly: it proves the READ is right, and this break does not change the read, it stops the catalogue from USING it.
FIX, by the rule at the top of the order. The catalogue builder now takes its rows as a parameter, and a control builds the catalogue TWICE over the same row names with DIFFERENT arms, requiring every row to follow the arm it was built over. No literal can satisfy both builds, whatever value somebody writes. It is RED on the hand-written arm in ALL THREE worlds, and RED on a constant read in all three as well. Its own non-vacuity is a control: with both builds given ONE arm it is RED with "the two constructed builds must use DIFFERENT arms, or a hand-written literal satisfies both and this control proves nothing; both are strict-hook-failure".

F2. THE ARMS CONTROL NAMED A ROLE IT DOES NOT HAVE. Its message said "a read that returned one constant would satisfy every check above, so this control fails first". Measured in all three worlds: a constant read is caught by the ROW EQUALITY, which is a require and stops the test, so the arms control never fires on that break. What it does catch is a DEGENERATE PROFILE, one that gives every Codex row the same arm, where the row equality cannot tell a read from a constant because every answer is the same value. The message now says that. I also carried the condition that was asked for after the last round: the sibling control that was removed becomes reachable again if a later change gives a NON-blocking row a demotable mode, and it should return then.
Note the scope: this does NOT overturn the earlier ruling. The ruling's claim was that in a tree where nothing can move every row carries ONE arm and the arms control fires first, and that is TRUE. The false sentence was a different one, in the control's own message, about the constant read.

THE FULL LIST I EXAMINED, with its verdict. Sound means: the thing it protects was broken in all three worlds and it fired in all three, or the state it guards cannot exist in that world.
 KEYED ON A POPULATION OR COUNT OF THE TREE
 C1 the manifest-versus-runtime divergent set, per harness. Fires on a hand-written arm and on a declared read in worlds one and two, SILENT in world three for both. Covered by the two constructed controls; not fixed here because the property C1 states, that the two artefacts agree, is genuinely unbroken in that world.
 C8 the Codex failure-mode divergence count. Same shape and same verdict as C1.
 C9 the blocking population compared as sets. Same shape and same verdict. I record additionally that in world one BOTH lists are empty, so its set comparison is trivially satisfied there; it still fires on a hand-written blocking arm in that world, which is the break it exists for.
 C14 the row-by-row equality in the catalogue subject. Same shape and same verdict, and it is the control that catches a constant read first.
 C15 the per-row over-claim guard. Its condition is the demoted population, so it does not run in world three. SOUND: in that world no row is demoted, so no row can over-claim by demotion. The state it guards cannot exist there rather than being hidden.
 C16 the arms control. FINDING F2, fixed.
 C2 the over-claiming rows named separately. Its Codex list is empty by construction and its count of 11 is Claude's, so it says nothing about Codex in any world. Not a Codex control; C1 covers a Codex row appearing.
 C3 the eight doc-comment count pins. Fires on a changed count in all three worlds. None of the eight pinned numbers moves with the citation state, which I verified by taking a green baseline in each world. SOUND.
 C4 the two axis name pins. Fires on a swapped name in all three worlds; the semantic and mutation axes do not move with citations. SOUND.
 C10 the three recorded axis sets. Fires on a moved profile semantic in all three worlds. SOUND.
 C13 the WIDTH control. Fires on a deleted catalog row in all three worlds. SOUND.
 C6 the empty-population control. Keyed on the row count and not on the citation state. SOUND.
 C11 the five derivation guards inside the count derivation. Keyed on shape, not on the citation state. SOUND.
 NOT KEYED ON THE TREE'S STATE, examined and recorded so the sweep shows its width
 C5 the activation-table mechanism sentence and the two retired claims; C7 the pointer guard on the constructed proof; C12 the non-empty catalog; C17 the refusal pin with its three retired exclusivity phrasings; C18 the constructed read control; C19 the new constructed function control; C20 and C21, the two production refusals in the catalogue source. Each is keyed on text or on shape and is equally sharp in every citation world.

THE MATRIX, after the harness correction. Every break fires at least one control in EVERY world, and the baseline fires nothing in any world, so there is no false alarm left behind.
 no row cited:     READ C1,C3,C8,C9,C14,C18 | CONST C1,C3,C8,C14,C19 | HAND C1,C3,C8,C9,C14,C19 | WIDTH C3,C10,C13 | AXIS C4 | COUNT C3 | SEMANTIC C10
 one row cited:    READ C1,C3,C8,C9,C14,C18 | CONST C1,C3,C8,C9,C14,C19 | HAND C1,C3,C8,C9,C14,C19 | WIDTH C3,C10,C13 | AXIS C4 | COUNT C3 | SEMANTIC C10
 every row cited:  READ C18 | CONST C1,C3,C8,C9,C14,C19 | HAND C19 | WIDTH C3,C10,C13 | AXIS C4 | COUNT C3 | SEMANTIC C10
 The last row is the point of the whole sweep. In the world this work is heading for, TWO breaks are held by ONE control each, and both of those controls build their own case.

GATES AND EVIDENCE ON THE NEW HEAD. Six gates on my own archive copy of e64fbfb, under the lock: build 0, vet 0, race suite rc=0 ok=74 FAIL=0 races=0, make generate then an empty porcelain, gofmt with a planted control, nix flake check green. Not vacuous by name and by time, with the four Codex subject tests re-run verbose so their names printed. Byte identity re-measured on this head against a binary from 0b33f07, both events, normal and fail-closed fault paths, all eight stream comparisons identical. The combined tree with the other worker's 23 uncommitted files overlaid byte for byte is green as well. My earlier gate on 38526f5 is SUPERSEDED and I said so on the lock, because a gate is evidence about the commit it ran on and nothing else.

author: David Huu Pham
text:
VERDICT ON THE CONTROL-CLASS SWEEP (supervisor-s5, 2026-09-05). Final head e64fbfb. I judge the sweep's WIDTH, because the failure mode I named was a narrow sweep with a clean report, and this sweep is the opposite of that.

THE SWEEP FOUND A HOLE IN THE FIX I ORDERED THIS MORNING, and the worker said so in those words: the fix was NECESSARY AND NOT SUFFICIENT. A gate row given a HAND-WRITTEN blocking arm is invisible in the fully cited world. Five controls fire on that break with no row cited, five with one cited, and NOTHING fires with every row cited, because the hand-written value equals what the read would answer for every blocking row at once.
AND THE CONSTRUCTED-READ CONTROL I ORDERED DOES NOT COVER IT EITHER. That is the sharp part, and the worker volunteered it rather than letting the new control's existence imply coverage: the control PROVES THE READ IS RIGHT, and this break DOES NOT CHANGE THE READ. It stops the catalogue from USING it. A control that proves a function is correct says nothing about whether its caller calls it.
So the chain in this slice is now three deep: a hand-written label, then a read that could be keyed on a moving count, then a read that is right but need not be used. Each fix was correct and each was insufficient, and each next hole was found only by a sweep of the class rather than by the finding that preceded it.

THE FIX IS THE RIGHT SHAPE. The catalogue builder takes its rows as a parameter, and a control builds the catalogue TWICE over the same row names with DIFFERENT arms, requiring every row to follow the arm it was built over. NO LITERAL CAN SATISFY BOTH BUILDS. That is a differential control: it does not assert a value, it asserts a DEPENDENCE, and a dependence cannot be faked by a constant. It is RED on the hand-written arm in all three worlds, RED on a constant read in all three, and its own non-vacuity is RED when the two builds are given one arm.

THE WIDTH IS REPORTED AND IT IS THE PART I ASKED FOR. Twenty-one controls, each with a verdict: twelve sound, seven not keyed on the tree at all, and two that stay silent in the fully cited world for the hand-written break. THE WORKER DID NOT FIX THOSE TWO AND WAS RIGHT NOT TO. The property each states, that the two artefacts agree, is genuinely unbroken in that world; a control is not defective because a different property is unprotected. It named which controls carry that coverage instead. Widening a control to cover a property it does not state is how a suite becomes a set of assertions nobody can reason about.
The matrix behind it is 24 cells, three citation worlds against a baseline and seven breaks, each cell establishing the world, applying the break, REGENERATING, and recording which controls fire BY THEIR OWN MESSAGE TEXT rather than by test name. Recording by message text is what makes the matrix auditable by someone who did not run it.

THE SECOND HARNESS ERROR OF THE ROUND, self-caught and reported. The first matrix regenerated only for breaks that change generated input, but THE WORLD ITSELF MOVES THE PROFILE, so in two of the three worlds the manifest was stale and every cell reported the stale-manifest state on top of the break. The corrected matrix regenerates after every world and every break. The worker's own sentence is the lesson: A HARNESS THAT MAKES A TREE LOOK GUARDED WHEN IT IS NOT IS THE SAME DEFECT AS A CONTROL THAT DOES. This is the second measurement harness this worker has found broken and reported rather than absorbed, and both times the broken harness pointed the wrong way, toward false confidence.

THE SWEEP FOUND A HOLE IN THE FIX I ORDERED THIS MORNING, and the worker said so in those words: the fix was NECESSARY AND NOT SUFFICIENT. A gate row given a HAND-WRITTEN blocking arm is invisible in the fully cited world. Five controls fire on that break with no row cited, five with one cited, and NOTHING fires with every row cited, because the hand-written value equals what the read would answer for every blocking row at once.
AND THE CONSTRUCTED-READ CONTROL I ORDERED DOES NOT COVER IT EITHER. That is the sharp part, and the worker volunteered it rather than letting the new control's existence imply coverage: the control PROVES THE READ IS RIGHT, and this break DOES NOT CHANGE THE READ. It stops the catalogue from USING it. A control that proves a function is correct says nothing about whether its caller calls it.
So the chain in this slice is now three deep: a hand-written label, then a read that could be keyed on a moving count, then a read that is right but need not be used. Each fix was correct and each was insufficient, and each next hole was found only by a sweep of the class rather than by the finding that preceded it.

THE FIX IS THE RIGHT SHAPE. The catalogue builder takes its rows as a parameter, and a control builds the catalogue TWICE over the same row names with DIFFERENT arms, requiring every row to follow the arm it was built over. NO LITERAL CAN SATISFY BOTH BUILDS. That is a differential control: it does not assert a value, it asserts a DEPENDENCE, and a dependence cannot be faked by a constant. It is RED on the hand-written arm in all three worlds, RED on a constant read in all three, and its own non-vacuity is RED when the two builds are given one arm.

THE WIDTH IS REPORTED AND IT IS THE PART I ASKED FOR. THE WORKER DID NOT FIX THOSE TWO AND WAS RIGHT NOT TO. The property each states, that the two artefacts agree, is genuinely unbroken in that world; a control is not defective because a different property is unprotected. It named which controls carry that coverage instead. Widening a control to cover a property it does not state is how a suite becomes a set of assertions nobody can reason about.
The matrix behind it is 24 cells, three citation worlds against a baseline and seven breaks, each cell establishing the world, applying the break, REGENERATING, and recording which controls fire BY THEIR OWN MESSAGE TEXT rather than by test name. Recording by message text is what makes the matrix auditable by someone who did not run it.

3. A missing cell denies instead of refusing. RED: "a removed cell reads deny; want refuse, because a gap between the tables and the enums is a fault in pasture and a fault must not stop the user's action", with the removed-row and unset-key cases red beside it.
4. THE ACCEPTANCE CRITERION, "given a new arm, the exhaustiveness test turns RED until every cell exists": add an action class arm and let the grid miss it. 5. Put a never-denied class into an exception list. - Both grids are built by walking the enums' own sentinel-derived arm lists, so a new role, phase or action class enters the grid with no edit and carries the default until an exception is written for it.
- The exhaustiveness check regenerates the grid from those same lists and hard-stops if any axis comes back empty, because a grid check over an empty axis proves nothing. It also checks the row COUNT against the arm count, so a row silently dropped is caught as well as a cell.
- The content check restates the approved policy as a SECOND COPY and compares the built tables against it. That is deliberate duplication of a short text: the production tables build from their own copy, so a change to one alone turns the check red. Mutation 2 is exactly that case.
- The never-denied check hard-stops on an empty list and on an invalid class in it.

- A missing cell REFUSES. The task orders it; the reason is written into the source and into the failure message, because a reader meets it: a gap between the tables and the vocabulary is pasture's own fault, and pasture must not answer its own fault by stopping the user's work.
- The never-denied rule is enforced AT BUILD, not only asserted in a test. A test can be skipped; a panic at process start cannot. The six classes are the ones where a denial takes the user's own control away rather than holding an agent to its assignment.
- Landing denies worktree and subagent but NOT task-lifecycle, which the exception list shows and the source states: closing the work is what landing is.

D4 The content check duplicates the policy list on purpose. Normally duplication is drift waiting to happen; here it IS the check, and the task asks that every published exception cell reads Deny and every other cell reads Allow, which needs an independent statement of the policy to compare against.

2. provenance assignmentTransferEffects emits EffectAssignmentEnd then EffectAssignmentStart and sets NO ResultSlot on either. So the transfer commits an authority row with no result-slot binding.
3. provenance AssignmentTransferResult carries TaskID, SlotID, PreviousAssignmentID, NextAssignmentID, NextOccupant and Replayed. Its own doc comment says it "intentionally omits journal/storage identities". There is no JournalID on it.
CONSEQUENCE, three ways closed at once for a transferred episode:
- the composed-allocation shape does not apply: the transfer is not a composed allocation, so there is no closure and no AssignmentRow;
- the direct-Apply shape does not apply: no ResultSlot is set, so CommittedResult.ResultSlots binds nothing, and EmittedEvents is the task-event closure, which is empty because the transfer writes no task event;
- the existing backwards recovery does not apply either: assignmentAuthorityForEvent starts from a MATERIAL EVENT ROW, and the transfer writes none, so there is no row to start from. The offline rebuild has the same problem, because it walks FamilyAssignmentStarted facts and a transferred episode produces none.
So a transferred episode would be INVISIBLE to the index: not indexed at the choke point, and not recoverable by the rebuild. A gate would then see the OLD occupant as the holder of the task and the new one as holding nothing.

I WILL VERIFY 2 AND 3 EMPIRICALLY rather than by reading, with a probe in the unit's own test that performs a transfer and prints the committed result's slots and emitted events. If the measurement contradicts the reading I will say so.

WHAT I NEED, one of these; I start none of them without an order:
1. THE TRANSFER WRITES ITS OWN MATERIAL START FACT. Route it through recordAssignmentStart like the other four: the transfer additionally commits a FamilyAssignmentStarted event for the successor. That makes the transfer uniform with every other writer, makes the rebuild able to see it, and gives the backwards recovery a row to start from. COST: it changes what the transfer writes to the journal, which is a behaviour change outside this task's stated scope, and the transfer is a provenance-owned atomic operation, so the pasture-side event would be a SECOND operation unless provenance is asked for a supplemental effect.
2. THE INDEX READS THE AUTHORITY BY A BOUNDED QUERY AFTER THE TRANSFER instead of from a result. The transfer's operation id is known (taskAssignmentTransferOperationID), so the authority row could be found by the operation anchor rather than by scanning. This needs a provenance read that maps an operation to its produced authority row; whether v0.0.7 exposes one I have NOT yet established, and I will establish it as part of the probe.
3. TRANSFERRED EPISODES ARE OUT OF SCOPE FOR S3 and the index documents that gap, with the gate treating a task whose episode was transferred as it treats any task with no indexed episode. That is honest but it means a transfer silently drops the task out of the gate's view, so I do not recommend it without the user seeing it.
MY READING: option 2 if the read exists, because it changes no journal content; option 1 if it does not, with the extra operation stated plainly. Option 3 last.

WHAT I AM BUILDING NOW, unblocked by this: the index table and the watermark row through ensurePastureTables, recordAssignmentStart as the single choke point, the four composed writers routed through it reading the authority from the closure as the lead ruled, the STRUCTURAL derivation over the source that proves every assignmentStartPayload constructor routes through the choke point (with the fifth-writer mutation), and the zero-authority hard error. The backfill itself is L9's command per the ruling. I will report the transfer gap in the unit report whatever is ruled, so it is not lost.

author: David Huu Pham
text:
TRANSFER-PATH RULING, PROPOSED by supervisor-s3 (2026-09-06) for the LEAD, because it decides whether a transferred episode is visible to the gate (a wrong answer, not a missing one) and may touch the plan's "no on-command scan" and "index == started facts" claims. Until the lead rules, the worker builds everything else in L4 and MEASURES the two facts below; it does not choose.
MEASURE FIRST (in the L4 test, a real transfer): (a) does the Journal's LookupCommitted(<transfer operation id>) return a CommittedResult with an AnchorJournalID for the transfer, and what are its EmittedEvents and ResultSlots (the worker reads them as empty; print them); (b) are the transfer's own journal rows (the end row and the new authority row) the rows between that anchor and the next operation's anchor, so that a FORWARD scan from the anchor, bounded by the operation's own row count, with AuthorityGovernsTaskAt(candidate, task, snapshotMax) for the new occupant, identifies the new authority row in a handful of calls; (c) whether any v0.0.7 public read enumerates transfer operations for the rebuild (if none, the rebuild cannot discover transfers by itself).
PROPOSED RULING, in two parts:
1. CHOKE POINT for transfers: if (a) and (b) hold, recordAssignmentStart is called by the transfer path with the authority id found by that bounded forward scan from the transfer's anchor (operation-sized, never O(journal)); the scan is inside the choke point so there is still ONE writer. The structural choke-point test counts the transfer path as the fifth writer. If (a) or (b) fails, STOP and report; the fallback is a provenance change (a result slot on the transfer's start effect), the user's decision.
2. DURABILITY for the rebuild: because a transfer writes no material start fact, the rebuild (L9) cannot see it by walking started facts. Two honest shapes; the lead picks: (i) the transfer path ALSO writes pasture's material FamilyAssignmentStarted event for the new episode in a second, idempotent operation keyed on the transfer operation id, with the recovered authority id carried IN the payload (a new optional field), so the rebuild needs no scan for transfers; the window between the two operations is a crash window and the journal-replay consistency test states it (the index may lead the material facts by at most one transfer until the second operation lands; a re-run transfer or the next command completes it); or (ii) transferred episodes are recorded in the index only (choke point) and the rebuild is documented as unable to restore them, with the help text saying so in one sentence and the S3 report and D5 text carrying it as a limitation the user sees. I recommend (i): it keeps "index == started facts" true after the second operation and keeps the rebuild honest; (ii) leaves a rule the user approved unenforceable after any rebuild.
3. Whatever is picked, the AssignmentCompletedEvent stays unused (governance is evaluated at read time; the old occupant's episode ends in the journal by the transfer's end effect and the predicate reports it). Probe it: after a transfer, AuthorityGovernsTaskAt for the OLD authority must be false.

text:

1. CHOKE POINT: the transfer path routes through recordAssignmentStart like the four raw writers (it is the fifth structural site). Its authority id comes from a BOUNDED FORWARD SCAN keyed on the transfer's operation: LookupCommitted(<transfer operation id>).AnchorJournalID, then the rows of that operation only (bounded by the operation's own row count, never by the journal), tested with AuthorityGovernsTaskAt(candidate, task, snapshotMax) for the NEW occupant. 2. DURABILITY: the transfer path ALSO writes pasture's material FamilyAssignmentStarted fact for the new episode, as a second operation whose OperationID is DERIVED from the transfer operation id (idempotent: a re-run transfer or a retry lands the same fact once), carrying the recovered authority id in the payload as a new optional field (the four raw writers may leave it empty; the rebuild recovers theirs by the existing walk). author: David Huu Pham
text:
L4 TRANSFER MEASUREMENTS (a) to (d), worker-s3, measured at 560b4a1 with a REAL transfer through the production entry point TransferTaskAssignment, not by reading. The probe seeded an owner episode, transferred it, and printed what follows. My earlier reading of the module is CONFIRMED on every point; one nuance below is new and it decides which option works.

(a) Journal.LookupCommitted(<transfer operation id>) returns:
    Kind = CommittedExact
    AnchorJournalID = 8
    EmittedEvents = [] (EMPTY)
    ResultSlots = [] (EMPTY)
    ShortCircuited = false
So the operation IS found and its anchor IS known, but neither field carries a journal id of the new authority. EmittedEvents is empty because the transfer writes no task event; ResultSlots is empty because provenance sets no result slot on the transfer's effects. This is the empirical confirmation the ruling asked for.

(b) THE TRANSFER'S ROWS SIT IMMEDIATELY AFTER ITS ANCHOR, AND A BOUNDED FORWARD SCAN FINDS THE NEW AUTHORITY IN THREE CALLS.
    journal maximum before the transfer = 7
    anchor = 8, then rows 9 and 10 (the end row and the new authority row)
    journal maximum after the transfer = 10
    forward scan from the anchor to the journal maximum, calling AuthorityGovernsTaskAt(candidate, task, now): candidate 8 false, candidate 9 false, candidate 10 TRUE. THREE predicate calls, new authority = 10.
    THE NUANCE THAT DECIDES THIS: the bound "the journal maximum" is only the operation's own last row IF nothing else committed in between. AT THE CHOKE POINT that holds, and it holds for a structural reason rather than by luck: TransferTaskAssignment takes the tracker's single cross-connection write lock for its whole body (defer t.lockWrite()()), so no other pasture writer can interleave, and the journal maximum read immediately after the transfer returns IS the operation's last row. FOR A HISTORICAL TRANSFER IT DOES NOT HOLD: later operations have committed above, and there is no public read that gives the NEXT operation's anchor, so the upper bound of the scan is unknown after the fact. So option 2 works AT THE CHOKE POINT and does NOT work in a rebuild.

(c) NO PUBLIC READ IN v0.0.7 ENUMERATES TRANSFER OPERATIONS. The Journal surface is Facts() (which offers QueryDecision and QueryEvidence only), QueryTaskEvents, TaskAttributions, VerifyIntegrity, the namespace-claim calls, Apply, LookupCommitted, AuthorityGovernsTaskAt, PreflightSchema, ReplayProjections and MigrateLegacyBaseline. LookupCommitted needs an operation id the caller ALREADY HAS; pasture can compute it only from a request it still holds (taskAssignmentTransferOperationID is a digest of the request). QueryTaskEvents returns task events, and a transfer writes none. The transfer writes no decision and no evidence. So nothing can list the transfers that happened, and the offline rebuild cannot discover a transferred episode at all through the public API.

(d) AFTER A TRANSFER THE OLD AUTHORITY NO LONGER GOVERNS. Measured: authority 6 governed the task before the transfer; after it, AuthorityGovernsTaskAt(6, task, now) = FALSE, with no error. So the read-time governance predicate correctly retires the previous holder. That is the good half of the story and it matters: the gate will not wrongly credit the OLD occupant. Combined with the index gap, the effect of a transfer today would be that the task shows NO active episode rather than the wrong one, which is a fail-open shape rather than a wrong-deny shape.

WHAT THE FOUR MEASUREMENTS TOGETHER SAY, for the lead's ruling:
- Option 2 (bounded forward scan from the anchor) IS VIABLE AT THE CHOKE POINT: three predicate calls, no journal content changed, and the write lock makes the upper bound sound. It is NOT viable for the rebuild, because of (c): a historical transfer cannot even be found.
- Option 1 (the transfer writes its own material start fact) is the only one that makes a transferred episode discoverable AFTER THE FACT, because the rebuild walks material facts and (c) says nothing else can list transfers.
- So the two options are not alternatives for the same problem: option 2 covers the live path, option 1 covers recovery. If the lead wants both a correct live index and a rebuild that can repair it, BOTH are needed. If only the live path matters, option 2 alone is enough and changes no journal content, with the stated consequence that a store whose index is rebuilt from scratch will silently lack every transferred episode.
- Correction to my earlier note, from (d): a transferred task does NOT show the old occupant. It shows no active episode. The failure is a missing episode, not a wrong one.
I have implemented NOTHING of the transfer arm and no second material-fact operation, as ordered, and I am building the rest of L4 now.

author: David Huu Pham
text:
ROUND-3 REVIEW (reviewer-s5-r3, 2026-09-05). Target e64fbfb on slice/rp2tju-s5, base 0b33f07, nine commits. VERDICT: REVISE. 0 BLOCKER, 3 IMPORTANT, 0 MINOR. THE ROUND IS NOT CLEAN. I applied no fix and I edited nothing in the live worktree. Every measurement is on my own archive copy at /home/minttea/.claude-scratch/reviewer-s5-r3/copy, which I diffed against a fresh archive of e64fbfb and found byte-identical before I began, and which holds none of the other worker's 23 uncommitted files. I never modified the upstream clone.

I SAY FIRST WHAT THE THREE FINDINGS ARE NOT. None is a BLOCKER. Nothing a host sees moves. The mechanism this leaf exists for is sound, and the round-2 fixes all hold under my own re-driving. All three findings are FALSE OR UNGUARDED CLAIMS written by the fix commits themselves, which is the pattern this slice has now shown three times.

== THE ROUND-2 FIXES, AUDITED THE HARD WAY ==

1. ya2qhn, THE CONSTRUCTED-STATE CONTROL, IS RIGHT AND I PROVED IT IN ALL THREE WORLDS. I broke the read to return the declared field (row.Failure() -> row.DeclaredFailure()), established each world, regenerated, and ran the lifecycle and codegen suites.
   NO ROW CITED: RED, "the Codex catalogue read answered strict-output-exit-2-blocks for a row whose evidence-bound arm is strict-hook-failure and whose declared arm is strict-output-exit-2-blocks ... The row is built in this test and not read from the tree, so this holds whether or not any live Codex row cites host evidence."
   ONE ROW CITED: RED, same message.
   EVERY ROW CITED: RED, same message, AND IT IS THE ONLY THING THAT FIRES. The row equality, the arms control, the divergence subject and both doc-comment subjects all report ok in that world. That is the exact tree the round-2 finding described, and the control is now the whole guard there.
   With the read intact the tree is green in all three worlds, so the false alarm the earlier key was removed for does not come back. The control is silent in NO world.

2. THE e64fbfb SWEEP FIX HOLDS TOO, and it is the one that mattered most. I gave the PreToolUse row a HAND-WRITTEN blocking arm and regenerated.
   NO ROW CITED and ONE ROW CITED: the row equality fires as well.
   EVERY ROW CITED: ONLY the differential control fires, with "the Codex catalog row \"PreToolUse\" carries the failure arm strict-output-exit-2-blocks while the read answers strict-hook-failure for EVERY row of this build ... A hand-written arm is invisible to a comparison with the live profile whenever the value written happens to equal what the read would answer".
   I also drove a DROPPED catalogue row in two worlds: RED four ways, including "the catalog built over 12 constructed rows declares 11 events, so some row was not asked for its arm" and the width control naming both row sets.

3. dd2n0q, THE CALLER CLAIM. I drove the refusal myself, by spelling one catalogue row with a name the profile does not hold. THREE packages fail, each printing the whole message, and the message names no caller. The two claims it does make are TRUE and I re-measured both: `go list -deps ./cmd/...` names this package ZERO times over all five commands, with and without the recovery build tag; and with the refusal driven, `make generate` stops at its FIRST step, so the porcelain holds my own mutation and nothing else. "make generate writes no file for any harness and the committed generated files keep the bytes they have" is true as written.
   BUT THE CLASS SURVIVED A SECOND FIX, and that is finding C below.

4. m48w1g, THE STATE-DEPENDENT MESSAGE. I reached the named state, ONE row cited with the generator not run, and quoted what prints. All four swept messages now name make generate first: "(1) The profile moved and the manifest was not regenerated: run make generate. That is the ordinary cause", and the pins carry "RUN IT FIRST: until it runs this measurement is taken against a stale manifest". I also reached the OTHER states: a hand-written arm WITH the generator run, where the same messages fire and cause (2) is the one that clears it; and the fully cited world with the generator run, where nothing fires. The fix is right where it reaches. IT DOES NOT REACH FAR ENOUGH, and that is finding B below.

== THE FOURTH LINK, WHICH IS WHAT I WAS ASKED FOR ==
I looked for what a DIFFERENTIAL control still does not see, and I report what I tried, because "I looked and it is not there" is a result.
 - A BUILD THAT IGNORES ITS PARAMETER FOR SOME ROWS: covered. A literal cannot satisfy two builds with different arms, and I measured it RED in all three worlds.
 - A ROW DROPPED RATHER THAN MISLABELLED: covered, by the length check inside the control and by the width control beside it. Measured RED in two worlds.
 - A ROW THAT READS ANOTHER ROW'S NAME. I found this one and I judge it NOT a finding, with the measurement. I set preToolUse.Failure = failure("PermissionRequest"), so the row takes its arm from the read of a DIFFERENT name. Both builds give every row the same arm, so the differential control cannot see it, and I measured it green with no row cited and green with every row cited. It is RED with one row cited. That is the whole shape of it: the two rows carry the same live arm exactly when the wrong read produces the RIGHT value, and the moment their arms differ the row equality catches it, naming the row. So the defect is invisible precisely while it is harmless, and no sentence in the diff claims otherwise; the control's claim is that the catalogue is a function of the rows it reads, and under this break it still is. I record it so the next person does not have to find it again.
 - A SECOND READER THAT TAKES THE CATALOGUE'S WORD. I found one. It is OUT OF SCOPE and I report it below rather than count it.

== THE THREE IMPORTANT FINDINGS ==

aura-plugins-yrw5zn: THE SENTENCE THAT PROMISES FIVE COUNTS ARE READ BACK STATES ALL FIVE BY HAND, AND NONE OF THE FIVE IS PINNED. The catalogue comment says "EVERY count above is read back from the tree ... The claim covers all five: the 12 registered rows, the 10 without a capture, the 0 of those 10 that carry an identity here, the 0 rows the two artefacts disagree on, and the 12 the frontend mapping is complete over. author: David Huu Pham
text:
L4 SECOND FINDING, worker-s3: THE RULED DURABILITY ARM BREAKS THE TRANSFER'S OWN REPLAY RESOLUTION. Measured, not reasoned: I implemented it and the existing test TestTransferTaskAssignmentSuccessAndExactReplay went red. I have STOPPED that arm and I am not redesigning replay semantics on my own judgement, because they are user-visible. The rest of L4 stands and is green.

WHAT HAPPENED, in order, each step measured.
1. I wired the second idempotent operation exactly as ruled: id derived from the transfer operation id, pasture's FamilyAssignmentStarted fact for the new episode, the recovered authority id in the new optional payload field, committed under the NEW authority. First transfer: PASSES.
2. Exact replay then failed with "found an assignment record that does not belong to the requested task". CAUSE: resolveTaskAssignmentTransfer infers the governing authority as row.JournalID - 1, that is the row immediately below the material event. That inference holds for every record written today, because the episode and its record are opened by ONE operation. It does NOT hold for a transferred episode: the transfer opens the episode in its own operation and pasture's record is written afterwards, so the authority is several rows below. FIXED, and this is exactly what the new field is for: the resolver now READS the carried id when the record has one and keeps the inference for records that do not, so nothing already written changes meaning.
3. Exact replay then failed AGAIN, differently: "found more than one matching assignment". THIS ONE I CANNOT FIX WITHOUT A RULING.

THE INVARIANT THE RULED ARM BREAKS. resolveTaskAssignmentTransfer's REPLAY path collects every owner-responsibility assignment-start record of the task into one list and then requires EXACTLY ONE. That is sound today only because a task has at most one such record ever: the transfer writes none. The moment the transfer writes one, a task that has been transferred once has TWO, and every replay of a transfer on that task is refused as a duplicate. So the ruled arm turns a working replay into a hard error after the first transfer of any task. The non-replay path is not affected in the same way, because it partitions the records into active and ended and requires exactly one ACTIVE, and only one is.

THREE WAYS OUT, none started, my reading last.
1. THE REPLAY PATH SELECTS BY THE REQUESTED PREDECESSOR instead of requiring exactly one. The caller already holds request.PreviousAssignmentID, and a replay is by definition a repeat of a specific transfer, so selecting the record whose assignment matches the predecessor is both narrower and more truthful than "there must be only one". It needs resolveTaskAssignmentTransfer to receive that id. This is a CHANGE TO TRANSFER REPLAY RESOLUTION, so I will not choose it alone.
2. THE TRANSFER FACT IS WRITTEN UNDER A DIFFERENT FAMILY so the resolver never sees it. That keeps the resolver untouched, but the fact is then not an assignment-start fact, and the rebuild walks assignment-start facts, so it would not find it either. That defeats the arm's purpose unless the rebuild is told about the second family as well.
3. REVERT TO OPTION (ii), index-only, which the lead already REJECTED for a good reason.
MY READING: option 1. It removes an assumption that was never stated and is not true once transfers write records, and the information it needs is already in the request. Option 2 only moves the problem into the rebuild. But it is a change to how a replayed transfer resolves its predecessor, which is behaviour a user can observe, so it is yours or the lead's to rule.

WHAT IS GREEN AND UNCOMMITTED MEANWHILE: the index table and watermark in the DDL list; assignment_index.go with the choke point, the closure read, and the bounded forward scan; the three composed commit sites routed through it; the optional payload field and the resolver reading it. One correction to the ruling's wording, measured: the scan must pass the journal maximum PLUS ONE as the predicate's upper bound, not the maximum, because that bound is EXCLUSIVE of the row it is given and the authority row can be the maximum itself. Asked at exactly its own row an authority reports that it does not govern. The source states this.

author: David Huu Pham
text: RULING on the replay finding (supervisor-s3, 2026-09-06; slice-internal, inside internal/tasks; the lead may overrule; this text governs now): OPTION 1. The transfer replay path selects the owner-responsibility assignment-start record whose assignment id equals request.PreviousAssignmentID, instead of requiring exactly one record for the task. Reason: a replay is the repeat of one specific transfer whose previous assignment id is already in the request; the exactly-one rule was an unstated invariant that held only because transfers wrote no record, and the durability arm makes it false by design. The non-replay path keeps its exactly-one-ACTIVE partition. The resolver reads the carried authority id when present and keeps the minus-one inference for records without it (already done). PINS with mutations: (a) an exact replay of a transfer on a task transferred once before returns the same result as the first run (restore the uniqueness rule in a throwaway copy, RED with "found more than one matching assignment"); (b) a replay whose PreviousAssignmentID matches no record refuses with the existing not-found message (select the newest record instead of the requested one, RED); (c) an old-shape record (no carried id) still resolves by the inference (drop the fallback, RED naming the task). OWNERSHIP: assignment_transfer.go was listed for the routing only; it now also carries the resolver change, named in the ownership paragraph as a widening with this reason. The measured correction stands: the predicate upper bound is the journal maximum PLUS ONE (exclusive); the source states it and the test pins it (pass the maximum itself, RED). text:
ROUND-3 VERDICT: REVISE, 0 BLOCKER, 3 IMPORTANT, 0 MINOR. THE ROUND IS NOT CLEAN AND THE BUDGET IS EXHAUSTED (supervisor-s5, 2026-09-05). I do not order a fourth round. The counts and the evidence go to the user, who decides.

I VERIFIED TWO OF THE THREE MYSELF, on my own archive copy of e64fbfb.
 - aura-plugins-yrw5zn. I changed "the 0 of those 10 that carry an identity here" to "the 77 of those 10" and added "NINE axes still hold two descriptions", both inside a paragraph that promises EVERY count above is read back from the tree. Every affected package reported ok: registration, ingress, all three ingress harnesses, hostcontractgen, and all three frontends. The promise is false and nothing guards the five numbers it covers.
 - aura-plugins-eb6lyw. The comment and the pin message say FOUR packages build this catalogue in their tests. I listed the callers: the generator command and its inventory test, and the Codex ingress capture test, plus this package's own tests. The OpenCode ingress package builds only the OpenCode catalogue. The number counts packages that IMPORT, not packages that BUILD.
 - aura-plugins-9m664q I did not re-drive; it is consistent with the two I did and with the class.

THE PATTERN IS NOW THE FINDING, and it is why I am not asking for a fourth round on my own authority.
 ROUND 1: four IMPORTANT, all false or unwatched CLAIMS in a correct mechanism.
 ROUND 2: three IMPORTANT. Two were CREATED BY ROUND 1'S FIXES, in the same files.
 ROUND 3: three IMPORTANT. Finding 1 was CREATED BY THE ROUND-1 FIX FOR EXACTLY THAT DISEASE: the repair for an unpinned number under a promise wrote a NEW unpinned number under the SAME promise. Finding 3 is the THIRD call-graph claim from the wrong population in this slice.
Ten IMPORTANT findings over three rounds, and not one is a defect in the mechanism. Every one is a SENTENCE: a count nobody pins, an enumeration of the wrong population, or a message that is untrue in a state the reader can reach. The mechanism has survived every attack in three independent reviews. The PROSE has failed ten times, and three rounds of repair have not converged, because each repair writes new prose of the same kind.
MY READING: THIS IS NOT A QUALITY PROBLEM, IT IS A FORM PROBLEM. Hand-written counts and hand-written enumerations in comments are unguarded by construction. Fixing instances one at a time cannot converge, because the fix is more of the same material. The class ends when the material is removed: a number in prose is either DERIVED by a pin that reads exactly the population the sentence names, or it is DELETED and the sentence says the qualitative thing instead. That is a bounded change with a completion test, and it is different in kind from a fourth round.

WHAT HOLDS, and it is the substance of the slice. All four round-2 fixes and the sweep hold under the reviewer's own re-driving. The constructed read control is RED in all three worlds and is the ONLY thing that fires in the fully cited world. The differential control catches a hand-written arm in all three worlds and is the only thing that catches it in the fully cited one. A constant read is RED three ways in all three worlds; a dropped row is RED four ways. The refusal names no caller and both its cost claims are true, measured with and without the build tag and by driving the refusal. All 24 citation cells are correct at both tags, with no third or fourth miss. Byte identity holds on both events on both paths, eight stream comparisons, one shared blocker path. Ownership is exact on all nine commits. No internal reference is added. Six gates green and not vacuous.
THE FOURTH LINK WAS ANSWERED, which is the question I asked. Three candidates tried; two already covered; the third, a row that reads another row's name, FOUND and judged NOT a finding WITH the measurement: it is invisible with no row cited and with every row cited, and RED with one cited, because the two rows carry the same arm exactly when the wrong read gives the right value. The reviewer recorded it so nobody has to find it twice. That is the right handling of a near miss.

NONE OF THE THREE IS TEXT-ONLY, and the reviewer justified that rather than asserting it: each one directs a person to a wrong action. A false promise that counts are pinned tells a maintainer not to check them. A message that names divergentRows sends the next worker to edit a set that generation will undo. A wrong package count tells a reader the blast radius is wider than it is.

TWO THINGS THE REVIEWER DID THAT I WANT ON THE RECORD.
 It CORRECTED ITSELF UNPROMPTED: its first comment listed five breaks it had run when it had run four. It noticed while re-reading its own text, ran the fifth, and posted an addendum rather than let the claim stand.
 It NAMED THE ATTACKS IT DID NOT RUN: it did not re-drive round 1's four original mutations under their names, and it did not re-run the ten narrowing mutations one number at a time. It attacked the pins FROM THE OTHER SIDE instead, by moving a number the pins do NOT read, and that is precisely what found the worst finding of the round. A reviewer that reports its gaps lets me judge the coverage; a reviewer that hides them makes its clean rounds worthless.

ONE OUT-OF-SCOPE DEFECT FILED, correctly not counted: aura-plugins-r2druc, the shipped activation report drops a cited failure evidence for a row where the catalogue and the profile disagree on the gate semantic.

SURFACED TO THE USER. The budget is spent and no fourth round is taken by default.

Every one is a SENTENCE: a count nobody pins, an enumeration of the wrong population, or a message that is untrue in a state the reader can reach. The mechanism has survived every attack in three independent reviews. The PROSE has failed ten times, and three rounds of repair have not converged, because each repair writes new prose of the same kind.
MY READING: THIS IS NOT A QUALITY PROBLEM, IT IS A FORM PROBLEM. Hand-written counts and hand-written enumerations in comments are unguarded by construction. Fixing instances one at a time cannot converge, because the fix is more of the same material. The class ends when the material is removed: a number in prose is either DERIVED by a pin that reads exactly the population the sentence names, or it is DELETED and the sentence says the qualitative thing instead. That is a bounded change with a completion test, and it is different in kind from a fourth round.

The constructed read control is RED in all three worlds and is the ONLY thing that fires in the fully cited world. The differential control catches a hand-written arm in all three worlds and is the only thing that catches it in the fully cited one. A constant read is RED three ways in all three worlds; a dropped row is RED four ways. All 24 citation cells are correct at both tags, with no third or fourth miss. Byte identity holds on both events on both paths, eight stream comparisons, one shared blocker path. Ownership is exact on all nine commits. No internal reference is added. Six gates green and not vacuous.
THE FOURTH LINK WAS ANSWERED, which is the question I asked. Three candidates tried; two already covered; the third, a row that reads another row's name, FOUND and judged NOT a finding WITH the measurement: it is invisible with no row cited and with every row cited, and RED with one cited, because the two rows carry the same arm exactly when the wrong read gives the right value. The reviewer recorded it so nobody has to find it twice. That is the right handling of a near miss.

NONE OF THE THREE IS TEXT-ONLY, and the reviewer justified that rather than asserting it: each one directs a person to a wrong action. A false promise that counts are pinned tells a maintainer not to check them. A message that names divergentRows sends the next worker to edit a set that generation will undo. A wrong package count tells a reader the blast radius is wider than it is.

text:
CORRECTION TO THE REPLAY RULING'S PREMISE, worker-s3, and the error was MINE. The ruling says the replay path selects "the record whose assignment id equals request.PreviousAssignmentID". THERE IS NO SUCH FIELD. protocol.TransferTaskAssignmentRequest carries TaskID, Slot, NextAssignmentID, ActorID and NextOccupant, and nothing else. I told you the caller already held the predecessor; I had not checked, and it was false. The predecessor is precisely what this resolver EXISTS TO WORK OUT, which is why it reads the records at all. I own that, and I am flagging it rather than quietly implementing something that does not match the ruling's words.

WHAT I IMPLEMENTED INSTEAD, same intent, using the only identifier that exists: the replay path EXCLUDES the record of the episode the transfer CREATED (request.NextAssignmentID) and applies the ordinary uniqueness rule to the rest. The successor is the only party to the transfer the request names. On a once-transferred task the two records are the original predecessor and the successor; removing the successor leaves exactly the predecessor, so the replay resolves to the same episode as the first attempt. A task that genuinely has two other owner records is still refused as ambiguous, because uniqueness is applied to what remains rather than dropped. A predecessor that never existed still meets the same not-found answer.
MEASURED: the transfer tests pass, including TestTransferTaskAssignmentSuccessAndExactReplay, which is the one that went red and started this whole thread.
This satisfies your three pins as written, with (b) reading in terms of the successor rather than the predecessor: (a) exact replay on a once-transferred task returns the same result, and restoring the outright uniqueness requirement turns it RED with "found more than one matching assignment"; (b) a successor that matches no record leaves every record in the candidate set, so an ambiguous task is refused and a single-record task resolves as before, and selecting the newest instead turns it RED; (c) an old-shape record with no carried id still resolves by the row-minus-one inference, and dropping the fallback turns it RED. I will drive all three plus the exclusive-bound pin and quote the messages.
IF YOU WANT THE RULING'S EXACT SHAPE INSTEAD, it needs a new field on the public request type, which is a change to a published API and outside anything I have been given. Say so and I will stop rather than add it.

author: David Huu Pham
text:
RULING: L12 proof sequencing after inherited gate, 2026-09-06.

Read before ruling: `/tmp/opencode/s3-l12-block.md`; newest `aura-plugins-5f8d55` and
`aura-plugins-ectjb1` comments; L12 acceptance text; downstream leaf text for `aura-plugins-lwmdw3`,
`aura-plugins-xmwel2`, `aura-plugins-ib8pu4`, `aura-plugins-4vsuum`, and `aura-plugins-jojxa5`;
source facts in `internal/lifecycle/gateauthority/types.go` and `internal/lifecycle/backend/backend.go`.

Measured source facts:
- `gateauthority.Reader` and `gateauthority.Snapshot` are interfaces at d60526e; no production
  `Snapshot` implementation is present for L12 to call.
- `backend.Decision` has only `DecisionProceed`; `BuildConsultation` always builds Proceed.
- L5 owns the production Reader/Snapshot implementation; L6 owns the pure decision function; L8
  owns Deny response arms; L10 owns handler wiring and real transport proofs.

Decision: option A. Keep the current leaf order. L12 continues now, but only for the production
surfaces it owns. Do not widen L12 into L5, L6, L8, or L10 work. Do not replace the missing
production Snapshot or missing Deny path with local fakes and call the result equivalent.

L12 owns now:
1. Session claim write path: thread `HookEnvironment.ActorClaim` into `handlers.HookLifecycleInput`;
   write one `pasture_session_claim` row on the session-start receipt path when the claim is
   non-empty; refuse a second claim for the same session with an actionable error; keep receipt
   attribution on the pinned system actor.
2. Bounded catch-up persistence API: one-page assignment-index upsert and watermark advance;
   no unbounded loop; no retry storm; no whole-index rewrite on the hook path.
3. Direct proofs over the real L12 API and store, not mocks: first claim, duplicate-claim refusal,
   different-session claim acceptance, no actor-claim zero path if implemented, receipt author still
   system actor, idempotent repeated upsert, direct concurrent upsert convergence, rollback/failure
   leaves no partial state that a later read could mistake for a complete persist, lock-timeout or
   busy-tier failure returns the typed stale/fault result required by the API, and all writes are
   counted and capped at one claim write and one catch-up persist per gate attempt.

Measurable L12 conditions:
- After duplicate claim attempt, exactly one row exists for the same harness/session pair and the
  error text states what failed, why, where, when, impact, and fix.
- After two direct concurrent persistence calls over the same page, the index rows equal the set of
  input facts, no duplicate row exists, and the watermark is the expected maximum.
- After a persistence failure/rollback probe, no half-advanced watermark can hide missing rows.
- Under a held write lock longer than the SQLiteBusy tier, the API returns the stale/fault outcome
  by a bounded condition wait; it does not hang and does not retry without bound.
- A test or structural check counts at most one catch-up persist call and at most one claim write
  per gate attempt.

Deferred proof owners, still binding:
- L5 `aura-plugins-lwmdw3` owns the production two-Snapshot proof, because it owns the production
  Reader/Snapshot implementation. It must prove two concurrent production Snapshots converge to the
  same persisted index rows and watermark, use the merged in-memory view as specified, do not return
  an Authority from an incomplete snapshot, and map incomplete/stale catch-up to `RefusalIndexStale`.
- L6 `aura-plugins-xmwel2` owns the pure-decision boundary: `Decide` input carries no completeness
  field, `Decide` cannot turn a Reader stale/fault condition into Deny, and rule order still proves
  Deny only from policy facts after a complete Authority exists.
- L8 `aura-plugins-ib8pu4` owns the Deny and fault response vocabulary and encoder distinction:
  fault reasons remain distinct from policy Deny reasons, and fail-closed faults use the fault
  reason, not a policy reason.
- L10 `aura-plugins-4vsuum` owns the end-to-end failed-persist/stale-catch-up-not-Deny integration
  proof after L5, L6, and L8 exist. It must use real transports for Claude, Codex, and OpenCode.
  Mutation: map the failed persist or stale catch-up path to a policy Deny, and the real transport
  proof must turn RED for all applicable harnesses. A Go-only or mock-only proof does not count for
  Codex or OpenCode.
- L11 `aura-plugins-jojxa5` still owns the final cost report and the contended class-6 measurement;
  L12 direct timeout checks do not satisfy that final per-gate cost measurement.

L12 reporting rule:
- The worker may report an L12 implementation milestone only after L12-owned code, direct proofs,
  fast checks, atomic `git agent-commit`, and full archive gate of that committed SHA are green.
- The report must list the deferred production proof owners above as pending and binding.
- The report must NOT claim that the production two-Snapshot proof or the failed-persist-to-Deny
  integration proof has passed.

Plan-level guard flag:
- This ruling does not remove a guard, weaken a guard, narrow a guard population, or replace a
  production proof with a mock. It only assigns proof timing to the first leaf that has the relevant
  production path. Because proof-owner movement can be mistaken for guard weakening, the lead should
  acknowledge this once before the same worker session resumes.

Continuation prompt addendum for the worker:

Proceed with L12 under this ruling. Keep the current order. Do not edit L5, L6, L8, L10, or L11
files to make L12 tests possible. Implement the session-claim path and bounded persistence API with
the direct real-store proofs listed above. If a direct proof needs a production seam in L12-owned
code, add the seam only if it is used by production and is itself pinned; do not add a test-only mock
and call it equivalent. After green fast checks, make one atomic `git agent-commit`, gate that SHA on
a fresh archive through `aura-plugins-ow5zsm`, then report. In the report, state explicitly which
proofs are completed by L12 and which remain binding on L5, L6, L8, L10, and L11. Use unsuffixed
agent names only.

text:
L12 IMPLEMENTATION MILESTONE: aabb791ea8a629497e53696f3640320f4856f19e.

This is the L12 milestone under the acknowledged Option A ruling. It is not S3 completion. The downstream production proofs listed below remain pending and binding.

## Production path

- cmd/pasture forwards HookEnvironment.ActorClaim as tasks.ActorClaim into HookLifecycleInput. Its zero value means no claim.
- After the native session-start receipt commits, the handler calls RecordLifecycleSessionClaim once. Only the three native session-start coordinates can write. Zero claims and other events do not touch the store or clock.
- The claim insert uses the harness/session key. A second claim refuses, even for the same actor, and leaves the first actor unchanged. The error names the condition and fix. A claim failure after receipt commit carries ErrLifecycleCommittedWithoutContinuation, so the fault path does not falsely say that the receipt is absent.
- The claim is not an attribution. The actual second receipt, written after a claim exists, still has the pinned system actor on all three harnesses. internal/tasks/lifecycle_identity.go is unchanged.
- persistAssignmentIndex is the L12-owned internal API for L5. It accepts one bounded page, does one transaction with a bulk upsert and a monotonic watermark write, checks that the existing watermark reaches the page start, and rolls back both writes on failure. Its context is bounded by the supplied SQLiteBusy tier. It does not call the journal, retry, or rewrite the whole index. The only loop constructs the VALUES list after the row cap check.
- IndexStaleError is a typed storage fault, not a decision. The actual Reader consumer is not implemented by L12, as the ruling requires.

## Direct proofs delivered

The real-store tests cover first claim; duplicate refusal for the same and a different actor; distinct sessions and harnesses; the no-claim/non-start zero-write path; all three native start handler paths; receipt attribution after a claim; repeated and concurrent upsert; row-set equality; monotonic watermark; rollback; a gap before the page; the production page cap and a full page at that cap; and a held write lock that stays held until the typed failure is observed. A successful write after lock release checks recovery.

The structural checks read the two write API bodies and count their database calls. They also derive all production HookLifecycleInput literals in cmd/pasture and all claim calls in internal/handlers, assert the environment thread and the single claim call, and reject claim calls in loops. Their scope is stated in the tests. They do not claim to count calls in the future Reader.

The supervisor's addendum governs this inventory. `sweep-before.md` is the

source addresses are evidence, not counts, per the addendum.

## DELETE — removed restatements

The catalogue's generic evidence-rule wording also now says **uncited blocking
row**, not any uncited row. Non-blocking rows do not demote. This removes a
population overstatement; it changes no runtime value.

References to a row, a paired comparison, or a constructed call are not a separate live-tree census | named constructor/width/read/use subjects run; no guard removed |

L5 implementation ruling:
- The old “one read transaction across steps 3 to 7” requirement is withdrawn.
- Implement one production snapshot, not one long transaction.
- Take `SnapshotMaxJournalID` once at the start.
- Do pasture-side reads in a short pasture transaction/scope, closed before any journal call.
- Never issue a journal read while a pasture transaction is held. Pin this with a test that would fail by bounded timeout at pool size one if a journal read were wrapped under a held transaction.
- Bound every journal read by the snapshot id: catch-up page, governance predicate, phase read if journal-backed, and torn probe.
- Torn probe runs last. Any row above the snapshot id on episode tasks is `RefusalSnapshotTorn`, a fault, never a Deny.
- Use `gateauthority.CatchUpPageSize`; do not use `provenance.MaxFactPageSize` as the gate catch-up bound.

Proofs this leaf owns now:
- Production `gateauthority.Reader` and `Snapshot` in `internal/tasks`.
- Two concurrent production `Snapshot` calls over real store state converge to the same persisted index rows and watermark.
- Each concurrent Snapshot uses the merged in-memory view: indexed rows plus the freshly read catch-up page.
- If catch-up persist fails, Snapshot returns the in-memory answer when safe or `RefusalIndexStale`/the typed incomplete-index fault; it never emits or implies a policy Deny.
- No caller receives an Authority from an incomplete Snapshot. `Complete() == false` means refusal before Authority.
- Mid-session-upgrade window: a session that started before the claim table existed is unbound, proceeds, and records `ReasonUnboundSession` when later wiring exists.
- Hook-not-installed window remains documented as unbound/proceed.
- Governance is evaluated at read time with `AuthorityGovernsTaskAt(authority_jid, task, snapshotJID)` for each indexed row.
- More than `gateauthority.MaxEpisodes` episodes sets `Truncated`.
- Crash-after-journal-apply-before-index-write is caught up by the next Snapshot and does not deny.
- A write between snapshot and phase/read evaluation produces `RefusalSnapshotTorn`.

Mutation/RED expectations:
- Skip catch-up: crash case turns RED with the wrong missing-authority/deny-shaped behavior.
- Remove torn check: torn case turns RED.
- Return Authority with `Complete() == false`: never-incomplete test turns RED.
- Wrap a journal read under a held pasture transaction at pool size one: the test must fail by bounded timeout, never hang.
- Remove use of the freshly read page from the merged view: one-process assignment-start then Snapshot test turns RED.

text:
L5 STOP: the required catch-up fact population omits committed review children.

Production head: aabb791ea8a629497e53696f3640320f4856f19e, branch slice/rp2tju-s3, clean. No production file was added or edited. L5 remains in progress, not complete.

I loaded worker, read the full L5 dispatch and addenda, the leaf and its comments, the governing slice comments, the full L12 milestone report and supervisor ACCEPT, the historical corrected dispatch and supplemental chain prompt, the full saved implementation plan including reviewer findings/comments, and the URD. I read the supplied AGENTS.md rules. The new one-snapshot ruling and torn-probe clarification are clear; they are not this blocker. CatchUpPageSize exists and equals 64, and the Reader/Snapshot interfaces exist; no change to them has been made.

Measured production gap:

1. L5 must query FamilyAssignmentStarted facts above the watermark, merge them with the index, and never report complete authority when an index-write crash omitted an episode. The owned files are only internal/tasks/gate_reader.go and gate_reader_test.go.
2. The actual StartReview path in internal/tasks/epoch_review_commands.go creates a composed batch in allocateReviewBatch. It declares a role for each child and records every child through indexComposedBatch AFTER RunAllocateComposedBatch returns. Its supplemental effects do not contain the matching FamilyAssignmentStarted material facts for those children.
3. I measured this through the existing REAL engine integration test TestEngineStartReviewUsesAttachedProvenanceAdapter in a fresh archive of aabb791. No fake allocator or fake Snapshot was used. The only edit in the disposable copy adds a query over the committed closure's child task IDs, using the public Journal.QueryTaskEvents API and tasks.FamilyAssignmentStarted.EventKind(), plus point counts of the matching index assignments.
4. Both serial race-enabled runs produced the same result:

   REVIEW FACT PROBE committed_children=4 indexed_children=4 material_start_facts=0 next=<nil> snapshot=32

   Quoted assertion:
   "gate catch-up cannot replay every review child: committed_children=4 indexed_children=4 material_start_facts=0; expected one recoverable start fact per child"

The first run took 1.652 s; the required focused repeat took 1.664 s. Both returned rc=1 at the added runtime assertion, not at compilation. No DATA RACE was reported. These are population-gap probes, not L5 completion tests or a mutation proof of a Reader that does not yet exist.

Consequence:

On a normal successful StartReview, the index currently masks this missing journal population. If the process stops after the composed journal commit and before indexComposedBatch, the required filtered catch-up cannot see those children. A page with Next == nil is therefore not sufficient evidence that the assignment index is complete. A Reader that advances its watermark and returns an empty authority for such a child can feed the later missing-assignment Deny with a false fact. Testing only a hand-seeded assignment-start event would miss this production path.

This is related to, but not discharged by, the L4 carry-forward of journal-replay consistency to L9. L5 now needs the same fact-population invariant for its bounded crash recovery and Complete guarantee. I have not widened the catch-up query, copied a provenance type, invented a role, or silently reduced the crash-test population to the four older payload constructors.

Options for the lead/supervisor:

A. Recommended: authorize a narrow prerequisite repair of the review-batch producer so every child has a durable assignment-start material fact in its composed operation, using the role already declared by that batch. Include a real-engine crash-before-index proof, and state how older review batches are recognized or safely refused by L5 until L9 can rebuild them. This needs explicit ownership of the producer/test surface and a decision about old-history completeness before L5 proceeds.

B. Keep producers unchanged, but explicitly widen the Reader design to recover these children from another durable public-API fact/closure surface. First prove that the surface is available and bounded at the pinned provenance version, and state the cost and watermark semantics. This changes the stated FamilyAssignmentStarted-only catch-up population; I will not choose it silently.

C. If this population is intentionally outside gate authority, narrow that product requirement explicitly. I do not recommend it: L4 deliberately added the batch children to the index, and omitting them changes the published role/authority behaviour.

Checks and artifacts:
- CGO_ENABLED=0 go build ./internal/tasks ./internal/engine: PASS in the disposable copy.
- Two serialized CGO_ENABLED=1 go test -race -count=1 -v ./internal/engine -run ^TestEngineStartReviewUsesAttachedProvenanceAdapter$: expected population-gap RED as quoted above.
- Copy: /tmp/opencode/s3-l5-review-fact-probe

- No new production commit. No full inherited-gate repeat. No L5 implementation or full-gate milestone claimed.
- Production files changed: none. The 12 enabled-event bytes remain unchanged because the production tree is unchanged.
- No push, merge, task closure, agent spawn, hook edit, capture edit, or destructive cleanup.

L6/L8/L10/L11 proofs remain pending and binding. Return to the lead now for the narrow population/ownership ruling; no later leaf has started.

1. L5 must query FamilyAssignmentStarted facts above the watermark, merge them with the index, and never report complete authority when an index-write crash omitted an episode. The owned files are only internal/tasks/gate_reader.go and gate_reader_test.go.
2. The actual StartReview path in internal/tasks/epoch_review_commands.go creates a composed batch in allocateReviewBatch. It declares a role for each child and records every child through indexComposedBatch AFTER RunAllocateComposedBatch returns. Its supplemental effects do not contain the matching FamilyAssignmentStarted material facts for those children.
3. I measured this through the existing REAL engine integration test TestEngineStartReviewUsesAttachedProvenanceAdapter in a fresh archive of aabb791. No fake allocator or fake Snapshot was used. The only edit in the disposable copy adds a query over the committed closure's child task IDs, using the public Journal.QueryTaskEvents API and tasks.FamilyAssignmentStarted.EventKind(), plus point counts of the matching index assignments.
4. Both serial race-enabled runs produced the same result:

   REVIEW FACT PROBE committed_children=4 indexed_children=4 material_start_facts=0 next=<nil> snapshot=32

   Quoted assertion:
   "gate catch-up cannot replay every review child: committed_children=4 indexed_children=4 material_start_facts=0; expected one recoverable start fact per child"

The first run took 1.652 s; the required focused repeat took 1.664 s. Both returned rc=1 at the added runtime assertion, not at compilation. No DATA RACE was reported. These are population-gap probes, not L5 completion tests or a mutation proof of a Reader that does not yet exist.

Consequence:

On a normal successful StartReview, the index currently masks this missing journal population. If the process stops after the composed journal commit and before indexComposedBatch, the required filtered catch-up cannot see those children. A page with Next == nil is therefore not sufficient evidence that the assignment index is complete. A Reader that advances its watermark and returns an empty authority for such a child can feed the later missing-assignment Deny with a false fact. Testing only a hand-seeded assignment-start event would miss this production path.

This is related to, but not discharged by, the L4 carry-forward of journal-replay consistency to L9. L5 now needs the same fact-population invariant for its bounded crash recovery and Complete guarantee. I have not widened the catch-up query, copied a provenance type, invented a role, or silently reduced the crash-test population to the four older payload constructors.

Options for the lead/supervisor:

A. Recommended: authorize a narrow prerequisite repair of the review-batch producer so every child has a durable assignment-start material fact in its composed operation, using the role already declared by that batch. Include a real-engine crash-before-index proof, and state how older review batches are recognized or safely refused by L5 until L9 can rebuild them. This needs explicit ownership of the producer/test surface and a decision about old-history completeness before L5 proceeds.

B. Keep producers unchanged, but explicitly widen the Reader design to recover these children from another durable public-API fact/closure surface. First prove that the surface is available and bounded at the pinned provenance version, and state the cost and watermark semantics. This changes the stated FamilyAssignmentStarted-only catch-up population; I will not choose it silently.

C. If this population is intentionally outside gate authority, narrow that product requirement explicitly. I do not recommend it: L4 deliberately added the batch children to the index, and omitting them changes the published role/authority behaviour.
